title: Grade 9 daily reading
overview: A year of authentic fiction, poetry, autobiography, and public reflection by twelve authors. Each night combines independent reading and purposeful rereading with three evidence-based conversations in about 25–30 minutes. The sequence develops attention to irony, narrative perspective, rhetoric, imagery, and the revision of judgment. Historical voices remain intact, with editorial orientation and content notes outside the source text; estimated times are flexible teaching judgments.

progression.focus: Reading social signals and testing testimony
progression.rationale: Austen’s changing social impressions, Douglass’s firsthand witness, and lyric arguments establish habits of separating observed detail, interpretation, and assertion. Rereading focuses on a named voice and a local turn in meaning.
Longer scenes and autobiographical accounts ask readers to follow motives across a complete episode, question a narrator’s framing, and explain how social or institutional pressures affect a choice.

Letters, recollections, and competing accounts require readers to hold earlier evidence in memory and explain revisions rather than defend an initial impression. Gothic narration extends the distinction between a speaker’s claims and the work’s implications.

progression.focus: Framed voices, causal arguments, and limits
progression.rationale: Nested narrators and reflective prose increase demands on attribution, causal reasoning, and recognizing omissions. Students assess the grounds and limits of an explanation while attending to historical context.

The creature’s developing perspective, public arguments, and concentrated poems connect close attention to language with questions about education, sympathy, and exclusion. Discussion increasingly compares plausible interpretations.

Odes, sonnets, essays, and narrative scenes ask readers to sustain interpretations through changes of image, syntax, speaker, or structure. Students select decisive evidence and qualify conclusions without a prescribed single moral.

days.title: Pride and Prejudice excerpt: A letter from the future heir
days.challenge: Reread Collins’s letter in two voices: the dignified voice he intends and the skeptical voice suggested by the family’s responses. Separate the legal situation from each character’s judgment.
days.focus: Distinguish an offered reconciliation from the social interests embedded in its language.
days.context: Elizabeth Bennet is one of five sisters. Their father’s estate is legally directed to a male relative, Mr. Collins, rather than to the daughters. In this chapter that unfamiliar cousin announces a visit. A living or rectory is a church position with an income.

excerpt.locator: Pride and Prejudice, Chapter XIII, paragraphs 1–30; opens ““I hope, my dear,” said Mr. Bennet to his wife, as they”; closes “but he continued to apologize for about a quarter of an hour.”.

questions.prompt: How does Collins combine humility and self-praise in the same letter? Identify a turn where one becomes the other.
facilitatorNotes: His wish to heal the breach is presented as duty, but he calls his own overtures commendable and advertises an aristocratic patron. The coexistence matters more than deciding that every phrase is insincere.
evidence: my present overtures of good-will are highly commendable

questions.prompt: Why do Jane, Elizabeth, and Mary respond differently to the letter? Which part does each attend to?
facilitatorNotes: Jane values the apparent wish to compensate; Elizabeth notices pomp and deference; Mary evaluates composition. Their selective attention introduces different habits of reading rather than three interchangeable reactions.
evidence: The idea of the olive branch perhaps is not wholly new

questions.prompt: What changes Mrs. Bennet’s attitude toward Collins, and why does admiration of the house still trouble her?
facilitatorNotes: A possible benefit to her daughters softens her hostility. Praise of the property also reminds her that Collins will inherit it. Her response is materially grounded even when the narration treats her reasoning comically.
evidence: the mortifying supposition of his viewing it all as his own future property

days.title: Pride and Prejudice excerpt: The art of the unstudied compliment
days.challenge: Mark ordinary favors that Collins describes as exceptional generosity. Then reread the exchange about prepared compliments to hear the irony without assuming the characters share it.
days.focus: Read praise at two levels: what Collins means and what the narrator invites readers to notice.
days.context: Mr. Collins, the Bennets’ visiting cousin and future heir, depends on Lady Catherine de Bourgh for his church appointment. Mr. Bennet has invited him to explain his patroness’s virtues. Fordyce’s Sermons was a conduct book addressed to young women.

excerpt.locator: Pride and Prejudice, Chapter XIV, paragraphs 1–17; opens “DURING dinner, Mr. Bennet scarcely spoke at all; but when the servants”; closes “seated himself at another table with Mr. Bennet, and prepared for backgammon.”.

questions.prompt: Which examples most undermine Collins’s claim that Lady Catherine is exceptionally generous? Why?
facilitatorNotes: Permission to socialize and suggestions about closet shelves are ordinary or intrusive acts inflated by his dependence. Accept a reading that she gives real assistance, provided the student distinguishes assistance from the excessive rhetoric.
evidence: some shelves in the closets upstairs

questions.prompt: What does the phrase “unstudied an air” reveal about Collins’s compliments and Mr. Bennet’s question?
facilitatorNotes: Collins admits rehearsal while valuing the appearance of spontaneity. Mr. Bennet’s polite question elicits this contradiction and entertains him without openly mocking the guest.
evidence: I always wish to give them as unstudied an air as possible

questions.prompt: How does the abandoned reading expose a mismatch between Collins’s stated purpose and his response to Lydia?
facilitatorNotes: He says serious books benefit young women, but Lydia’s interruption immediately turns instruction into personal offense. He moves to backgammon despite assurances of no resentment; students can also acknowledge Lydia’s discourtesy.
evidence: I have often observed how little young ladies are interested by books of a serious stamp

days.title: Pride and Prejudice excerpt: Choices made at a glance
days.challenge: Track how quickly Collins changes his proposed bride and how quickly the sisters approve of Wickham. Keep the visible encounter with Darcy distinct from explanations not yet supplied.
days.focus: Contrast explicit narrative judgment with judgments characters make from appearance.
days.context: Collins has come to the Bennets intending to marry one of their daughters. Jane, the eldest, appears attached to the wealthy Mr. Bingley. Elizabeth and her sisters meet a newly arrived officer, Wickham, while walking to Meryton.

excerpt.locator: Pride and Prejudice, Chapter XV, paragraphs 1–13; opens “MR. COLLINS was not a sensible man, and the deficiency of nature”; closes “met with so much attention in the whole course of his life.”.

questions.prompt: How does the timing of Collins’s switch from Jane to Elizabeth shape our view of his intended marriage?
facilitatorNotes: The change happens while Mrs. Bennet stirs the fire. Rank among sisters and eligibility replace individual attachment, exposing the self-interested practicality behind his supposed atonement.
evidence: done while Mrs. Bennet was stirring the fire

questions.prompt: What does the narration establish about Wickham, and what does it leave unproved?
facilitatorNotes: It establishes handsome appearance, ease of conversation, and favorable impressions. These are evidence of social skill, not yet of honesty or moral worth. Ask students to distinguish observation from the characters’ inference.
evidence: His appearance was greatly in his favour

questions.prompt: What can Elizabeth reasonably infer from the meeting between Darcy and Wickham? What remains uncertain?
facilitatorNotes: Both change color and exchange a restrained greeting, suggesting a charged prior connection. The text does not assign the colors or explain the cause; naming a guilty man would exceed the evidence.
evidence: Both changed colour, one looked white, the other red.

days.title: Pride and Prejudice excerpt: Wickham begins his account
days.challenge: Separate Wickham’s verifiable details from claims about motives and private events. Reread the moments when he appears reluctant to speak, and notice how Elizabeth responds.
days.focus: Examine how a speaker establishes trust before presenting an accusation.
days.context: At an evening gathering, Elizabeth sits beside Wickham. She has seen him and Darcy exchange a cold greeting but does not know their history. A church living is a paid religious appointment that a patron could help bestow. This is the opening part of their conversation.

excerpt.locator: Pride and Prejudice, Chapter XVI, paragraphs 1–31; opens “AS no objection was made to the young people’s engagement with their”; closes “such feelings, and thought him handsomer than ever as he expressed them.”.

questions.prompt: How does Wickham make an ordinary conversation feel special to Elizabeth before discussing Darcy?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator stresses his skill with a threadbare topic and her pleasure in being his chosen listener. This social appeal prepares her receptiveness, though charm alone neither proves nor disproves his story.
evidence: the commonest, dullest, most threadbare topic might be rendered interesting

questions.prompt: How does claiming that he cannot be impartial affect Wickham’s credibility?
facilitatorNotes: The admission can sound candid and modest while allowing him to deliver damaging claims. His avowed restraint should be compared with how much he actually tells a new acquaintance.
evidence: It is impossible for me to be impartial.

questions.prompt: Which parts of the story about the living would require evidence beyond Wickham’s account?
facilitatorNotes: The wording of the bequest, the asserted legal defect, Darcy’s reasons, and Wickham’s conduct all need corroboration. His named circumstances make the story detailed, but detail is not independent confirmation.
evidence: There was just such an informality in the terms of the bequest

days.title: Pride and Prejudice excerpt: An explanation for every contradiction
days.challenge: Make a two-column map of Darcy’s alleged faults and admitted good actions. Examine how Wickham explains both through pride, then reconsider the narrator’s emphasis on graceful manners.
days.focus: Test a persuasive account that absorbs apparently contradictory evidence.
days.context: Wickham has told Elizabeth that Darcy denied him a church appointment intended by Darcy’s late father. Elizabeth now asks why Darcy would act that way. The conversation continues directly from the preceding selection; these are Wickham’s claims, not independently established facts.

excerpt.locator: Pride and Prejudice, Chapter XVI, paragraphs 32–60; opens ““But what,” said she, after a pause, “can have been his motive?”; closes “than he could well manage before the carriage stopped at Longbourn House.”.

questions.prompt: How does Wickham explain Darcy’s generosity without revising his unfavorable portrait?
facilitatorNotes: He attributes aid to tenants, the poor, and his sister chiefly to family and social pride. This makes generous behavior fit the same accusation; students may question whether the explanation can be tested from this conversation alone.
evidence: pride has often been his best friend

questions.prompt: Why does Elizabeth find Darcy’s friendship with Bingley difficult to explain? How does Wickham resolve it?
facilitatorNotes: She takes Bingley’s amiability as established and sees friendship as evidence against the portrait. Wickham claims Darcy treats social equals differently, preserving his account while appealing to Elizabeth’s class-based grievance.
evidence: Among those who are at all his equals in consequence, he is a very different man

questions.prompt: What caution does the ending suggest about judging a story by the manner of its telling?
facilitatorNotes: The close emphasizes that Wickham says things well and acts gracefully, then shows Elizabeth preoccupied with him. It records the success of his performance without independently confirming its claims.
evidence: Whatever he said, was said well; and whatever he did, done gracefully.

days.title: Narrative excerpt: family ties, inherited enslavement, and Aunt Hester
days.challenge: Separate remembered encounters, admitted uncertainty, and claims about the institution while following long conditional sentences; then follow how a single witnessed scene is framed as a turning point.
days.focus: How a personal account becomes an argument against laws that turn family relationships into property, and why Douglass presents his aunt’s whipping as the entrance to his story of slavery.
days.context: Douglass opens his 1845 autobiography by describing the family knowledge and relationships that slavery denied him. This excerpt begins after his discussion of his unknown birth date and continues to the end of chapter I, where he describes the first whipping he witnessed. A cowskin is a heavy whip.
days.contentNote: Discusses forced family separation and sexual exploitation implicit in enslavers’ paternity, and describes in detail the stripping and whipping of Douglass’s aunt, witnessed by him as a child; the enslaver’s oaths appear as printed with dashes; historical racial language is retained.

excerpt.locator: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, Chapter I, consecutive paragraphs to the end of the chapter; opens “My mother was named Harriet Bailey. She was the daughter of Isaac”; closes “the way of the bloody scenes that often occurred on the plantation.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Douglass distinguish what he knows about his mother from what he cannot verify about his father?
facilitatorNotes: His named maternal relatives contrast with withheld paternal knowledge. His refusal to certify a rumor limits his claim and builds credibility while showing how slavery controls access to family history.
evidence: of the correctness of this opinion, I know nothing

questions.prompt: How do the night visits complicate his statement that he received news of his mother’s death almost as if she were a stranger?
facilitatorNotes: The twelve-mile walks show sustained maternal care despite compulsory separation. His emotional distance is presented as an injury produced by the institution, not proof that his mother lacked affection.
evidence: travelling the whole distance on foot, after the performance of her day's work

questions.prompt: Why does the passage move from disputed paternity to the law governing children’s status?
facilitatorNotes: The law is central regardless of the rumor: it lets an enslaver claim his own children as property. Discuss how the family example exposes the contradiction in a racial or biblical justification without accepting that justification.
evidence: shall in all cases follow the condition of their mothers

questions.prompt: Douglass calls his aunt’s whipping “the blood-stained gate, the entrance to the hell of slavery.” Why present this scene as an entrance rather than only as the worst thing he saw?
facilitatorNotes: It is the first such scene he witnessed, and the chapter’s last sentence explains why: he had lived with his grandmother “out of the way” of plantation violence. The gate image turns the scene into a threshold for the child and for the narrative, which he says will make him “a witness and a participant.”
A defensible alternative stresses knowledge rather than place: the child now understands what his status means. Both readings fit the passage; ask students which words support each.
evidence: It was the blood-stained gate, the entrance to the hell of slavery, through which I was about to pass.
I had therefore been, until now, out of the way of the bloody scenes that often occurred on the plantation.

questions.prompt: What does Douglass imply about Captain Anthony’s motive when he writes that it “may be safely left to conjecture” why the master guarded Aunt Hester? Why imply this instead of stating it?
facilitatorNotes: The surrounding sentences point to sexual jealousy: he forbade her the company of a young man, punished that meeting as “the chief offence,” and is said to lack “pure morals.” The implication connects to the chapter’s earlier account of enslavers fathering children.

Leaving the inference to the reader matches his earlier refusal to assert what he cannot verify about his father, and it observes 1845 decorum while still making the point unmistakable. Students may reasonably weigh which motive, caution or decorum, matters more.
evidence: Why master was so careful of her, may be safely left to conjecture.
Had he been a man of pure morals himself, he might have been thought interested in protecting the innocence of my aunt

days.title: Narrative excerpt: the plantation as a system, and its songs
days.challenge: Track how lists of resources and a hierarchy of overseers accumulate an argument rather than merely describe a setting, then follow Douglass’s shift from description to his own retrospective interpretation of the songs.
days.focus: Abundance, administrative control, and deprivation in the same economic system, and the songs as testimony against it.
days.context: Douglass describes Colonel Lloyd’s home plantation and the surrounding farms it administered, the overseers who ran them, and the songs sung on the way to collect the monthly allowance. The opening reference is to an assault narrated earlier in the book. The selection ends with Douglass’s reflection on the songs; his next paragraph, on northern listeners who take singing as evidence of contentment, is part of the Grade 9 weekly course (week 16).
days.contentNote: Enslavement, threatened sale, childhood deprivation, and whipping are discussed, including a woman whipped in front of her children; historical terminology is retained.

excerpt.locator: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, Chapter II, consecutive paragraphs through the paragraph ending “there is no flesh in his obdurate heart”; opens “My master's family consisted of two sons, Andrew and Richard; one daughter,”; closes “will only be because “there is no flesh in his obdurate heart.””.

questions.prompt: What does calling the plantation a “seat of government” add to the description of its farms?
facilitatorNotes: The phrase emphasizes organized authority over many sites, not isolated acts by a single cruel person. Punishment, trade, and management converge there.
evidence: It was the seat of government for the whole twenty farms.

questions.prompt: How does the detailed list of food and clothing change the force of the earlier account of crops raised in abundance?
facilitatorNotes: The contrast shows that productive wealth does not translate into adequate provisions for the people producing it. Students can compare the ship’s continuous trade with children lacking clothing.
evidence: These were raised in great abundance

questions.prompt: Why does Douglass say the lack of sleep matters more than the lack of beds?
facilitatorNotes: The workday continues through washing, mending, and cooking; the missing resource is time as well as material comfort. The horn and threatened punishment make this deprivation systematic.
evidence: than from the want of time to sleep

questions.prompt: Douglass says he did not understand the songs “when a slave” because he “was myself within the circle.” What does distance let him hear in them now?
facilitatorNotes: Inside the experience he heard sounds; outside it, writing later, he hears testimony, prayer, and complaint. Retrospection and distance turn music into evidence, which is why he says the songs could teach more than “whole volumes of philosophy.”

Students may note that he also says the words were “full of meaning to themselves”: the singers understood what an outsider would call jargon. The insider and outsider views are different kinds of knowledge rather than one simply correcting the other.
evidence: I was myself within the circle; so that I neither saw nor heard as those without might see and hear.
Every tone was a testimony against slavery, and a prayer to God for deliverance from chains.

questions.prompt: The enslaved people called Mr. Hopkins “a good overseer.” What does that label reveal when it follows the portrait of Mr. Severe?
facilitatorNotes: “Good” is relative: Hopkins still whipped, but without visible pleasure, after a man whose field was “the field of blood and of blasphemy.” The praise measures how low the standard had fallen, and it anticipates the irony of the “first-rate overseer” in chapter IV.
A defensible alternative reads the label as genuine relief recorded without irony. Ask whether Douglass’s flat sentences invite one reading or allow both.
evidence: He whipped, but seemed to take no pleasure in it. He was called by the slaves a good overseer.
His presence made it both the field of blood and of blasphemy.

days.title: Narrative excerpt: the garden and the stable
days.challenge: Read apparently admiring descriptions against the punishments that follow them; distinguish suspicion from evidence.
days.focus: How luxury depends on arbitrary power over hungry and vulnerable people.
days.context: In chapter III, Douglass turns from provisions on Lloyd’s plantation to its celebrated garden, carriages, horses, and keepers.
days.contentNote: Contains descriptions of whipping, hunger, and humiliating treatment of enslaved people; discussion should analyze the testimony without reenacting it.

excerpt.locator: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, Chapter III, consecutive paragraphs; opens “COLONEL LLOYD kept a large and finely cultivated garden, which afforded almost”; closes “his whip, and at every stroke raise great ridges upon his back.”.

questions.prompt: How does the tarred fence turn the garden into a system of accusation?
facilitatorNotes: A trace of tar counts as proof of either entering or merely trying to enter; the rule makes suspicion sufficient for punishment. The garden’s beauty is therefore paired with coercive control.
evidence: it was deemed sufficient proof

questions.prompt: What effect do the paired complaints about horses being too hot or too cold, or fed too soon or too late, create?
facilitatorNotes: The opposite possibilities make the demands impossible to predict and suggest that no performance can secure safety. The repeated alternatives reproduce the keepers’ trapped situation.
evidence: he got it too soon or too late

questions.prompt: What does the contrast between the horses’ treatment and old Barney’s treatment reveal?
facilitatorNotes: The account lavishes care on valuable animals while denying a person explanations, safety, and dignity. Accept formulations grounded in the contrast rather than claims that the horses themselves are at fault.
evidence: They never knew when they were safe from punishment.

days.title: Narrative excerpt: the danger of telling the truth
days.challenge: Distinguish reported anecdote from personal testimony and interpret apparently positive testimony under coercion.
days.focus: Why statements of contentment cannot be separated from the risks of speaking.
days.context: Douglass recounts an encounter between Lloyd and a man Lloyd enslaved, then explains how threats shape what enslaved people say about their conditions.
days.contentNote: Describes forced sale and separation; historical racial and ownership language is retained.

excerpt.locator: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, Chapter III, consecutive paragraphs; opens “To describe the wealth of Colonel Lloyd would be almost equal to”; closes “but to be a poor man's slave was deemed a disgrace indeed!”.

questions.prompt: Why does it matter that neither man recognizes the other’s position at the beginning of the roadside exchange?
facilitatorNotes: Lloyd’s wealth is so extensive that personal recognition disappears; the other man therefore answers without knowing the danger. The mismatch between ordinary questions and later punishment exposes arbitrary authority.
evidence: nor did all the slaves of the out-farms know him

questions.prompt: How should a reader evaluate a statement that an enslaved speaker is contented, according to this passage?
facilitatorNotes: The statement may reflect fear of spies and retaliation, not freely expressed satisfaction. Douglass explains a survival strategy rather than inviting readers to dismiss the speaker as inherently dishonest.
evidence: They suppress the truth rather than take the consequences of telling it

questions.prompt: Why end with arguments among enslaved people over whose master is greater?
facilitatorNotes: The ending complicates the analysis: coercion is joined by identification with a powerful owner and familiar human pride. Students may see irony in the belief that greatness transfers to the people being owned.
evidence: the greatness of their masters was transferable to themselves

days.title: Narrative excerpt: what counts as a “first-rate overseer”
days.challenge: Follow irony in praise-like vocabulary and explain how repeated sentence structures expose a moral reversal; then test the portrait against the killing that shows what Gore’s “firmness” means.
days.focus: A system that rewards ambition, consistency, and obedience when they serve cruelty, and that leaves a killing unpunished.
days.context: Chapter IV profiles Austin Gore, who replaces an overseer considered insufficiently severe, and then narrates his killing of Demby and the plantation’s response. Enslaved people could not testify against a white man in a Maryland court.
days.contentNote: Describes coercion and whipping, and the shooting of an enslaved man, Demby, including the sight of his body in the water; the killer is never prosecuted.

excerpt.locator: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, Chapter IV, consecutive paragraphs through “stained with his brother’s blood”; opens “MR. HOPKINS remained but a short time in the office of overseer.”; closes “though his guilty soul had not been stained with his brother's blood.”.

questions.prompt: Why is the phrase “first-rate overseer” not straightforward praise in this portrait?
facilitatorNotes: The traits qualifying Gore for promotion are immediately linked to cruelty and manipulation. The phrase exposes the institution’s standards of success rather than endorsing them.
evidence: what is called a first-rate overseer

questions.prompt: What happens to the possibility of innocence in the sequence “accused,” “convicted,” and “punished”?
facilitatorNotes: The repeated progression makes punishment automatic; there is no meaningful hearing or distinction between allegation and proof. Its rhythm models the closed process.
evidence: To be accused was to be convicted, and to be convicted was to be punished

questions.prompt: How does the contrast between Gore’s pride before enslaved people and servility before the master sharpen the portrait?
facilitatorNotes: His authority is hierarchical rather than principled: he demands submission below while performing it above. The balanced phrasing links domination to dependence.
evidence: quite servile enough to crouch, himself, at the feet of the master

questions.prompt: Gore defends the killing by predicting “the freedom of the slaves, and the enslavement of the whites.” How does Douglass let Gore’s own reasoning condemn him?
facilitatorNotes: Douglass reports the argument without rebuttal, then adds the flat sentence “Mr. Gore’s defence was satisfactory.” The understatement makes the community’s acceptance the indictment: the system admits it rests on terror and accepts that as justification.
Students may also read Gore’s fear as an unwitting admission that slavery depends on force rather than consent; both readings use the same evidence.
evidence: the result of which would be, the freedom of the slaves, and the enslavement of the whites
Mr. Gore's defence was satisfactory.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter section end with Gore “as highly esteemed” as though his soul “had not been stained with his brother’s blood”? What does the word “brother” claim?
facilitatorNotes: The phrase echoes Cain and Abel, where a brother’s blood cries out from the ground: Douglass insists on a shared humanity that the law denied. The preceding sentences explain the legal mechanism of impunity, since enslaved witnesses could neither sue nor testify.
Some readers emphasize the biblical judgment, others the bitter social observation about esteem; the sentence holds both.
evidence: as though his guilty soul had not been stained with his brother's blood
they of course could neither institute a suit, nor testify against him

days.title: On Virtue
days.challenge: Reread the twenty-one lines aloud, trace changes in address, and distinguish comprehending an ideal from following it.
days.focus: Personification turns an abstract virtue into an active poetic guide.
days.context: Wheatley addresses the personified idea Virtue in a Christian and classical poetic vocabulary. Read the full poem once for movement and again to mark each request.

excerpt.locator: On Virtue; complete poem, Memoir and Poems of Phillis Wheatley (Boston, 1834); opens “ON VIRTUE. O THOU bright jewel, in my aim I strive To”; closes “nobler lay, O thou, enthroned with cherubs in the realms of day.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker first stop trying to fathom Virtue, then ask Virtue to attend her?
facilitatorNotes: Distinguish mastering a lofty idea from accepting it as a guide. The movement from intellectual defeat to relationship supports a reading of humility without surrender.
evidence: But O my soul, sink not into despair;

questions.prompt: How does the bright jewel become a queen, companion and teacher across the poem?
facilitatorNotes: Trace the movement from a desired object to an active person with wings, attendants and instruction. Readers may stress aspiration or dependence, but should connect specific changes.
evidence: Teach me a better strain, a nobler lay,

questions.prompt: Does the final request concern moral conduct, poetry, or both?
facilitatorNotes: The requests to guide steps and teach a better strain connect ethics with the poet’s craft. Do not require the reader to share the poem’s religious beliefs.
evidence: But guide my steps to endless life and bliss.

days.title: Hymn to the Morning
days.challenge: Read twice for the change from invocation to sensory description to interruption; annotate the linked images of heat and inspiration.
days.focus: An apparently celebratory dawn poem ends by exposing the limits of its own song.
days.context: Aurora names dawn; Calliope and her sisters are the classical Muses, figures of artistic inspiration. These terms are supplied as orientation, outside Wheatley’s text.

excerpt.locator: Hymn to the Morning; complete poem, Memoir and Poems of Phillis Wheatley (Boston, 1834); opens “HYMN TO THE MORNING. ATTEND my lays, ye ever honored Nine, Assist”; closes “his fervid beams too strong, And scarce begun, concludes the abortive song.”.

questions.prompt: What help does the speaker request before describing the morning itself?
facilitatorNotes: The opening invocation to the nine Muses asks for refined language and musical skill; the poem presents description as artistic labour, not merely spontaneous looking.
evidence: Assist my labors, and my strains refine;

questions.prompt: How do the birds and the poet resemble one another, and where does that resemblance break down?
facilitatorNotes: Both begin songs at dawn. The birds resume their lays, while the poet’s song is cut short by excessive heat; discuss this comic or humbling difference.
evidence: Harmonious lays the feathered race resume,

questions.prompt: What changes when the king of day becomes too powerful for the speaker?
facilitatorNotes: The celebrated light also overwhelms the celebrant. The abrupt ending complicates simple praise: nature inspires art but can also limit it.
evidence: And scarce begun, concludes the abortive song.

days.title: Hymn to the Evening
days.challenge: Reread with attention to imperative verbs and personified powers; follow how a landscape description becomes a prayer.
days.focus: Sound and colour lead into a cyclical meditation on rest and renewed attention.
days.context: The poem uses Christian praise alongside classical personifications of dawn and night. Its moral and devotional voice is Wheatley’s poetic construction.

excerpt.locator: Hymn to the Evening; complete poem, Memoir and Poems of Phillis Wheatley (Boston, 1834); opens “HYMN TO THE EVENING. SOON as the sun forsook the eastern main,”; closes “seals my drowsy eyes, Then cease my song, till fair Aurora rise.”.

questions.prompt: Which sounds make evening seem active rather than empty?
facilitatorNotes: Thunder, streams and birds create a layered soundscape. Encourage discussion of the transition from majestic noise to softer music.
evidence: Soft purl the streams, the birds renew their notes,

questions.prompt: How does the red western sky become a model for human conduct?
facilitatorNotes: The wish that breasts glow with virtue translates visible colour into a moral aspiration. Identify the comparison rather than treating the sunset as a literal moral lesson.
evidence: So may our breasts with ev'ry virtue glow,

questions.prompt: Compare the poem’s final command with its hope for the next morning. Does the ending close or continue the cycle?
facilitatorNotes: The song stops under Night’s sceptre, yet the promised return of Aurora projects renewed song and labour. Both closure and continuation are defensible when supported.
evidence: Then cease my song, till fair Aurora rise.

days.title: On Recollection
days.challenge: Track the changing role of one personification over a longer poem; reread the first and last praise passages against the central self-reproach.
days.focus: Memory is represented as both artistic resource and moral witness.
days.context: Mneme is the personification of memory; the nine are the Muses. Wheatley names herself an African poet within the classical invocation.
days.contentNote: The poem discusses sin, divine punishment and remorse; treat its religious claims as the poem’s perspective.

excerpt.locator: On Recollection; complete poem, Memoir and Poems of Phillis Wheatley (Boston, 1834); opens “ON RECOLLECTION. MNEME begin. Inspire, ye sacred Nine, Your vent'rous Afric, in”; closes “who, in her sacred shrine, Feels himself sheltered from the wrath divine!”.

questions.prompt: How does Mneme first help the poet create, before becoming a judge?
facilitatorNotes: At first memory orders recovered events and offers images; later it condemns vice and praises virtue. Trace this expansion from artistic faculty to conscience.
evidence:
The acts of long-departed years, by thee
Recovered, in due order ranged we see:

questions.prompt: What is troubling about follies being written in brass?
facilitatorNotes: The durable material opposes the wish that youthful errors pass unnoticed. Readers may discuss permanence, visibility or accountability, grounding the interpretation in the return of those follies.
evidence: Unnoticed, but behold them writ in brass!

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker address Virtue after describing memory’s power?
facilitatorNotes: Recollection alone can intensify remorse; Virtue offers guidance for future days. The poem turns from recalling acts to changing action, without erasing the remembered past.
evidence: Be thine employ to guide my future days,

days.title: Thoughts on the Works of Providence
days.challenge: Track changes of scale and distinguish descriptive claims, rhetorical questions and personified argument; reread the Love–Reason exchange.
days.focus: A sustained devotional argument moves from cosmic scale to mental life and a dialogue between Love and Reason.
days.context: This eighteenth-century poem presents natural and mental phenomena through a Christian devotional argument. Its numerical astronomy is historical language in a poem, not a current science reference.
days.contentNote: Contains historical religious claims, references to death, and outdated astronomical measurement; discussion evaluates the poem’s argument rather than endorsing its factual measurements.

excerpt.locator: Thoughts on the Works of Providence; complete poem, Memoir and Poems of Phillis Wheatley (Boston, 1834); opens “THOUGHTS ON THE WORKS OF PROVIDENCE. ARISE, my soul; on wings enraptured,”; closes “arrayed in mercy shine, What songs should rise, how constant, how divine!”.

questions.prompt: Why does the poem imagine both too little and too much sunlight?
facilitatorNotes: The paired counterfactuals present benefit as a balance rather than unlimited abundance. Ask how this supports the speaker’s argument about wise ordering.
evidence: In their excess how would our race complain,

questions.prompt: What does sleep contribute to an argument that begins with planetary motion?
facilitatorNotes: The poem moves from immense visible systems to ordinary consciousness. Its questions about dreams and the return of reason treat private experience as another arena for its devotional interpretation.
evidence: What power, O man! thy reason then restores,

questions.prompt: When Love and Reason speak, does either simply defeat the other?
facilitatorNotes: Reason acknowledges Love’s divine origin and embraces her. The reconciliation lets the poem bring intellectual understanding and affection into the same account; readers should not turn the scene into a rejection of thought.
evidence: She clasped the blooming goddess in her arms.

days.title: Pride and Prejudice excerpt: Two sisters weigh a story
days.challenge: Reread the sisters’ reasons for belief, not just their conclusions. Track how the narrator connects Elizabeth’s expectations for the ball to her wish for confirmation.
days.focus: Compare competing errors in assessing testimony: excessive charity and excessive certainty.
days.context: Elizabeth tells Jane that Wickham blames Darcy for depriving him of a promised church living. Neither sister has heard Darcy’s account. An invitation to a ball then redirects the household’s attention.

excerpt.locator: Pride and Prejudice, Chapter XVII, paragraphs 1–15; opens “ELIZABETH related to Jane, the next day, what had passed between Mr.”; closes “such a Friday, Saturday, Sunday, and Monday endurable to Kitty and Lydia.”.

questions.prompt: What is strong and what is weak about Jane’s refusal to condemn either man?
facilitatorNotes: She recognizes incomplete knowledge and the possibility of error, but her commitment to everyone’s goodness generates an unsupported theory about intermediaries. Uncertainty is reasonable; that specific explanation remains conjecture.
evidence: Interested people have perhaps misrepresented each to the other.

questions.prompt: Does Elizabeth apply the same evidentiary standard to Wickham and Darcy? Explain using her own words.
facilitatorNotes: She treats names, details, and looks as sufficient for Wickham while requiring Darcy to contradict an accusation he has not been shown to know about. Her confidence goes beyond the evidence available.
evidence: Besides, there was truth in his looks.

questions.prompt: How does the invitation scene turn Elizabeth’s wit against her?
facilitatorNotes: Her teasing question about Collins dancing prompts him to claim the first two dances she wanted for Wickham. The reversal makes her social confidence vulnerable and reveals a marriage intention she had not taken seriously.
evidence: Elizabeth felt herself completely taken in.

days.title: Pride and Prejudice excerpt: A dance and a disputed portrait
days.challenge: Follow the changing subjects of the dance dialogue. Notice when the narrator reports Elizabeth’s inference and when it reveals something she does not know about Darcy.
days.focus: Trace how prior belief shapes the interpretation of absence, silence, and conversation.
days.context: Elizabeth arrives at the Netherfield ball hoping to dance with Wickham. He is absent. After dancing with Collins, she unexpectedly accepts Darcy as a partner. The selection ends when that dance and its uneasy conversation finish.

excerpt.locator: Pride and Prejudice, Chapter XVIII, paragraphs 1–43; opens “TILL Elizabeth entered the drawing-room at Netherfield, and looked in vain for”; closes “which soon procured her pardon, and directed all his anger against another.”.

questions.prompt: How does Elizabeth keep Darcy responsible for Wickham’s absence after her first explanation proves incorrect?
facilitatorNotes: She first suspects an omitted invitation; Denny’s suggestion that Wickham avoided Darcy supplies a replacement explanation. Her disappointment preserves the conclusion while its supposed basis changes.
evidence: not less answerable for Wickham’s absence than if her first surmise had been just

questions.prompt: Why is Elizabeth’s warning about judging properly at first ironic within this scene?
facilitatorNotes: She warns someone she believes inflexible while relying heavily on a single account herself. The scene supports questioning her certainty without requiring readers to decide Darcy innocent of every fault.
evidence: It is particularly incumbent on those who never change their opinion, to be secure of judging properly at first.

questions.prompt: What does the final sentence let the reader know that Elizabeth may not understand?
facilitatorNotes: Darcy’s attraction makes him forgive her relatively quickly and direct anger elsewhere. The access to his feeling complicates her interpretation of his cold manner and their supposedly mutual dislike.
evidence: on each side dissatisfied, though not to an equal degree

days.title: Pride and Prejudice excerpt: Advice that fails to persuade
days.challenge: For each warning or claim, identify the speaker’s actual knowledge, social prejudice, and motive. Compare Elizabeth’s criticism of others’ evidence with Collins’s confident misreading of a reception.
days.focus: Distinguish a weak argument from the truth or falsity of its conclusion.
days.context: After Elizabeth’s dance with Darcy, Miss Bingley warns her against Wickham. Jane then reports Bingley’s defense of his friend. Finally Collins discovers Darcy’s connection to Lady Catherine and decides to introduce himself.

excerpt.locator: Pride and Prejudice, Chapter XVIII, paragraphs 44–62; opens “They had not long separated when Miss Bingley came towards her, and,”; closes “very handsome thought. Upon the whole, I am much pleased with him.””.

questions.prompt: Why is Elizabeth justified in challenging Miss Bingley’s argument even if the warning might contain truth?
facilitatorNotes: Miss Bingley admits ignorance of particulars and treats Wickham’s parentage as evidence of guilt. Rejecting that class prejudice is justified; it does not establish that every accusation is false.
evidence: His guilt and his descent appear, by your account, to be the same

questions.prompt: What limitation does Elizabeth correctly identify in Bingley’s testimony?
facilitatorNotes: Bingley relies on Darcy and cannot recall key circumstances. His sincerity and loyalty do not amount to firsthand knowledge; readers can recognize this valid criticism alongside Elizabeth’s favorable treatment of Wickham.
evidence: you must excuse my not being convinced by assurances only

questions.prompt: How does Collins’s report of meeting Darcy differ from the narrated encounter?
facilitatorNotes: The narration shows astonishment, distant civility, and increasing contempt; Collins reports pleasure and admiration. His desire for connection makes him convert a rebuff into a compliment.
evidence: Mr. Darcy seemed much pleased with the attention.

days.title: Pride and Prejudice excerpt: The family on display
days.challenge: Track Elizabeth’s changing attention across mother, sister, father, and guests. Reread the difference between the marriage Mrs. Bennet imagines and the evidence actually supplied.
days.focus: Analyze how a scene moves between comedy, embarrassment, and economic anxiety.
days.context: At the ball’s supper, Elizabeth watches her mother discuss Jane’s expected marriage to Bingley within Darcy’s hearing. Singing and more speeches follow. No engagement has been announced.

excerpt.locator: Pride and Prejudice, Chapter XVIII, paragraphs 63–77; opens “As Elizabeth had no longer any interest of her own to pursue,”; closes “her, the worth of each was eclipsed by Mr. Bingley and Netherfield.”.

questions.prompt: What practical hopes are mixed into Mrs. Bennet’s excitement about Jane’s possible marriage?
facilitatorNotes: Money, proximity, opportunities for younger daughters, and relief from responsibility accompany pleasure in Bingley. Her public certainty is comic, but these interests reflect the daughters’ financial vulnerability.
evidence: consign her single daughters to the care of their sister

questions.prompt: Why does stopping Mary’s song fail to relieve Elizabeth completely?
facilitatorNotes: Her father’s public remark embarrasses Mary, so Elizabeth becomes sorry for the sister whose performance she wanted stopped. The scene complicates the idea that a witty intervention is automatically kind.
evidence: Elizabeth, sorry for her, and sorry for her father’s speech

questions.prompt: How does the departure scene expose a gap between Mrs. Bennet’s confidence and the guests’ response?
facilitatorNotes: Several hosts are impatient, and the family sees that it is wished away, yet Mrs. Bennet leaves certain of two marriages. Bingley’s warmth provides some grounds for hope, but not for the settled outcome she imagines.
evidence: under the delightful persuasion

days.title: Pride and Prejudice excerpt: A refusal that will not be heard
days.challenge: Track each refusal and Collins’s reinterpretation of it. Read Elizabeth’s final appeal aloud, stressing the difference between a social stereotype and an individual speaker.
days.focus: Examine how a ready-made belief can prevent a person from hearing explicit evidence.
days.context: The morning after the ball, Collins proposes to Elizabeth. Her mother welcomes the proposal because Collins will inherit the family estate. Elizabeth does not want to marry him. This chapter presents the entire proposal and refusal.
days.contentNote: A comic scene depicts repeated dismissal of a woman’s explicit refusal and family pressure to marry.

excerpt.locator: Pride and Prejudice, Chapter XIX, paragraphs 1–22; opens “THE next day opened a new scene at Longbourn. Mr. Collins made”; closes “not be mistaken for the affectation and coquetry of an elegant female.”.

questions.prompt: What do Collins’s ordered reasons for marrying reveal about the place Elizabeth occupies in his proposal?
facilitatorNotes: His professional example, personal happiness, patroness’s advice, and inheritance plan dominate. Elizabeth is positioned as suitable to a preexisting project; the language of violent affection contrasts with the calculated list.
evidence: My reasons for marrying are, first

questions.prompt: Why can Elizabeth’s increasingly direct refusals not persuade Collins?
facilitatorNotes: He assumes that women conventionally refuse wanted offers and that his advantages must be desirable. The assumption converts disconfirming evidence into encouragement, leaving her no verbal response he will accept.
evidence: I shall choose to attribute it to your wish of increasing my love by suspense

questions.prompt: What does Elizabeth ask him to recognize when she calls herself a “rational creature”?
facilitatorNotes: She asks that her words be treated as sincere judgment from an individual with agency. This rejects his stereotype of an elegant female and his reliance on parental authority; her refusal does not need a better bargain to be valid.
evidence: a rational creature speaking the truth from her heart

days.title: Narrative excerpt: a changed mistress and an overheard lesson
days.challenge: Reread the compressed contrast in sound, facial imagery, and metaphor to distinguish cause from mere character labeling; then follow how Douglass turns an enslaver’s argument against him.
days.focus: The corrupting effects of unchecked power on a person initially presented as kind, and the link between literacy and freedom revealed by a prohibition.
days.context: After moving to Baltimore, Douglass describes Sophia Auld’s first response to him, her husband’s prohibition of the reading lessons she had begun, and the lesson Douglass drew from it. An ell is an old measure of about a yard. The selection ends mid-paragraph; the remaining sentences, beginning with his resolution to learn without a teacher, are part of the Grade 9 weekly course (week 36).
days.contentNote: Historical enslavement and dehumanizing treatment. Hugh Auld’s quoted speech repeatedly uses a racial slur, which Douglass records as evidence of the enslaver’s reasoning.

excerpt.locator: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, Chapter VI, consecutive paragraphs, ending mid-paragraph at “I had gained from my master”; opens “My new mistress proved to be all she appeared when I first”; closes “instruction which, by the merest accident, I had gained from my master.”.

questions.prompt: Which earlier experiences make Douglass uncertain how to behave toward Sophia Auld?
facilitatorNotes: He has learned submissive behavior, but it does not win her approval. His uncertainty reveals the prior system through the unexpected experience of being treated with ordinary regard.
evidence: My early instruction was all out of place.

questions.prompt: Trace the change in the description of her voice. What argument does the sound imagery help make?
facilitatorNotes: Tranquil music becomes harsh discord, making the institutional change perceptible rather than abstract. Students can also trace the parallel changes in eyes and face.
evidence: that voice, made all of sweet accord, changed to one of harsh and horrid discord

questions.prompt: Why call the cause a “poison” rather than simply say she became a bad person?
facilitatorNotes: Poison depicts a destructive influence entering and altering someone, while “irresponsible” identifies power without accountability. Discuss how the metaphor locates a structural cause without erasing individual actions.
evidence: The fatal poison of irresponsible power

questions.prompt: Why does Douglass call his master’s warning “invaluable instruction” gained “by the merest accident”? What did Auld teach that he did not intend to teach?
facilitatorNotes: Auld’s explanation that reading would “unfit” a person for slavery reveals that the system depends on enforced ignorance. The prohibition therefore teaches Douglass the route to freedom more clearly than the lessons themselves.
Students may question “from that moment”: a retrospective narrator may compress a gradual understanding into one revelation. That compression is itself a narrative choice worth discussing.
evidence: From that moment, I understood the pathway from slavery to freedom.
I was gladdened by the invaluable instruction which, by the merest accident, I had gained from my master.

questions.prompt: Douglass reproduces Auld’s words exactly, slur included, introducing them with “To use his own words.” What does direct quotation accomplish that a summary would not?
facilitatorNotes: Quotation makes the enslaver’s language and logic the evidence: readers judge Auld by what he said, and the key argument, that literacy makes a person unfit to be enslaved, comes from his own mouth. Douglass then reinterprets it as a “new and special revelation.”
Students may note the cost of reproducing such language; Douglass’s choice is testimony rather than endorsement, and the passage frames the words as damning the speaker.
evidence: To use his own words, further, he said,
It would forever unfit him to be a slave.

days.title: Narrative excerpt: valuation and division
days.challenge: Track changes between legal-administrative vocabulary and the language of relationships, memory, and fear.
days.focus: How treating people as inherited property destroys their control over their lives.
days.context: After Captain Anthony dies without a will, Douglass is recalled from Baltimore for the valuation and division of the estate.
days.contentNote: Includes forced family separation and a graphic recollection of violence against a child; adult guidance and an option to pause are appropriate.

excerpt.locator: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, Chapter VIII, consecutive paragraphs; opens “IN a very short time after I went to live at Baltimore,”; closes “division, just about one month, and it seemed to have been six.”.

questions.prompt: What does the alternating list of people and animals achieve beyond saying both are property?
facilitatorNotes: The sequence puts specific human life stages and relationships into the same categories as livestock, forcing the reader to confront the reduction. The effect depends on syntax as well as information.
evidence: There were horses and men, cattle and women, pigs and children

questions.prompt: How does the power of “a single word” contrast with the bonds at risk?
facilitatorNotes: A minimal act by an owner can override wishes, prayers, and lifelong relationships. The imbalance shows that separation is not a negotiation among people with equal standing.
evidence: A single word from the white men was enough

questions.prompt: Why does the last sentence compare one month with six?
facilitatorNotes: The comparison records experienced time under fear rather than revising the chronology. Returning to Baltimore brings relief, but the valuation still exposes the insecurity of even relatively better treatment.
evidence: it seemed to have been six

days.title: Narrative excerpt: the grandmother and the deserted hearth
days.challenge: Distinguish known events, conditional speculation, borrowed verse, and imagined scene while tracing an appeal to justice.
days.focus: How a lifetime of service is answered with abandonment, and how the prose makes that injustice felt.
days.context: Douglass describes the treatment of his grandmother after the deaths of members of the family that claimed ownership of her. He includes lines attributed in the source to the poet Whittier.
days.contentNote: Family separation, abandonment of an elderly person, anticipated death, and historical racial language.

excerpt.locator: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, Chapter VIII, consecutive paragraphs; opens “Very soon after my return to Baltimore, my mistress, Lucretia, died, leaving”; closes “her fallen remains. Will not a righteous God visit for these things?”.

questions.prompt: How does the repeated account of what the grandmother did for the family prepare the charge of ingratitude?
facilitatorNotes: Her care spans the owner’s infancy, adulthood, and death, building a record of intimate service. The inheritance system returns no freedom or security for that lifetime.
evidence: She had rocked him in infancy, attended him in childhood, served him through life

questions.prompt: What does the inserted verse contribute that differs from the surrounding explanation?
facilitatorNotes: The repeated “gone” gives the losses a lamenting rhythm and a first-person cry. It connects the particular grandmother’s separation to a wider pattern while changing the passage’s sound and pace.
evidence: Gone, gone, sold and gone

questions.prompt: Where does Douglass signal uncertainty, and how should that affect our reading of the final scene?
facilitatorNotes: “If” identifies uncertainty about whether she is still alive. The final scene dramatizes the condition and its probable end; do not label every imagined gesture an eyewitness observation.
evidence: If my poor old grandmother now lives

days.title: Narrative excerpt: separation and a route north
days.challenge: Follow the turn from retrospective regret to practical observation in a brief narrative transition.
days.focus: How geographical knowledge restores a possibility of action within coercive movement.
days.context: A dispute between Thomas Auld and Hugh Auld results in Douglass being moved from Baltimore to St. Michael’s. His departure also separates him from boys who had helped him learn.
days.contentNote: Enslavement, forced movement, and separation; references to alcohol and changed behavior.

excerpt.locator: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, Chapter VIII, consecutive paragraphs; opens “In about two years after the death of Mrs. Lucretia, Master Thomas”; closes “a favorable opportunity. When that came, I was determined to be off.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Douglass distinguish the Aulds from the people he truly regrets leaving?
facilitatorNotes: The distinction prevents the reader from treating his attachment to Baltimore as loyalty to enslavers. His most important relationships are with the boys who shared knowledge.
evidence: But it was not to them that I was attached.

questions.prompt: What changes between regretting an earlier failure to escape and watching the steamboats?
facilitatorNotes: Regret becomes active observation: the direction of travel supplies usable knowledge. The passage does not show an escape yet, only a revived plan grounded in what he sees.
evidence: I paid particular attention to the direction which the steamboats took

questions.prompt: How does the closing determination complicate the fact that this journey itself is involuntary?
facilitatorNotes: The enforced journey unexpectedly provides information he can use toward freedom. The ending converts a scene of lost control into the preparation for a future choice.
evidence: My determination to run away was again revived.

days.title: Narrative excerpt: an address to the ships
days.challenge: Track changing emotional positions inside an apostrophe, including accusation, questioning, planning, and self-consolation.
days.focus: The gulf between visible movement on the bay and a person denied freedom.
days.context: During his time with Edward Covey, Douglass describes exhaustion and his private address to ships on Chesapeake Bay. An apostrophe addresses something absent, abstract, or unable to answer.
days.contentNote: Depicts physical and psychological harm under enslavement and mentions thoughts of suicide and violence without instructions; discussion need not invite personal disclosures.

excerpt.locator: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, Chapter X, consecutive paragraphs; opens “If at any one time of my life more than another, I”; closes “one moment, and at the next reconciling myself to my wretched lot.”.

questions.prompt: Why are the white sails both beautiful and terrifying in the narrator’s description?
facilitatorNotes: The same sight means free movement to others but intensifies his confinement. “Ghosts” changes a conventional pleasant view into a reminder of deprivation.
evidence: so many shrouded ghosts

questions.prompt: How does the repeated opposition between “you” and “I” organize the speech to the ships?
facilitatorNotes: Each contrast pairs their mobility with his restraint, making unequal freedom the organizing rhythm. Students can trace a shift from envy to imagining how the bay might carry him away.
evidence: You are loosed from your moorings, and are free; I am fast in my chains

questions.prompt: Does the speech end in a simple, permanent triumph of hope?
facilitatorNotes: No. It includes a concrete plan and future hope, but the framing sentence describes recurring swings between protest and reconciliation to his lot. Accept readings of hope as persistent but unstable.
evidence: at the next reconciling myself to my wretched lot

days.title: To the Earl of Dartmouth
days.challenge: Distinguish ceremonial address, personification and autobiographical claim; reread the transition beginning Should you, my lord.
days.focus: Public praise becomes an argument for freedom through the speaker’s personal testimony.
days.context: Wheatley’s poem addresses a British political officeholder while linking colonial grievances to her own forcible removal from Africa. Its praise and its demands need to be read together.
days.contentNote: Contains a first-person account of enslavement, family separation and a kidnapped child; no graphic violence.

excerpt.locator: TO THE RIGHT HONORABLE WILLIAM, EARL OF DARTMOUTH, His Majesty's Principal Secretary of State for North America, &c.; complete poem, Memoir and Poems of Phillis Wheatley (Boston, 1834); opens “TO THE RIGHT HONORABLE WILLIAM, EARL OF DARTMOUTH, His Majesty's Principal Secretary”; closes “that blest abode, Where, like the prophet, thou shalt find thy God.”.

questions.prompt: How does the personal account of being taken from Africa change the earlier public praise of Freedom?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker grounds political language in the grief of an actual child and parent. This makes freedom more than an abstract compliment to a statesman.
evidence: Was snatched from Afric's fancied happy seat:

questions.prompt: Whose pain does the poem ask the reader to imagine when it describes the father and babe?
facilitatorNotes: The focus extends beyond the speaker’s suffering to her parent and the captor’s hardened feeling. Avoid treating the passage as acceptance of enslavement.
evidence: That from a father seized his babe beloved:

questions.prompt: Is the poem only flattery, or does its praise also make a demand?
facilitatorNotes: The appeal for renewed favours and the prayer against tyrannic sway permit reading praise as a claim upon power. Ask which exact requests support that interpretation.
evidence: Others may never feel tyrannic sway?

days.title: A Hymn to Humanity
days.challenge: Read twice to distinguish the heavenly figure, the praised addressee and the speaking poet; trace the shift from universal ideals to personal gratitude.
days.focus: Personified benevolence becomes a statement about friendship and the conditions that support art.
days.context: The poem is addressed to S. P. G. and uses the Muses and Graces as classical figures of art and friendship. Its speaker explicitly identifies herself as Africa’s muse.

excerpt.locator: A HYMN TO HUMANITY. To S. P. G. Esq.; complete poem, Memoir and Poems of Phillis Wheatley (Boston, 1834); opens “A HYMN TO HUMANITY. To S. P. G. Esq. Lo! for this”; closes “Immortal Friendship laurel-crowned, The smiling Graces all around, With ev'ry heavenly Art.”.

questions.prompt: How does the poem make Humanity seem at once universal and located in particular people?
facilitatorNotes: The heavenly prince descends to inspire each human heart, but the empire is said to be in the great and good. Explore the tension between a universal invitation and selective praise.
evidence: Each human heart inspire:

questions.prompt: What does enlarging the contracted mind suggest about the relation between feeling and action?
facilitatorNotes: Bounty requires overcoming narrowness, not merely feeling pity. The metaphor connects generosity to an expansion of attention and conduct.
evidence: Enlarge the close contracted mind,

questions.prompt: How does the speaker connect a friend’s compassion with her own ability to write?
facilitatorNotes: The pitying eye responds to the languid muse, after which the Muses string her lyre. Acknowledge gratitude while asking how support makes artistic production possible.
evidence: And deigned to string my lyre.

days.title: A Farewell to America
days.challenge: Reread the successive stanzas to trace changing addressees and shifting emotional direction rather than assuming one consistent farewell mood.
days.focus: A departure poem balances illness, attachment, curiosity and spiritual caution.
days.context: The dated poem presents a speaker departing New England for Britain. Read its travel, health and affection claims as the poem supplies them; its religious ending belongs to the speaker’s perspective.
days.contentNote: References illness and separation.

excerpt.locator: A FAREWELL TO AMERICA. To Mrs. S. W.; complete poem, Memoir and Poems of Phillis Wheatley (Boston, 1834); opens “A FAREWELL TO AMERICA. To Mrs. S. W. ADIEU, New England's smiling”; closes “on the field Of all its power disarms! Boston, May 7th, 1773.”.

questions.prompt: Why do spring’s flowers and birds initially fail to comfort the departing speaker?
facilitatorNotes: Their abundance cannot restore her denied health or remove the pain of departure. The repeated in vain makes landscape joy and personal feeling diverge.
evidence: I mourn for health deny'd.

questions.prompt: How does the speaker hold her own hope for recovery together with Susannah’s grief?
facilitatorNotes: She imagines Health approaching and wants to see London, yet carefully asks that Susanna not grieve for her. Readers can distinguish affection, reassurance and divided loyalties.
evidence: But let no sighs, no groans for me,

questions.prompt: Why does the poem turn from anticipation of London to resisting Temptation?
facilitatorNotes: The closing stanzas treat travel’s attractive prospects as also requiring moral vigilance. This prevents a purely triumphant departure ending; interpretations should cite both joy and the final shield image.
evidence: But thou, Temptation, hence away!

days.title: The New Colossus
days.challenge: Read the sonnet aloud twice, mark the turn into direct speech, and trace conflicting words for strength and exclusion.
days.focus: A sonnet transforms a monument from a symbol of conquest into a speaking invitation.
days.context: This poem was written for the Statue of Liberty pedestal fundraising effort, as the historical edition’s footnote records. That footnote and its reference marker are omitted from the supplied poem. Read aloud twice and mark the turn from description into direct speech.
days.contentNote: Includes historical language describing displaced and impoverished people as refuse; discuss whose rejection the poem invokes rather than adopting that language.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem; The Poems of Emma Lazarus, vol. I (1889), scan pages 216, 217, printed pages 202, 203. Page URLs: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Page:The_poems_of_Emma_Lazarus_volume_1.djvu/216; https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Page:The_poems_of_Emma_Lazarus_volume_1.djvu/217; opens “THE NEW COLOSSUS. Not like the brazen giant of Greek fame, With”; closes “homeless, tempest-tost to me, I lift my lamp beside the golden door!””.
excerpt.inlineReason: The library text keeps the edition's footnote on THE NEW COLOSSUS. (its reference [2] after the title and the note "Written in aid of Bartholdi Pedestal Fund, 1883." after the poem); this night omits the marker and note, as its edition statement declares, so it keeps its own text.

blocks.text: THE NEW COLOSSUS.

Not like the brazen giant of Greek fame,
With conquering limbs astride from land to land;
Here at our sea-washed, sunset gates shall stand
A mighty woman with a torch, whose flame
Is the imprisoned lightning, and her name
Mother of Exiles. From her beacon-hand
Glows world-wide welcome; her mild eyes command
The air-bridged harbor that twin cities frame.
“Keep, ancient lands, your storied pomp!” cries she
With silent lips. “Give me your tired, your poor,
Your huddled masses yearning to breathe free,
The wretched refuse of your teeming shore.
Send these, the homeless, tempest-tost to me,
I lift my lamp beside the golden door!”

questions.prompt: How does the opening contrast two kinds of power represented by monuments?
facilitatorNotes: The conquering giant is opposed to a torch-bearing woman whose authority welcomes rather than dominates. Attend to the fact that mild eyes still command.
evidence: With conquering limbs astride from land to land;

questions.prompt: What effect does the statue’s direct speech have after eight lines of description?
facilitatorNotes: It gives a silent object a public voice and changes description into invitation and challenge. The apparent contradiction of silent lips is central to the personification.
evidence: With silent lips.

questions.prompt: Who calls the arriving people refuse, and how does the poem challenge or reuse that description?
facilitatorNotes: The quoted invitation adopts the language of rejection to offer welcome; readers may hear compassion alongside troubling social labels. Require attention to the pronouns your and me.
evidence: I lift my lamp beside the golden door!

days.title: Long Island Sound
days.challenge: Reread while marking visual and auditory details, then explain how the last line reframes the whole catalogue.
days.focus: A sensory sonnet considers how attention turns a passing landscape into memory and art.
days.context: The speaker recalls an August afternoon on Long Island Sound. The complete sonnet is supplied; use the reading budget for an initial reading, a voiced rereading and brief annotations.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem; The Poems of Emma Lazarus, vol. I (1889), scan pages 225, 226, printed pages 211, 212. Page URLs: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Page:The_poems_of_Emma_Lazarus_volume_1.djvu/225; https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Page:The_poems_of_Emma_Lazarus_volume_1.djvu/226; opens “LONG ISLAND SOUND. I see it as it looked one afternoon In”; closes “gazed thereon. All these fair sounds and sights I made my own.”.

questions.prompt: What does the opening tell us about whether the landscape is being observed now or remembered?
facilitatorNotes: I see it as it looked makes present imagination recover a specific past afternoon. Discuss how precise details make memory feel immediate.
evidence: I see it as it looked one afternoon

questions.prompt: How do the unseen children and the rippling tide broaden the poem beyond a picture?
facilitatorNotes: Sound supplies life outside the visible frame. The low lisp and laughter make the remembered scene something heard as well as seen.
evidence: Laughter of unseen children, cheerful chirp

questions.prompt: What might the final claim that the speaker made the sights and sounds her own mean?
facilitatorNotes: Possible readings include memory, artistic shaping or emotional possession. Distinguish these from literal ownership of the place and support the reading with the preceding act of gazing.
evidence: All these fair sounds and sights I made my own.

days.title: Pride and Prejudice excerpt: The family answers a refusal
days.challenge: Compare what each parent believes Elizabeth’s interests to be. Reread the narrator’s account of Collins’s hurt pride beside his own language of resignation.
days.focus: Analyze how authority and humor change the balance of a family dispute.
days.context: Elizabeth has refused Collins repeatedly. He assumes she is merely following a convention of modest reluctance; Mrs. Bennet now learns that the refusal is serious and asks her husband to intervene.
days.contentNote: The scene depicts family pressure to accept an unwanted marriage.

excerpt.locator: Pride and Prejudice, Chapter XX, paragraphs 1–35; opens “MR. COLLINS was not left long to the silent contemplation of his”; closes “manner has been at all reprehensible, I here beg leave to apologize.””.

questions.prompt: How does Mr. Bennet turn his wife’s threat into protection for Elizabeth?
facilitatorNotes: He mirrors the threatened loss of a parent but reverses its condition, making refusal the choice he supports. The comic symmetry reassures Elizabeth while exposing the pressure in her mother’s demand.
evidence: I will never see you again if you do.

questions.prompt: What real concern lies beneath Mrs. Bennet’s exaggerated complaint, and what does it fail to justify?
facilitatorNotes: She fears who will support Elizabeth after her father dies. That economic concern is real in this inheritance system, but it does not establish that coercing this particular marriage is right or that Elizabeth cannot judge happiness.
evidence: who is to maintain you when your father is dead

questions.prompt: How does the narrator’s explanation of Collins differ from his final speech?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator identifies imaginary affection and injured pride. Collins recasts withdrawal as duty, resignation, and concern for everyone’s advantage; the mismatch lets readers see self-protection in moral language.
evidence: His regard for her was quite imaginary;

days.title: Pride and Prejudice excerpt: Caroline’s letter and two interpretations
days.challenge: Distinguish Caroline’s stated wishes from her brother’s unreported choices. Compare Jane’s charitable reading and Elizabeth’s strategic reading without treating either as complete knowledge.
days.focus: Evaluate what a letter establishes and what readers infer about its author’s intentions.
days.context: Collins has turned his attention toward Charlotte Lucas after Elizabeth’s refusal. Meanwhile Jane receives a letter from Caroline Bingley announcing that the Netherfield household has left for London. Jane hopes to marry Caroline’s brother.

excerpt.locator: Pride and Prejudice, Chapter XXI, paragraphs 1–28; opens “THE discussion of Mr. Collins’s offer was now nearly at an end,”; closes “a family dinner, she would take care to have two full courses.”.

questions.prompt: What does Caroline’s letter actually establish about Bingley’s future, and what does it merely predict or desire?
facilitatorNotes: It establishes the household’s departure and her wish for a connection with Georgiana. Her certainty about his remaining in London is not a statement from him; Elizabeth correctly distinguishes a sister’s intention from a brother’s decision.
evidence: It is only evident that Miss Bingley does not mean he should.

questions.prompt: How can affectionate language carry an unwelcome message in this letter?
facilitatorNotes: The repeated dear-friend address surrounds news of separation and a rival marriage hope. Students can argue calculated discouragement or tactless confidence, but should explain how the form softens or disguises the impact.
evidence: am I wrong, my dearest Jane, in indulging the hope

questions.prompt: Where does Elizabeth’s attempt to comfort Jane itself become overconfident?
facilitatorNotes: She dismisses the possibility that friends could influence an independent young man. Her insight into Caroline’s interest does not prove Bingley immune to pressure or guarantee his return.
evidence: so totally independent of everyone

days.title: Pride and Prejudice excerpt: Charlotte’s calculation
days.challenge: Separate Charlotte’s stated expectations from Elizabeth’s expectations for her. Reread the narrator’s ironic description of a “disinterested” desire for an establishment.
days.focus: Hold practical necessity and personal cost together in interpreting a choice.
days.context: Charlotte Lucas, Elizabeth’s close friend, has listened patiently to Collins after Elizabeth rejected him. She has little money of her own and limited socially acceptable means of supporting herself. Her attention now has an unexpected result.

excerpt.locator: Pride and Prejudice, Chapter XXII, paragraphs 1–19; opens “THE Bennets were engaged to dine with the Lucases; and again, during”; closes “that friend to be tolerably happy in the lot she had chosen.”.

questions.prompt: What does the apparently accidental meeting in the lane reveal about Charlotte’s agency?
facilitatorNotes: She deliberately places herself in Collins’s path after seeing him arrive. Her constrained economic options do not make her passive; she pursues a practical goal with clear knowledge of the man.
evidence: instantly set out to meet him accidentally in the lane

questions.prompt: Why is marriage described as a “preservative from want,” and how does that phrase limit the promised happiness?
facilitatorNotes: Charlotte understands marriage as financial protection rather than a guarantee of affection. The metaphor frames her choice as prevention of deprivation, helping explain a decision Elizabeth finds degrading.
evidence: their pleasantest preservative from want

questions.prompt: Does Elizabeth understand Charlotte’s reasoning by the end? What separates understanding from agreement here?
facilitatorNotes: Elizabeth knows their views differ but assumes Charlotte cannot be tolerably happy. Readers may share her concern about the match while recognizing that she judges Charlotte through her own requirements rather than Charlotte’s stated aim.
evidence: I ask only a comfortable home;

days.title: Pride and Prejudice excerpt: A match becomes a family grievance
days.challenge: Trace Mrs. Bennet’s successive explanations and the narrator’s compressed passage of time. Ask which observations support her fears and which are interpretations driven by loss.
days.focus: Distinguish a feared future from evidence of another person’s intentions.
days.context: Charlotte’s engagement to Collins is formally announced. Mrs. Bennet had hoped he would marry one of her daughters and keep the future control of their home within that immediate family. Bingley remains away in London.

excerpt.locator: Pride and Prejudice, Chapter XXIII, paragraphs 1–25; opens “ELIZABETH was sitting with her mother and sisters, reflecting on what she”; closes “anybody else?” “I leave it to yourself to determine,” said Mr. Bennet.”.

questions.prompt: How does the numbered list of Mrs. Bennet’s reactions expose contradictions in her thinking?
facilitatorNotes: She disbelieves the match, explains it as deception, wishes unhappiness, and hopes it will end. The list gives orderly form to mutually shifting claims, all returning to her sense of injury.
evidence: In the first place, she persisted in disbelieving the whole of the matter;

questions.prompt: What happens to Elizabeth and Charlotte’s friendship when Elizabeth cannot accept the marriage?
facilitatorNotes: Mutual silence replaces confidence. Elizabeth turns more intensely toward Jane; the cost of judgment is thus relational, not only an opinion about Collins. Students can discuss whether the silence is protective or damaging.
evidence: a restraint which kept them mutually silent on the subject

questions.prompt: How does the narration separate Mrs. Bennet’s fear of displacement from proof of Charlotte’s plans?
facilitatorNotes: It repeatedly frames hostile interpretations as what Mrs. Bennet regards, concludes, and is convinced of. The entail makes displacement conceivable, but the low-voiced conversations do not establish a plot.
evidence: she concluded her to be anticipating the hour of possession

days.title: Pride and Prejudice excerpt: Kind intentions and harmful effects
days.challenge: Follow the shifts from Jane’s hurt to Charlotte’s situation and back to Bingley. Reread both sisters’ strongest claims and identify a limitation in each rather than choosing a wholly correct sister.
days.focus: Assess an argument about responsibility that separates intention from consequence.
days.context: A second letter confirms that the Bingleys will remain in London. Jane tries to accept disappointment without blaming anyone; Elizabeth suspects interference. Their disagreement expands to Charlotte’s marriage and the possibility of causing harm without intending it.

excerpt.locator: Pride and Prejudice, Chapter XXIV, paragraphs 1–31; opens “MISS BINGLEY’S letter arrived, and put an end to doubt. The very”; closes “by everybody else Mr. Darcy was condemned as the worst of men.”.
