questions.prompt: How does Jane explain her disappointment in a way that protects Bingley? What does that explanation cost her?
facilitatorNotes: She calls it an error of her own imagination and claims no one else has been harmed. This preserves goodwill but assigns the misunderstanding to herself and may hide the depth of her pain.
evidence: an error of fancy on my side

questions.prompt: What principle does Elizabeth defend when she says harm can occur “without scheming”?
facilitatorNotes: She distinguishes malicious intention from thoughtlessness, insensitivity, or weak resolve. A person can be responsible for consequences without deliberately plotting them; whether her diagnosis of Bingley is established remains a separate issue.
evidence: without scheming to do wrong, or to make others unhappy, there may be error and there may be misery

questions.prompt: Why is the community’s final condemnation of Darcy a warning about shared certainty?
facilitatorNotes: The neighbors enjoy seeing an old dislike apparently justified by Wickham’s story. Repetition and agreement add social force but no new firsthand evidence; Jane alone leaves room for unknown circumstances.
evidence: everybody was pleased to think how much they had always disliked Mr. Darcy

days.title: Narrative excerpt: seeking protection and resisting Covey
days.challenge: Follow a long episode through changing locations and distinguish what the narrator observes, infers, and retrospectively explains.
days.focus: The failure of an appeal to authority and the unexpected reversal of a power relationship.
days.context: The passage recounts Douglass’s collapse while working for Covey, his attempt to obtain protection from Thomas Auld, Sandy Jenkins’s advice, and the subsequent struggle with Covey.
days.contentNote: Sustained accounts of severe beating, blood, physical injury, and self-defense; a historical account rather than a model for reenactment.

excerpt.locator: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, Chapter X, consecutive paragraphs; opens “I have already intimated that my condition was much worse, during the”; closes “need not; for you will come off worse than you did before.””.

questions.prompt: How does Thomas Auld’s reference to losing a year’s wages answer Douglass’s request for protection?
facilitatorNotes: It redirects a plea about survival into a property-and-contract calculation. Compare the narrator’s injured condition with Auld’s concern for the financial arrangement.
evidence: he would lose the whole year's wages

questions.prompt: Does the passage establish that Sandy’s root causes Covey’s changed conduct?
facilitatorNotes: No. Douglass begins skeptical, briefly considers the possibility, and notes the alternative significance of Sunday. The later confrontation changes the conditions more clearly; distinguish sequence from demonstrated cause.
evidence: had it been on any other day than Sunday

questions.prompt: Why include Bill’s refusal to help Covey?
facilitatorNotes: His reply draws a limit around the work for which he was hired and deprives Covey of expected support. The scene reveals that the outcome involves others’ choices as well as the two combatants.
evidence: his master hired him out to work, and not to help to whip me

days.title: Narrative excerpt: freedom “in form” and “in fact”
days.challenge: Separate psychological transformation, continued legal status, and a tentative explanation of another person’s motives.
days.focus: A turning point whose meaning exceeds its immediate legal consequences.
days.context: After resisting Covey, Douglass explains why he regards the struggle as a turning point. He remains legally enslaved for several more years.
days.contentNote: Refers to whipping, violent resistance, and the risk of death; retains the historical term used for Covey’s reputation.

excerpt.locator: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, Chapter X, consecutive paragraphs; opens “This battle with Mr. Covey was the turning-point in my career as”; closes “lost; so, to save his reputation, he suffered me to go unpunished.”.

questions.prompt: What distinction does Douglass make between remaining enslaved “in form” and being enslaved “in fact”?
facilitatorNotes: His legal position has not changed, but his self-understanding and willingness to submit have. Do not read the assertion as a claim that the material dangers disappear.
evidence: however long I might remain a slave in form

questions.prompt: How do the ember and resurrection images develop the turning point?
facilitatorNotes: Both describe something apparently extinguished or buried returning to life. They make restored self-confidence a rebirth, and students may compare the quiet rekindling with the more dramatic resurrection.
evidence: It rekindled the few expiring embers of freedom

questions.prompt: How certain is his explanation for Covey’s failure to seek official punishment?
facilitatorNotes: He explicitly presents it as an unsatisfying inference about reputation, not witnessed knowledge. That qualification invites attention to the limits of retrospective explanation.
evidence: does not entirely satisfy me

days.title: Narrative excerpt: holidays and counterfeit liberty
days.challenge: Distinguish a practice’s stated benevolent purpose from the mechanism the narrator argues it serves.
days.focus: Control through excess and the manipulation of what freedom appears to mean.
days.context: At the end of his year with Covey, Douglass examines the holiday period between Christmas and New Year’s Day, using it as evidence about the institution’s methods.
days.contentNote: Alcohol abuse, coercive feeding, whipping, and racist ownership language are discussed as historical practices.

excerpt.locator: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, Chapter X, consecutive paragraphs; opens “My term of actual service to Mr. Edward Covey ended on Christmas”; closes “cases I have cited sufficient. The practice is a very common one.”.

questions.prompt: Why call the holidays “safety-valves” rather than simply rest?
facilitatorNotes: The mechanical image makes the break a way to release pressure that might threaten the system. It assigns the practice a controlling function despite its appearance as a gift.
evidence: These holidays serve as conductors, or safety-valves

questions.prompt: What distinction does Douglass insist on between liberty and the behavior encouraged during these holidays?
facilitatorNotes: He distinguishes self-directed freedom from imposed or encouraged dissipation. The institution falsely labels an exhausting excess as liberty so that returning to work can seem welcome.
evidence: artfully labelled with the name of liberty

questions.prompt: How do the molasses and extra-food examples support the holiday argument?
facilitatorNotes: Each gives a desired thing in an abusive form until it becomes repellent. The examples claim a shared mechanism; readers may assess how well these observations support the wider generalization.
evidence: by allowing him to see only the abuse of it

days.title: Narrative excerpt: teaching and solidarity
days.challenge: Trace the relation between emotional language, dangerous collective action, and a rebuttal to a general claim.
days.focus: Learning as mutual commitment rather than an individual achievement alone.
days.context: While working under William Freeland, Douglass holds a clandestine Sabbath school and teaches fellow enslaved people during winter evenings.
days.contentNote: Threats of whipping for learning, enslavement, and references to oppression in religious language.

excerpt.locator: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, Chapter X, consecutive paragraphs; opens “I held my Sabbath school at the house of a free colored”; closes “hardships to which we were necessarily subjected by our condition as slaves.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Douglass withhold the host’s name even though the school met ten years earlier?
facilitatorNotes: Publication can still expose someone to danger. The omission is part of responsible testimony, and the ironic reference to the “crime” highlights the injustice of banning education.
evidence: whose name I deem it imprudent to mention

questions.prompt: What evidence distinguishes the students’ motives from a desire for popularity or status?
facilitatorNotes: They risk punishment and attend because they want to learn; the account explicitly rules out social approval. Their persistence gives force to the starvation and darkness metaphors.
evidence: They came because they wished to learn.

questions.prompt: How does the final paragraph answer the claim that enslaved people do not trust one another?
facilitatorNotes: Douglass counters with specific collective practices, including consultation and refusal to act separately. His testimony presents bonds under pressure, not the absence of personhood assumed by the stereotype.
evidence: We never undertook to do any thing, of any importance, without a mutual consultation.

days.title: Narrative excerpt: preparing the canoe escape
days.challenge: Read a quoted document inside a memoir while tracking the difference between its claimed destination and the group’s actual plan.
days.focus: Literacy, coordinated decision-making, and concealment under a pass system.
days.context: Douglass and several companions plan an escape by canoe before Easter in 1835. Sandy has withdrawn from the plan but continues to encourage them. The quoted protections are documents Douglass says he wrote for the attempt.
days.contentNote: Enslavement, restricted movement, danger of capture, and historically necessary concealment; the excerpt is not a present-day procedural assignment.

excerpt.locator: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, Chapter X, consecutive paragraphs; opens “Sandy, one of our number, gave up the notion, but still encouraged”; closes “feelings as much as possible; and I think we succeeded very well.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the group choose the water route over the land route?
facilitatorNotes: They expect to be mistaken for fishermen and encounter fewer demands to explain their movement. The comparison reveals the unequal surveillance built into the environment.
evidence: we hoped to be regarded as fishermen

questions.prompt: How does the protection’s stated destination differ from the group’s intention, and why does the distinction matter?
facilitatorNotes: The document claims permission for Baltimore, while the actual aim is freedom beyond Maryland. It is designed to cover only the part of the journey during which the routes align.
evidence: We were not going to Baltimore

questions.prompt: How does Douglass’s account of his own encouragement balance confidence and anxiety?
facilitatorNotes: His energetic persuasion does not erase the hazard; the group renews its pledge while concealing intense feelings. A strong response distinguishes the confidence needed to act from certainty of success.
evidence: We tried to conceal our feelings as much as possible

days.title: Success
days.challenge: Reread the sonnet’s opening qualification, public commands and final contrast; evaluate the rhetoric rather than simply agreeing with its ideal.
days.focus: An emphatic celebration of achievement is complicated by its deliberate exclusions.
days.context: The complete sonnet is supplied. Read aloud, annotate the language of public celebration, then revisit the speaker’s acknowledged decision to ignore defeat.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem; The Poems of Emma Lazarus, vol. I (1889), scan pages 216, printed pages 202. Page URLs: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Page:The_poems_of_Emma_Lazarus_volume_1.djvu/216; opens “SUCCESS. Oft have I brooded on defeat and pain, The pathos of”; closes “’Midst flippant, feeble crowds of spectres wan, The bold, significant, successful man.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker tell us about earlier attention to defeat before announcing today’s song?
facilitatorNotes: The opening makes the praise a chosen change of emphasis, rather than proof that pain has disappeared. The temporary to-day qualifies the celebration.
evidence: These I ignore to-day and only long

questions.prompt: What do the trumpet and choral voice images ask a reader to do?
facilitatorNotes: They turn private admiration into shared audible celebration; the commands rejoice and salute recruit an audience.
evidence: Salute him with free heart and choral voice,

questions.prompt: Does the successful man’s contrast with the crowd strengthen or trouble the poem’s praise?
facilitatorNotes: Both responses can be defended: it magnifies persistence, but labels others as feeble spectres. Require readers to notice the poem’s cost to those outside its ideal.
evidence: The bold, significant, successful man.

days.title: Critic and Poet
days.challenge: Read the prose premise alongside the sonnet; map critic, rule and poet onto the fable without reducing it to an anti-science slogan.
days.focus: A fable exposes a definition that refuses to learn from the thing it claims to explain.
days.context: An apologue is a short illustrative fable. The prose epigraph belongs to the historical poem and is included; it frames the naturalist’s encounter as a problem in literary judgment.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem; The Poems of Emma Lazarus, vol. I (1889), scan pages 229, printed pages 215. Page URLs: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Page:The_poems_of_Emma_Lazarus_volume_1.djvu/229; opens “CRITIC AND POET. AN APOLOGUE. (“Poetry must be simple, sensuous, or impassioned;”; closes “my line, Were it a bird, ’t would answer to my law.””.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with the naturalist’s method before the nightingale arrives?
facilitatorNotes: He treats an existing definition as a fixed limit on what a bird can be. Observation is subordinated to classification rather than allowed to revise it.
evidence: To classify by rote and book,

questions.prompt: How does the naturalist protect his rule after hearing the bird?
facilitatorNotes: He denies that the observed creature is a bird instead of admitting the rule’s inadequacy. Connect his explicit refusal of error to the final conditional claim.
evidence: Were it a bird, ’t would answer to my law.”

questions.prompt: How does the prefatory argument connect the bird fable to criticism of poetry?
facilitatorNotes: The syllogism predetermines the category poet just as the naturalist predetermines bird. Readers can discuss how new art tests old criteria rather than assuming all criteria are useless.
evidence: therefore he is not a poet.

days.title: Life and Art
days.challenge: Reread its temporal signals and the shift from general poet to first-person speaker; distinguish a literary claim from a universal psychological rule.
days.focus: The sonnet argues that artistic expression may follow, rather than coincide with, overwhelming experience.
days.context: The Muse is a personification of artistic inspiration. This poem supplies its own account of how feeling becomes art; no biographical incident is needed to discuss it.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem; The Poems of Emma Lazarus, vol. I (1889), scan pages 230, 231, printed pages 216, 217. Page URLs: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Page:The_poems_of_Emma_Lazarus_volume_1.djvu/230; https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Page:The_poems_of_Emma_Lazarus_volume_1.djvu/231; opens “LIFE AND ART. Not while the fever of the blood is strong,”; closes “kiss his brow. Then his lips ope to sing—as mine do now.”.

questions.prompt: Why is the Muse absent when feeling is most intense?
facilitatorNotes: The poem distinguishes living an experience from shaping it into song. Its claim is not that intense experience lacks value: life itself is called the poem at that moment.
evidence: Life is his poem then;

questions.prompt: What changes at the turn beginning But when the dream is done?
facilitatorNotes: The imagery moves from strong pulse and full strings to failure, twilight and solitude. Distance from experience creates the opening for a new kind of expression.
evidence: But when the dream is done, the pulses fail,

questions.prompt: How do the final words as mine do now affect the apparently general claim about poets?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker discloses a present instance of the process being described. This makes the account self-reflective and personal, though readers need not identify the speaker directly with the author’s biography.
evidence: Then his lips ope to sing—as mine do now.

days.title: Sympathy
days.challenge: Trace shifts in pronouns and the boundary of the quoted voice; reread images that hold similarity and distance together.
days.focus: A poem about private imperfection constructs an answering voice and a shared relationship.
days.context: The sonnet imagines a reader responding to the speaker’s disclosure. Its images of cross, rose and thorn present pain and relief through figurative language.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem; The Poems of Emma Lazarus, vol. I (1889), scan pages 231, printed pages 217. Page URLs: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Page:The_poems_of_Emma_Lazarus_volume_1.djvu/231; opens “SYMPATHY. Therefore I dare reveal my private woe, The secret blots of”; closes “my soul’s need can understand, Stretching o’er silent gulfs her sister hand.””.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker promise neither to beautify nor hide her faults?
facilitatorNotes: Disclosure is offered as a basis for recognition, not an exhibition of perfection. The promise joins honesty with an appeal to a reader who shares weakness.
evidence: Nor beautify nor hide.

questions.prompt: What changes when the poem gives the imagined reader a quoted response?
facilitatorNotes: The reader becomes a speaking partner rather than a silent audience. Private suffering is reframed as shared, and the poem performs the connection it proposes.
evidence: Not I alone am weak, not I apart

questions.prompt: How does the final sister hand alter the image of silent gulfs?
facilitatorNotes: The gulfs preserve distance and separation, while a reaching hand proposes connection across them. Accept readings of literary, emotional or communal solidarity grounded in both images.
evidence: Stretching o’er silent gulfs her sister hand.”

days.title: Influence
days.challenge: Track who can see or know each detail and distinguish the narrator’s arrangement from the characters’ evidence.
days.focus: A sonnet joins two partial viewpoints to make unseen care legible to a reader.
days.context: The poem presents a religious observer and a skeptical poet in separate places. Its interest lies in the relation between their viewpoints, not in identifying a real historical pair.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem; The Poems of Emma Lazarus, vol. I (1889), scan pages 234, 235, printed pages 220, 221. Page URLs: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Page:The_poems_of_Emma_Lazarus_volume_1.djvu/234; https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Page:The_poems_of_Emma_Lazarus_volume_1.djvu/235; opens “INFLUENCE. The fervent, pale-faced Mother ere she sleep, Looks out upon the”; closes “and knows not whence Falls this unwonted peace on heart and sense.”.

questions.prompt: How does the earthly star connect the two people in the poem?
facilitatorNotes: The tower light gives the praying observer a sign of a real person beneath the larger sky. The metaphor links her cosmic vision to a particular act of attention.
evidence: High in the tower, an earthly star of even.

questions.prompt: What do the Mother and the poet each know, and what remains unavailable to them?
facilitatorNotes: She sees a tired watcher and prays; he experiences peace without knowing its source. The narrator supplies both perspectives, so readers should distinguish narration from either character’s knowledge.
evidence: He the shrewd, skeptic poet unaware

questions.prompt: Does the poem settle the cause of the poet’s peace, or invite readers to consider a possible connection?
facilitatorNotes: Its arrangement strongly suggests influence, but the poet himself cannot verify a cause. Discuss how dramatic irony and the title guide inference without demanding agreement with a religious explanation.
evidence: Feels comforted and stilled, and knows not whence

days.title: Pride and Prejudice excerpt: Charlotte at home
days.challenge: Compare the home Collins performs for visitors with the home Charlotte quietly organizes. Notice how Elizabeth recognizes management and contentment without suddenly admiring the marriage.
days.focus: Reassess an earlier prediction in light of observed daily arrangements.
days.context: Several months later, Charlotte is married to Collins. Elizabeth visits their parsonage at Hunsford with Charlotte’s father and sister. The intervening chapters have included Jane’s stay in London and plans for Elizabeth’s journey; this selection begins their arrival.

excerpt.locator: Pride and Prejudice, Chapter XXVIII, paragraphs 1–20; opens “EVERY object in the next day’s journey was new and interesting to”; closes “the whole party was asked to dine at Rosings the next day.”.

questions.prompt: What does Collins’s tour reveal about the difference between counting possessions and appreciating a place?
facilitatorNotes: His detailed enumeration leaves little room for guests’ impressions; the narrator says minuteness leaves beauty behind. The view of Rosings matters most to him because it displays patronage and status.
evidence: a minuteness which left beauty entirely behind

questions.prompt: How does Charlotte create room for comfort within a marriage Elizabeth dislikes?
facilitatorNotes: She encourages gardening, avoids hearing some remarks, arranges the house, and enjoys showing it without him. These are practical accommodations; readers may interpret them as resourcefulness, a cost, or both.
evidence: When Mr. Collins could be forgotten, there was really a great air of comfort

questions.prompt: How does the excitement over the visitors at the gate expose different measures of importance?
facilitatorNotes: Maria and Sir William respond to rank as spectacle; Elizabeth expected an actual disturbance and notices discourtesy in keeping Charlotte outside. Her response punctures the social awe without proving her own judgments always fair.
evidence: I expected at least that the pigs were got into the garden

days.title: Pride and Prejudice excerpt: Dinner at Rosings
days.challenge: Follow who asks questions, who may answer briefly, and who claims the right to pronounce judgments. Track Elizabeth’s composure through intrusive questions about money, education, and age.
days.focus: Study how rank becomes conversational authority and how that authority is resisted.
days.context: Elizabeth and the Collins household dine with Lady Catherine, their wealthy neighbor and Collins’s patroness. Collins has prepared the visitors to be overwhelmed. Being “out” means taking part in adult social gatherings.

excerpt.locator: Pride and Prejudice, Chapter XXIX, paragraphs 1–42; opens “MR. COLLINS’S triumph, in consequence of this invitation, was complete. The power”; closes “very soon obliged to take her Ladyship’s praise into his own hands.”.

questions.prompt: How does Collins’s clothing advice define the kind of welcome guests should expect?
facilitatorNotes: He reassures Elizabeth that plain clothing is acceptable because Lady Catherine wants distinctions of rank preserved. The apparent kindness maintains hierarchy rather than making guests forget it.
evidence: She likes to have the distinction of rank preserved.

questions.prompt: What does Elizabeth concede about her education, and what assumption does she challenge?
facilitatorNotes: She admits less supervision than some families and room for idleness, yet says interested learners had books and masters. She challenges Lady Catherine’s certainty that one prescribed arrangement is the only possible education.
evidence: such of us as wished to learn never wanted the means

questions.prompt: Why is the closing description of Lady Catherine determining the weather comic?
facilitatorNotes: Her habit of issuing instructions extends rhetorically to something she cannot control. The narration compresses her self-importance into the form of an ordinary social forecast treated like a decree.
evidence: hear Lady Catherine determine what weather they were to have on the morrow

days.title: Pride and Prejudice excerpt: The arrangement of a quiet life
days.challenge: Map the rooms and paths that allow privacy. Then distinguish what Elizabeth observes during Darcy’s visit from what she hopes his reaction will reveal.
days.focus: Read domestic space and routine as evidence of power and adaptation.
days.context: Elizabeth’s visit at Hunsford settles into a routine. Charlotte manages life with Collins and their demanding patroness. Darcy arrives at Rosings with his cousin, Colonel Fitzwilliam; Jane is still in London after Bingley’s departure.

excerpt.locator: Pride and Prejudice, Chapter XXX, paragraphs 1–12; opens “SIR WILLIAM stayed only a week at Hunsford; but his visit was”; closes “subject was pursued no further, and the gentlemen soon afterwards went away.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Charlotte choose the less attractive room for the women’s daily use?
facilitatorNotes: The better room keeps Collins occupied in his own apartment; Charlotte trades a pleasant view for greater independence. Elizabeth’s changed assessment shows her learning to read the practical purpose of an arrangement.
evidence: Mr. Collins would undoubtedly have been much less in his own apartment

questions.prompt: What criticism is compressed into “scold them into harmony and plenty”?
facilitatorNotes: The phrase exposes the fantasy that authority and rebuke can remedy conflict or poverty. Lady Catherine treats being poor as a condition to correct by discipline, while the ironic wording reveals the inadequacy of that response.
evidence: scold them into harmony and plenty

questions.prompt: What makes Elizabeth’s question about Jane a test rather than a simple request for information?
facilitatorNotes: She already believes Darcy has not seen Jane and watches for awareness of the separation from Bingley. The reported slight confusion is an interpreted sign, not yet a confession of involvement.
evidence: she wished to see whether he would betray any consciousness

days.title: Pride and Prejudice excerpt: Practice at the pianoforte
days.challenge: Listen for several meanings of performance: playing music, speaking to strangers, and presenting a social self. Reread the analogy Elizabeth makes without assuming it settles every difference in temperament.
days.focus: Compare claims of natural ability with the work of practice in music and sociability.
days.context: At Rosings, Elizabeth talks and plays music with Colonel Fitzwilliam nearby. Darcy joins them. Lady Catherine claims expert taste despite never having learned to play, and repeatedly directs the conversation.

excerpt.locator: Pride and Prejudice, Chapter XXXI, paragraphs 1–30; opens “COLONEL FITZWILLIAM’S manners were very much admired at the Parsonage, and the”; closes “instrument till her Ladyship’s carriage was ready to take them all home.”.

questions.prompt: How do Lady Catherine’s claims about herself and Anne undermine her advice about practice?
facilitatorNotes: She insists that excellence needs constant practice yet confidently awards hypothetical excellence to herself and her daughter without it. The inconsistency exposes rank-based entitlement to praise.
evidence: If I had ever learnt, I should have been a great proficient.

questions.prompt: How does Elizabeth use her own imperfect playing to answer Darcy’s account of social difficulty?
facilitatorNotes: She attributes her limitations to insufficient practice and implies that conversation likewise requires effort. Students may see a useful challenge while noting that temperament and musical technique are not identical.
evidence: because I would not take the trouble of practising

questions.prompt: What makes Darcy’s statement that neither performs to strangers both a connection and an evasion?
facilitatorNotes: It groups them together and compliments her playing, softening criticism. It also redirects the question of whether his reserved behavior is changeable; the exchange sustains ambiguity rather than ending in a verdict.
evidence: We neither of us perform to strangers.

days.title: Pride and Prejudice excerpt: A visit with no clear explanation
days.challenge: Reread the discussion of distance through both characters’ economic situations. Keep a list of observable actions and the competing motives Elizabeth or Charlotte assigns them.
days.focus: Interpret ambiguous behavior without turning a plausible explanation into a fact.
days.context: Darcy calls at the parsonage and unexpectedly finds Elizabeth alone. Their conversation turns from Bingley to Charlotte’s marriage and the distance from home. Charlotte later tries to interpret Darcy’s repeated visits.

excerpt.locator: Pride and Prejudice, Chapter XXXII, paragraphs 1–31; opens “ELIZABETH was sitting by herself the next morning, and writing to Jane,”; closes “patronage in the church, and his cousin could have none at all.”.

questions.prompt: Why do Elizabeth and Darcy initially disagree about whether fifty miles is near?
facilitatorNotes: Darcy treats a good road and half-day journey as sufficient; Elizabeth adds the cost and frequency a modest income permits. Distance is not only geographical but experienced through resources.
evidence: The far and the near must be relative

questions.prompt: How does Elizabeth’s reading of Darcy’s smile limit her understanding of the conversation?
facilitatorNotes: She assumes he alludes to Jane and Netherfield, while his movement closer and questions about her attachment permit other readings. The narration explicitly marks her interpretation as something she fancied she understood.
evidence: a sort of smile, which Elizabeth fancied she understood

questions.prompt: What makes Charlotte’s investigation inconclusive despite repeated observation?
facilitatorNotes: Looking, visiting, and silence can fit attraction, awkwardness, or distraction. Charlotte’s wish for a good match guides her attention, but the expression remains disputable; observation alone does not eliminate ambiguity.
evidence: the expression of that look was disputable

days.title: Narrative excerpt: the morning of arrest
days.challenge: Follow suspense created by incomplete knowledge and compare a character’s certainty with what the scene actually reveals.
days.focus: Solidarity, constrained speech, and the struggle over evidence during capture.
days.context: On the morning before the planned canoe escape, Douglass and his companions are working as usual when he fears the plan has been betrayed.
days.contentNote: Arrest, gun threats, assault, profanity, and racist insults occur in the historical dialogue.

excerpt.locator: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, Chapter X, consecutive paragraphs; opens “After a painful waiting, the Saturday morning, whose night was to witness”; closes “So we were not yet convicted of the intention to run away.”.

questions.prompt: How does the scene build suspense after Douglass says he is certain they have been betrayed?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator’s fear is definite, but the approaching riders and hurried movements are observed without a full explanation. The step-by-step arrival makes readers share the delay before arrest.
evidence: I was not yet certain as to what the matter was.

questions.prompt: What does Henry’s refusal contribute to the scene beyond delaying the constables?
facilitatorNotes: His dialogue asserts agency under a threat intended to remove it. Readers can discuss the cost and force of that defiance without assuming everyone must respond identically under violence.
evidence: I won't be tied!

questions.prompt: What does Betsy Freeland’s speech assume about Henry and John, and how does that contrast with the group’s planning?
facilitatorNotes: She blames Douglass as the source of their desire for freedom, denying their own thought and commitment. Her biscuits and accusations divide people the narrative has shown acting together.
evidence: Henry nor John would never have thought of such a thing.

days.title: Narrative excerpt: separation in prison
days.challenge: Track the shifting meaning of togetherness and the narrator’s qualified explanations for decisions made by others.
days.focus: Why release for some can intensify suffering for the person left behind.
days.context: After the escape plan is discovered, the group is taken toward St. Michael’s and then to Easton jail. They try to avoid supplying evidence against one another.
days.contentNote: Imprisonment, threatened sale, racial exploitation, and forced separation.

excerpt.locator: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, Chapter X, consecutive paragraphs; opens “When we got about half way to St. Michael's, while the constables”; closes “great prejudice in the community, and he feared I might be killed.”.

questions.prompt: Why does “Own nothing” represent solidarity as well as a response to questioning?
facilitatorNotes: In this usage it means admit nothing. The repeated pledge protects the group and shows their commitment continuing after the plan fails.
evidence: Our confidence in each other was unshaken.

questions.prompt: Why does the relatively clean jail not make the account a simple story of improved circumstances?
facilitatorNotes: Material conditions are described separately from the danger of sale and separation. When the others leave, isolation becomes the most painful part of the experience.
evidence: It caused me more pain than any thing else in the whole transaction.

questions.prompt: Which parts of the explanation for leaving Douglass behind are presented as inference rather than certainty?
facilitatorNotes: He says “I supposed” about the owners’ reasoning and later admits not knowing why Alabama is abandoned as a destination. Those limits distinguish his fears and interpretations from verified decisions.
evidence: But, from some cause or other, he did not send me to Alabama

days.title: Narrative excerpt: wages without ownership
days.challenge: Follow the shift from narrative about skilled work to a tightly structured argument about right and power.
days.focus: The difference between improved conditions and freedom to own the product of one’s labor.
days.context: After violence at a previous shipyard, Douglass learns calking at another yard and begins finding work and negotiating wages himself, while remaining enslaved.
days.contentNote: Enslavement, earlier injury, and compelled surrender of earnings are discussed.

excerpt.locator: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, Chapter X, consecutive paragraphs; opens “Master Hugh, finding he could get no redress, refused to let me”; closes “of the grim-visaged pirate upon the high seas is exactly the same.”.

questions.prompt: Why does improved work and leisure increase rather than reduce the desire for freedom?
facilitatorNotes: Reduced immediate danger leaves room to think about rights and possibilities. Douglass uses this experience to reject the assumption that comfort produces legitimate contentment with enslavement.
evidence: it only increased my desire to be free

questions.prompt: How does the sequence “contracted,” “earned,” “paid,” and “rightfully” build the claim about wages?
facilitatorNotes: It establishes each ordinary basis for ownership before the sentence turns to compelled surrender. The parallel clauses make the reversal conspicuous.
evidence: I contracted for it; I earned it; it was paid to me; it was rightfully my own

questions.prompt: What work does the pirate comparison do at the end?
facilitatorNotes: It strips the transaction of a lawful or moral appearance and identifies force as its only basis. A response should connect the analogy to the preceding rejected reasons, not merely call it insulting.
evidence: solely because he had the power to compel me to give it up

days.title: Narrative excerpt: what an escape narrative must withhold
days.challenge: Evaluate a narrator’s reasons for intentional omission and the competing interests of audience, witnesses, and future escapees.
days.focus: The ethics and consequences of publishing information.
days.context: At the start of chapter XI, Douglass announces his successful escape but explains why he will not disclose every circumstance.
days.contentNote: Discusses enslavement, recapture, persecution, and figurative threats of violence.

excerpt.locator: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, Chapter XI, consecutive paragraphs; opens “I NOW come to that part of my life during which I”; closes “and for which no one can be made to suffer but myself.”.

questions.prompt: What two kinds of harm justify withholding the details of escape?
facilitatorNotes: Disclosure might expose helpers and alert enslavers to routes still available to others. His argument weighs ongoing consequences against the reader’s curiosity and his own wish to tell the story.
evidence: guarding a door whereby some dear brother bondman might escape

questions.prompt: How does “upperground railroad” sharpen his criticism without denying helpers’ courage?
facilitatorNotes: The wordplay points to the contradiction between a clandestine purpose and public declarations. He explicitly honors courage while questioning a tactic’s effect on those still seeking freedom.
evidence: the upperground railroad

questions.prompt: What happens to the usual positive association of enlightenment in this passage?
facilitatorNotes: Information becomes dangerous when it enlightens the enslaver rather than the person escaping. The final light metaphor asks readers to judge knowledge by whom it helps in this context.
evidence: let us not hold the light by which he can trace the footprints of our flying brother

days.title: Narrative excerpt: revising beliefs in New Bedford
days.challenge: Distinguish observed evidence, reported incidents, broad comparisons, and the limits of an initial impression.
days.focus: A free labor economy challenges old assumptions, while racial exclusion complicates the new beginning.
days.context: After escaping and reaching New Bedford with his wife, Douglass compares the town with the places he knew while enslaved and seeks paid work. The source retains an asterisk marking an author’s note outside this selected passage.
days.contentNote: Includes historical racial language, threatened violence against an informer, kidnapping fears, and discrimination in employment.

excerpt.locator: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, Chapter XI, consecutive paragraphs; opens “I was quite disappointed at the general appearance of things in New”; closes “years in New Bedford, before I became known to the anti-slavery world.”.

questions.prompt: What belief about wealth is overturned by the wharves and warehouses?
facilitatorNotes: He had assumed that wealth and refinement required enslaved labor. Productive, orderly work without whipping provides evidence against that belief, though it remains his observed comparison rather than a complete economic survey.
evidence: in the absence of slaves, there could be no wealth

questions.prompt: How does Nathan Johnson’s example challenge the idea that manual labor and informed judgment are incompatible?
facilitatorNotes: Johnson’s hardened hands coexist with newspapers, hospitality, and knowledge of national affairs. The specific household counters a class-based assumption about refinement.
evidence: Yet Mr. Johnson was a working man.

questions.prompt: Why does the final paragraph contain both joy and a barrier to the trade Douglass has learned?
facilitatorNotes: Owning his earnings changes work’s meaning, but white calkers refuse to work alongside him. The distinction prevents readers from mistaking escape from slavery for the disappearance of racism.
evidence: such was the strength of prejudice against color

days.title: The Raven
days.challenge: Read the full poem, then reread three exchanges to track the speaker’s interpretation separately from what the bird actually says.
days.focus: A fixed refrain gains destructive meaning through the grieving speaker’s changing questions.
days.context: The speaker mourns Lenore. Pallas evokes wisdom; nepenthe is imagined relief from sorrow; the mythological and biblical references intensify his search for consolation.
days.contentNote: Bereavement, despair and frightening supernatural imagery; no graphic violence.

excerpt.locator: The Raven; complete poem in The Raven and Other Poems (1845); https://www.eapoe.org/works/poems/ravenj.htm; opens “ONCE upon a midnight dreary, while I pondered, weak and weary, Over”; closes “shadow that lies floating on the floor Shall be lifted — nevermore!”.

questions.prompt: What explanation does the speaker offer for the raven’s one word before treating it as prophecy?
facilitatorNotes: He imagines a previous master taught a stock phrase. Compare that plausible account with the increasingly personal questions he then chooses to ask.
evidence: what it utters is its only stock and store

questions.prompt: How does Nevermore change its effect while remaining the same word?
facilitatorNotes: It moves from an odd name or learned response to denial of relief and reunion. The speaker’s questions create much of its apparent meaning.
evidence: Though its answer little meaning — little relevancy bore;

questions.prompt: Why does the ending shift from events in the chamber to the speaker’s soul and the shadow?
facilitatorNotes: The image makes grief enduring and internal, whether the bird is read literally or symbolically. Require attention to the shadow’s persistence rather than a single supernatural explanation.
evidence: And my soul from out that shadow that lies floating on the floor

days.title: The Valley of Unrest
days.challenge: Reread to distinguish the stated history from suggested causes; annotate repetitions that turn natural description into mourning.
days.focus: An emptied landscape expresses unresolved human loss through unnatural movement.
days.context: This is the complete 1845 poem. Compare its former quiet with its present motion, without treating the imagined valley as a documented place.
days.contentNote: War, a grave and mourning are referenced without graphic description.

excerpt.locator: The Valley of Unrest; complete poem in The Raven and Other Poems (1845); https://www.eapoe.org/works/poems/valleye.htm; opens “Once it smiled a silent dell Where the people did not dwell;”; closes “weep: — from off their delicate stems Perennial tears descend in gems.”.

questions.prompt: What difference does the move from Once to Now establish?
facilitatorNotes: A formerly quiet dell becomes restless after its people leave for war. Do not invent their fate beyond what the grave and absence suggest.
evidence: They had gone unto the wars,

questions.prompt: Why does the poem insist that no wind moves the trees and clouds?
facilitatorNotes: It removes an ordinary physical explanation and makes the motion uncanny or emotionally charged. The landscape seems to enact grief.
evidence: Ah, by no wind are stirred those trees

questions.prompt: How do the eye-like violets and weeping lilies make human absence present?
facilitatorNotes: Personification and visual analogy transfer watching and mourning to flowers. Readers may see remembrance or haunting, supported by the nameless grave.
evidence: And weep above a nameless grave!

days.title: Bridal Ballad
days.challenge: Read each stanza aloud and identify the subject of happy now each time; notice how the refrain’s certainty erodes.
days.focus: A repeated assurance unravels through the conflict between public ceremony and private grief.
days.context: The dramatic speaker is a bride haunted by a former lover’s death in battle. The poem supplies a troubled voice, not a reliable report of a supernatural event.
days.contentNote: Bereavement, guilt and marital distress.

excerpt.locator: Bridal Ballad; complete poem in The Raven and Other Poems (1845); https://www.eapoe.org/works/poems/bridale.htm; opens “THE ring is on my hand, And the wreath is on my”; closes “— Lest the dead who is forsaken May not be happy now.”.

questions.prompt: Which early objects seem intended to prove happiness, and why is that proof unstable?
facilitatorNotes: Ring, wreath and riches provide outward signs, but the repeated insistence is interrupted by bereavement and fear. Distinguish possession from feeling.
evidence: Satins and jewels grand

questions.prompt: How does the bride confuse the living groom with the lost lover?
facilitatorNotes: The vow sounds like a knell and his voice evokes the fallen man. The dreamlike substitution makes the wedding scene an encounter with memory.
evidence: For the words rang as a knell,

questions.prompt: What changes in the final recurrence of happy now?
facilitatorNotes: The phrase no longer asserts the bride’s state; it expresses anxiety about the abandoned dead. Track the changed subject and the uncertain may.
evidence: May not be happy now.

days.title: The Sleeper
days.challenge: Follow the change from euphemism to funerary detail and reread the childhood recollection as a structural reversal.
days.focus: The poem delays the naming of death by surrounding it with seductive images of sleep.
days.context: The speaker addresses Irene as if she could hear. Lethe is the mythological river of forgetfulness; its name contributes to the poem’s language of sleep.
days.contentNote: Death, burial, ghosts and a brief reference to worms; students may discuss the figurative effects without personal disclosure.

excerpt.locator: The Sleeper; complete poem in The Raven and Other Poems (1845); https://www.eapoe.org/works/poems/sleeperh.htm; opens “AT midnight, in the month of June, I stand beneath the mystic”; closes “think, poor child of sin! It was the dead who groaned within.”.

questions.prompt: How does the opening make sleeping seem to include an entire landscape?
facilitatorNotes: Moon, lake, ruin and valley are personified as drowsy or at rest. This prepares for the ambiguous transition from ordinary sleep to death.
evidence: All Beauty sleeps!

questions.prompt: Which details eventually make Irene’s sleep different from an ordinary night’s rest?
facilitatorNotes: Enduring sleep, the changed chamber, worms and a family vault point to death. Ask readers to locate how recognition is delayed rather than naming it immediately.
evidence: Forever with unopened eye,

questions.prompt: Why end with the childhood memory of stones thrown at a tomb?
facilitatorNotes: The former child who imagined the dead answering will now belong to the silent tomb herself. The reversal adds vulnerability and finality to the grand funeral imagery.
evidence: She ne'er shall force an echo more,

days.title: The Coliseum
days.challenge: Distinguish the speaker’s voice from the Echoes and follow repeated spatial contrasts between past spectacle and present ruins.
days.focus: A ruined monument becomes a debate over whether material loss also destroys cultural power.
days.context: The title names Rome’s ancient amphitheatre. The poem is an imaginative meditation; its allusive claims about magical power are part of the speaker’s rhetoric.
days.contentNote: Alludes to fallen heroes, ruin and religious or mythological power.

excerpt.locator: The Coliseum; complete poem in The Raven and Other Poems (1845); https://www.eapoe.org/works/poems/colisemj.htm; opens “TYPE of the antique Rome! Rich reliquary Of lofty contemplation left to”; closes “as a garment, “Clothing us in a robe of more than glory.””.

questions.prompt: How does the speaker’s imagined thirst change the ruined building from an object into a resource?
facilitatorNotes: He seeks knowledge and drinks in grandeur, treating the monument as nourishment for thought. The kneeling posture also makes his encounter humble or reverential.
evidence: Thirst for the springs of lore that in thee lie,

questions.prompt: What is the effect of pairing a fallen hero with a falling column?
facilitatorNotes: The repeated verb joins human mortality to architectural decay. Other substitutions—bat for eagle and plants for spectators—extend the collapse of former power.
evidence: Here, where a hero fell, a column falls!

questions.prompt: When the Echoes answer Not all, what survives according to their speech?
facilitatorNotes: Influence, memory, mystery and imaginative authority survive beyond intact stone. Debate whether the echoes correct the speaker or give voice to his own developing answer.
evidence: We are not impotent — we pallid stones.

days.title: Pride and Prejudice excerpt: A confidence on the walk
days.challenge: Underline Fitzwilliam’s qualifications about names and particulars. Compare them with Elizabeth’s later certainty, while recognizing the real circumstantial evidence that makes her inference plausible.
days.focus: Trace the movement from qualified secondhand report to confident personal conclusion.
days.context: Darcy repeatedly meets Elizabeth on her favorite path. During a different walk, Colonel Fitzwilliam discusses dependence, marriage, and a confidence Darcy shared about preventing a friend’s marriage. Elizabeth connects it to Jane and Bingley.

excerpt.locator: Pride and Prejudice, Chapter XXXIII, paragraphs 1–41; opens “MORE than once did Elizabeth, in her ramble within the park, unexpectedly”; closes “apprehension of Lady Catherine’s being rather displeased by her staying at home.”.

questions.prompt: How does Elizabeth challenge Fitzwilliam’s account of a younger son’s hardship?
facilitatorNotes: She distinguishes lack of aristocratic freedom to marry without money from ordinary deprivation. His admission about habits of expense shows how dependence can be produced by expected lifestyle as well as scarcity.
evidence: Our habits of expense make us too dependent

questions.prompt: What does Fitzwilliam know directly, and what does he only suppose about the prevented marriage?
facilitatorNotes: He knows Darcy claimed to have saved a friend; he does not know the names or details and infers Bingley. This is evidence of intervention but qualified evidence about the particular couple.
evidence: without mentioning names or any other particulars

questions.prompt: What does Elizabeth add to the report once alone, and how secure are those additions?
facilitatorNotes: She identifies Jane and Bingley, gives Darcy chief responsibility, and assigns motives involving rank and his sister. Some fit known circumstances, but they are further inferences beyond the cousin’s account.
evidence: It was not to be supposed that any other people could be meant

days.title: Pride and Prejudice excerpt: A proposal becomes an accusation
days.challenge: Track the shift from proposal to dispute. Separate the faults Darcy openly admits, allegations he has not yet answered, and Elizabeth’s judgment of his manner.
days.focus: Analyze how sincere feeling can coexist with insulting assumptions and failed persuasion.
days.context: Elizabeth has just heard that Darcy claims to have prevented an imprudent marriage and believes he separated Jane from Bingley. Alone at the parsonage, she rereads Jane’s letters. Darcy arrives and makes an unexpected proposal.
days.contentNote: The scene includes class-based insults during an unwanted marriage proposal.

excerpt.locator: Pride and Prejudice, Chapter XXXIV, paragraphs 1–31; opens “WHEN they were gone, Elizabeth, as if intending to exasperate herself as”; closes “was to encounter Charlotte’s observation, and hurried her away to her room.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Darcy’s declaration of overcoming obstacles offend rather than reassure Elizabeth?
facilitatorNotes: He treats her family and social position as degradation and assumes acceptance despite his struggle. His sincere attachment does not remove the insult of presenting her as a difficulty he has generously overcome.
evidence: he was not more eloquent on the subject of tenderness than of pride

questions.prompt: What has Darcy admitted by the end, and what remains unresolved in this scene?
facilitatorNotes: He admits trying to separate Bingley from Jane and rejoicing in success. He reacts to the Wickham accusation but has not supplied his account; silence or anger cannot by itself settle every claim.
evidence: I did everything in my power to separate my friend from your sister

questions.prompt: What distinction does Elizabeth make between gentlemanly rank and gentlemanly conduct?
facilitatorNotes: She judges his treatment of others and his manner, not the wealth that gives him social standing. Her criticism makes courtesy and regard ethical standards rather than inherited privileges.
evidence: had you behaved in a more gentlemanlike manner

days.title: Pride and Prejudice excerpt: Darcy’s letter: the separation
days.challenge: Mark where Darcy admits an action, allows the possibility of error, or defends a motive. Reread his claim of impartiality beside his acknowledged wish that Jane be indifferent.
days.focus: Evaluate a self-defense that combines concessions, interpretation, and rationalization.
days.context: The morning after Elizabeth refuses Darcy, he gives her a letter answering two accusations. This first part contains the narrative opening, his request for a fair hearing, and his account of separating Bingley from Jane. The excerpt stops at the transition within the long printed letter paragraph.

excerpt.locator: Pride and Prejudice, Chapter XXXV, opening through first charge, paragraphs 1–5; opens “ELIZABETH awoke the next morning to the same thoughts and meditations which”; closes “very naturally appear insufficient, I have not yet learnt to condemn them.”.

questions.prompt: What distinction does Darcy make between the two charges before answering either?
facilitatorNotes: He presents deliberately ruining Wickham as much graver than separating a brief attachment. That framing guides the reader’s scale of judgment and also minimizes the emotional harm Elizabeth assigns to Jane’s separation.
evidence: Two offences of a very different nature, and by no means of equal magnitude

questions.prompt: Where does Darcy acknowledge the limits of his reading of Jane, and where does he still insist on his judgment?
facilitatorNotes: He admits Elizabeth knows her sister better and that an error could justify resentment. Yet he defends his observation as impartial despite wanting that conclusion, a tension readers should assess rather than simply accept.
evidence: That I was desirous of believing her indifferent is certain;

questions.prompt: What action does Darcy concede was questionable, and how does he qualify that concession?
facilitatorNotes: He admits concealing Jane’s presence in London, calls the disguise perhaps beneath him, then says it was for the best. The qualified apology shows both self-awareness and continuing self-justification.
evidence: Perhaps this concealment, this disguise, was beneath me.

days.title: Pride and Prejudice excerpt: Darcy’s letter: the missing transactions
days.challenge: Compare the financial sequence with Wickham’s earlier account. Separate reported acts from Darcy’s interpretations of motives, and consider what an offered corroborating witness adds.
days.focus: Identify evidence that can distinguish competing accounts and the limits of a proposed witness.
days.context: The letter continues at its turn to Wickham. Darcy supplies an account of money accepted instead of a church appointment and an attempted elopement involving his fifteen-year-old sister, Georgiana. These are his claims; he names a person Elizabeth can consult. The excerpt begins within the same printed paragraph and completes the letter.
days.contentNote: The letter reports an adult man’s attempted elopement with a fifteen-year-old girl for financial advantage; no sexual detail is supplied.

excerpt.locator: Pride and Prejudice, Chapter XXXV, second charge through signature, paragraphs 1–2; opens “—With respect to that other, more weighty accusation, of having injured Mr.”; closes “of the morning. I will only add, God bless you. “Fitzwilliam Darcy.””.

questions.prompt: Which transaction, if confirmed, most changes the account of the church living?
facilitatorNotes: Darcy says Wickham renounced the church claim and accepted three thousand pounds, then later sought the living again. This missing agreement changes the meaning of refusal; students should retain the condition that it is corroborated.
evidence: He resigned all claim to assistance in the church

questions.prompt: What does Darcy state about Georgiana’s actions, and what does he infer about Wickham’s motives?
facilitatorNotes: He reports her consent to elope and her eventual disclosure to him. He identifies her fortune as the chief motive and supposes revenge was another; the latter is explicitly an interpretation rather than directly quoted admission.
evidence: I cannot help supposing that the hope of revenging himself on me was a strong inducement

questions.prompt: How does the offer to consult Colonel Fitzwilliam strengthen the letter without making him wholly independent?
facilitatorNotes: He was an executor and co-guardian, so he can know relevant transactions and events. He is also Darcy’s cousin and intimate; the offer makes checking possible, but readers should still consider the scope and relationship of a witness.
evidence: one of the executors of my father’s will

days.title: Pride and Prejudice excerpt: Elizabeth learns to reread
days.challenge: Compare the speed and purpose of Elizabeth’s first reading with her later rereading. Distinguish changed judgment about specific acts from an automatic reversal of every opinion.
days.focus: Study revision of belief as a process of testing evidence and examining personal investment.
days.context: Elizabeth has read Darcy’s letter defending his conduct toward Jane and Wickham. She initially resists it. This chapter follows her repeated reading and comparison with remembered events, including Wickham’s avoidance of the ball and his public accusations after Darcy left.

excerpt.locator: Pride and Prejudice, Chapter XXXVI, paragraphs 1–13; opens “ELIZABETH, when Mr. Darcy gave her the letter, did not expect it”; closes “was no longer an object. She could think only of her letter.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Elizabeth’s first rapid reading fail to produce understanding?
facilitatorNotes: She anticipates the next objection and refuses the possibility of an explanation, so attention outruns comprehension. The later command to examine each sentence marks a change in reading practice, not just a change of allegiance.
evidence: incapable of attending to the sense of the one before her eyes

questions.prompt: What remembered conduct helps her assess the rival assertions about Wickham?
facilitatorNotes: She recalls no substantial good act, his immediate disclosure to a stranger, avoidance of the ball, and wider accusations only after Darcy left. These consistencies and inconsistencies provide more than charm or repeated assertion, though some conclusions still rely on probability.
evidence: On both sides it was only assertion.

questions.prompt: What does “Till this moment, I never knew myself” add beyond discovering that Wickham misled her?
facilitatorNotes: She recognizes how flattery and offended pride shaped her supposedly superior discernment. The discovery concerns her own participation in error; it does not mean all her earlier criticisms, including rude conduct, were imaginary.
evidence: Till this moment, I never knew myself.

days.title: Family records and the limits of certainty
days.challenge: Track the difference between a record, an inference, and a remembered conversation.
days.focus: Autobiographical evidence and family resemblance.
days.context: Franklin addresses his son while reconstructing the history of an English family from which he descended.

excerpt.locator: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin, Ancestry and Early Youth in Boston, consecutive paragraphs; opens “And now I speak of thanking God, I desire with all humility”; closes “on the same day," you said, "one might have supposed a transmigration."”.

questions.prompt: Where does Franklin mark the boundary between what he knows and what he can only suppose?
facilitatorNotes: Compare the dated parish register with the parenthetical conjecture about the surname. His limits make the account more accountable, though not independently proven.
evidence: there being no registers kept in that parish at any time preceding

questions.prompt: How does the portrait of his uncle Thomas begin to turn genealogy into a portrait of Franklin himself?
facilitatorNotes: Thomas moves from a craft into learning and public undertakings; the son recognizes the likeness. Distinguish this selected family pattern from proof of inherited character.
evidence: from its similarity to what you knew of mine

questions.prompt: Why begin this family history by admitting the possibility of a fatal reverse?
facilitatorNotes: The providential opening frames past happiness as contingent, not an assurance of future success. Ask how that qualification affects the tone of the following achievements.
evidence: I desire with all humility to acknowledge

days.title: A father’s table as a school
days.challenge: Reread one long paragraph for its turning points and qualified praise.
days.focus: Characterization through ordinary routines.
days.context: Franklin recalls his father, a Boston tradesman whose family responsibilities limited formal public service.

excerpt.locator: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin, Ancestry and Early Youth in Boston, consecutive paragraphs; opens “I think you may like to know something of his person and”; closes “suitable gratification of their more delicate, because better instructed, tastes and appetites.”.

questions.prompt: How does Franklin distinguish holding public office from exercising public influence?
facilitatorNotes: The father lacks time and money for office, yet neighbors and leading people seek his judgment. Locate the qualification introduced by “indeed.”
evidence: frequently chosen an arbitrator between contending parties

questions.prompt: What does the dinner-table routine teach, and what does it train the children not to notice?
facilitatorNotes: Connect deliberate conversation about conduct with inattention to food; the narrator presents habits of attention as products of education.
evidence: little or no notice was ever taken of what related to the victuals on the table

questions.prompt: Is the final description of his companions entirely complimentary? Explain its irony.
facilitatorNotes: “Better instructed” usually praises education, but here cultivated taste produces unhappiness. Students may read gentle teasing or a defense of practical simplicity.
evidence: their more delicate, because better instructed, tastes and appetites

days.title: Books, ballads, and an argument on paper
days.challenge: Separate popularity, fluency, correctness, and clarity as competing measures of writing.
days.focus: Revision of judgments about literary ability.
days.context: As a twelve-year-old apprentice in his brother James’s printing business, Franklin gains access to books and experiments with writing.
days.contentNote: Includes historical claims denying women’s intellectual equality, which Franklin disputes, and a reference to a fatal drowning.

excerpt.locator: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin, Beginning Life As a Printer, consecutive paragraphs; opens “This bookish inclination at length determined my father to make me a”; closes “attentive to the manner in writing, and determined to endeavor at improvement.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the successful sale of the ballad fail to establish its literary merit?
facilitatorNotes: Its topical subject explains sales; the older narrator calls the poems wretched while the younger writer feels flattered. Attend to the two time perspectives.
evidence: The first sold wonderfully, the event being recent

questions.prompt: How does the move from speaking to letters expose a different weakness in Franklin’s argument?
facilitatorNotes: Collins’s fluency had seemed overwhelming; written exchange allows the father to assess organization and clarity rather than merely performance.
evidence: bore me down more by his fluency than by the strength of his reasons

questions.prompt: What limits does Franklin place on his own defense of women’s education?
facilitatorNotes: He admits disputatious motives and never reproduces the argument itself. Readers can identify his position without treating this episode as a fully developed defense.
evidence: I took the contrary side, perhaps a little for dispute's sake

days.title: Buying time to learn
days.challenge: Trace several consequences of one decision without treating the narrator’s causal claims as established science.
days.focus: Money, time, and self-directed learning.
days.context: Franklin recalls his teenage apprenticeship and the practical arrangements that enabled private study.
days.contentNote: Historical diet claims are the narrator’s interpretation, not nutritional guidance.

excerpt.locator: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin, Beginning Life As a Printer, consecutive paragraphs; opens “When about 16 years of age I happened to meet with a”; closes “Human Understanding, and the Art of Thinking, by Messrs. du Port Royal.”.

questions.prompt: How does the boarding arrangement produce two different resources for reading?
facilitatorNotes: Half the boarding payment supports his meals; savings buy books, while quick solitary meals create study time. Reconstruct the sequence precisely.
evidence: This was an additional fund for buying books.

questions.prompt: Which benefits are directly described, and which depend on Franklin’s explanation of his own mind?
facilitatorNotes: Distinguish saved money and uninterrupted time from the claimed mental effects of temperance. Both appear in the memoir, but with different kinds of evidence.
evidence: greater clearness of head and quicker apprehension

questions.prompt: Why include both earlier failure in arithmetic and the limit of his later geometry?
facilitatorNotes: The account makes self-directed progress striking while qualifying the scope of mastery; it does not claim universal effortless learning.
evidence: but never proceeded far in that science

days.title: An anonymous writer claims his freedom
days.challenge: Follow the changing meanings of a name on a newspaper and an apprenticeship agreement.
days.focus: Authority, authorship, and retrospective self-criticism.
days.context: Franklin works for his older brother James on the New England Courant in Boston. He describes both family conflict and political censorship.
days.contentNote: Includes physical abuse of an apprentice, imprisonment, and religious prejudice.

excerpt.locator: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin, Beginning Life As a Printer, consecutive paragraphs; opens “My brother had, in 1720 or 1721, begun to print a newspaper.”; closes “person in the place, and with very little money in my pocket.”.

questions.prompt: How does anonymity first help Franklin, and why does revealing himself complicate that success?
facilitatorNotes: The hidden name allows assessment without the brother’s assumptions about age; disclosure brings recognition but also vanity and rivalry.
evidence: none were named but men of some character among us for learning and ingenuity

questions.prompt: Explain how the plan to evade the Assembly’s order also creates an opportunity for Franklin to leave.
facilitatorNotes: The public discharge makes Benjamin appear independent, while the secret second agreement preserves James’s claim. Exposure would undermine the evasion.
evidence: new indentures for the remainder of the term, which were to be kept private

questions.prompt: Does the older narrator wholly excuse the way he gains his freedom?
facilitatorNotes: He labels it unfair and an erratum while reporting violence and restricted employment. Keep the tension between self-criticism and contextual explanation.
evidence: It was not fair in me to take this advantage

days.title: Lenore
days.challenge: Mark changes of speaker and compare the vocabulary of descent, ascent, public ritual and accusation.
days.focus: A funeral dialogue questions who has authority to mourn and how grief should be voiced.
days.context: Lenore is the subject of mourning in this poem; the dramatic voices should not automatically be equated with Poe. Peccavimus means we have sinned; a paean is a song of praise.
days.contentNote: Death of a young woman, mourning and accusations of social cruelty.

excerpt.locator: Lenore; complete poem in The Raven and Other Poems (1845); https://www.eapoe.org/works/poems/lenoref.htm; opens “AH, broken is the golden bowl! the spirit flown forever! Let the”; closes “grief and groan, to a golden throne, beside the King of Heaven.””.

questions.prompt: How do the voices disagree about what a proper funeral should sound like?
facilitatorNotes: One asks for bells, tears and a dirge; the grieving speaker refuses that ritual and proposes a paean of ascent. Compare commands rather than treating the poem as a single uninterrupted voice.
evidence: Let no bell toll!

questions.prompt: What accusation makes the refusal more than a preference in music?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker charges the mourners with loving wealth, hating pride and harming Lenore through slander. The ritual becomes morally compromised by who performs it.
evidence: ye loved her for her wealth and hated her for her pride,

questions.prompt: Does the final upward movement erase grief or transform its expression?
facilitatorNotes: The soul’s rise reframes departure as deliverance from a hostile world. Readers may hear consolation, anger or insistence; require support from the paired oppositions.
evidence: To friends above, from fiends below,

days.title: Israfel
days.challenge: Reread the shift from praise to comparison and conditional exchange; separate the poem’s invented angelic setting from factual religious description.
days.focus: Praise of a supernatural singer becomes an argument about the conditions under which art is made.
days.context: Poe uses Israfel as an imaginative heavenly singer. The poem’s mixture of celestial and cultural references belongs to its poetic world, not to a neutral account of a religious tradition.

excerpt.locator: Israfel; complete poem in The Raven and Other Poems (1845); https://www.eapoe.org/works/poems/israfelf.htm; opens “IN Heaven a spirit doth dwell “Whose heart-strings are a lute;” None”; closes “bolder note than this might swell From my lyre within the sky.”.

questions.prompt: What makes Israfel’s instrument different from an ordinary lute?
facilitatorNotes: His own heart-strings become the instrument, making emotion inseparable from the song. The listening stars magnify its power.
evidence: Whose heart-strings are a lute;

questions.prompt: How does the comparison between earthly sunshine and heavenly shadow complicate the praise?
facilitatorNotes: Even the shadow of perfect bliss exceeds earthly joy. The comparison makes artistic excellence partly a matter of conditions, not simply talent.
evidence:
And the shadow of thy perfect bliss
Is the sunshine of ours.

questions.prompt: What does the imagined exchange of places allow the speaker to claim without directly boasting?
facilitatorNotes: He suggests the angel might struggle on earth and a mortal might sing more boldly in heaven. The conditional ending tests the fairness of comparing unlike circumstances.
evidence: He might not sing so wildly well

days.title: Dream-Land
days.challenge: Compare the opening and closing frames, then reread the stanza explaining why the traveller cannot look openly.
days.focus: Dream travel offers a paradoxical refuge whose consolation depends on obscurity.
days.context: Eidolon means an image or phantom; Thule here suggests a remote limit. These brief glosses orient the poem’s invented geography.
days.contentNote: Ghostly memories of dead friends and unsettling dream imagery.

excerpt.locator: Dream-Land; complete poem in The Raven and Other Poems (1845); https://www.eapoe.org/works/poems/drmlandc.htm; opens “BY a route obscure and lonely, Haunted by ill angels only, Where”; closes “upright, I have wandered home but newly From this ultimate dim Thule.”.

questions.prompt: How does the poem make this landscape resist ordinary measures of place and time?
facilitatorNotes: Boundless floods, bottomless valleys and a realm outside space and time deny familiar limits. Ask how repeated spatial excess creates dream logic.
evidence: Out of SPACE — out of TIME.

questions.prompt: Why might a frightening region be called peaceful and soothing?
facilitatorNotes: For a sorrowing heart, it offers encounters with memories and lost friends. Comfort and terror coexist; a response that calls the setting simply pleasant misses the contrast.
evidence:
For the heart whose woes are legion
’Tis a peaceful, soothing region

questions.prompt: What does the changed final route tell us about the speaker’s journey?
facilitatorNotes: The opening reports reaching the land; the ending reports wandering home from it. The repeated frame makes a completed passage through an experience whose mysteries remain partially hidden.
evidence: I have wandered home but newly

days.title: The City in the Sea
days.challenge: Reread the negative statements about wind and waves, then chart the final stanza’s escalation in motion.
days.focus: A static city of death becomes unsettling through inverted light and the delayed arrival of movement.
days.context: The imagined city is ruled by personified Death. Biblical and ancient architectural allusions contribute to its scale; the poem is not a report of a historical place.
days.contentNote: Death, graves and a final image of Hell; no graphic violence.

excerpt.locator: The City in the Sea; complete poem in The Raven and Other Poems (1845); https://www.eapoe.org/works/poems/cityseae.htm; opens “LO! Death has reared himself a throne In a strange city lying”; closes “settle hence. Hell, rising from a thousand thrones, Shall do it reverence.”.

questions.prompt: What does the city’s upward light reverse about an ordinary landscape?
facilitatorNotes: Light comes from below rather than heaven. It makes architecture visible while denying the usual reassuring source of illumination.
evidence: But light from out the lurid sea

questions.prompt: Why describe the sea as hideously serene rather than merely calm?
facilitatorNotes: Repeated absence of motion makes calm feel deathlike and unnatural. The adjective prevents readers from treating stillness as peace.
evidence: On seas less hideously serene.

questions.prompt: How does the small initial movement prepare the final collapse?
facilitatorNotes: A stir, slight sinking and faint breathing enlarge into the city’s descent. The slow sequence makes tiny changes ominous after the sustained stillness.
evidence: But lo, a stir is in the air!

days.title: To One in Paradise
days.challenge: Reread personifications of time and the final recurring dream; build an interpretation that can account for comfort and paralysis.
days.focus: A grief lyric sets the language of onward time against a speaker held by memory.
days.context: The unnamed beloved is addressed directly throughout. Read the landscapes as images within a dramatic grief lyric rather than as locations to identify.
days.contentNote: Bereavement and despair.

excerpt.locator: To One in Paradise; complete poem in The Raven and Other Poems (1845); https://www.eapoe.org/works/poems/paradsm.htm; opens “THOU wast all that to me, love, For which my soul did”; closes “thy footstep gleams — In what ethereal dances, By what eternal streams.”.

questions.prompt: What kinds of shelter does the lost beloved provide in the opening metaphors?
facilitatorNotes: Island, fountain and shrine imply refuge, sustenance and devotion. Discuss how the possessive final line may add intensity or an uncomfortable sense of ownership.
evidence: A fountain and a shrine,

questions.prompt: How does the poem set the Future’s command against the speaker’s position over the Past?
facilitatorNotes: The Future urges onward motion while the spirit hovers motionless. The contrasting actions enact the difficulty of moving beyond loss.
evidence: A voice from out the Future cries,

questions.prompt: Does the last stanza fulfil the command to move onward?
facilitatorNotes: It locates the beloved in recurring trances and dreams rather than ordinary present life. Readers may find consolation or continuing suspension, but should connect the nightly repetition to the earlier stillness.
evidence: And all my nightly dreams

days.title: Frankenstein introduction: learning to invent
days.challenge: Track the contrast between the child’s stories and waking dreams. Reread the account as a crafted memory written years after the events, noticing changes in the narrator’s attitude toward fame.
days.focus: Distinguish private imaginative freedom, public writing, and later recollection.
days.context: In 1831 Mary Shelley supplied an account of how she began Frankenstein in 1816. This is her retrospective author’s introduction, not Victor Frankenstein’s fictional narration. The opening ends with her difficulty finding a ghost-story idea.
days.contentNote: The introduction recounts supernatural tales involving death and frightening apparitions.

excerpt.locator: Frankenstein (1831), Author’s Introduction, paragraphs 1–8; opens “The Publishers of the Standard Novels, in selecting "Frankenstein" for one of”; closes “and each morning I was forced to reply with a mortifying negative.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Shelley value childhood daydreams more than the stories she wrote?
facilitatorNotes: The written stories imitate others and anticipate a reader, whereas dreams are private, unaccountable, and freely invented. The contrast complicates an account in which publication alone measures creativity.
evidence: my dreams were all my own;

questions.prompt: How can the same landscape be “blank and dreary” in retrospect but an “eyry of freedom” in childhood?
facilitatorNotes: The adult names its physical bleakness while remembering the child’s imaginative freedom there. Place acquires meaning through the perceiver and time; the account explicitly distinguishes these perspectives.
evidence: Blank and dreary on retrospection I call them;

questions.prompt: What standards make the proposed ghost story difficult for her to begin?
facilitatorNotes: She wants a bodily effect on readers—fear, quickened pulse, reluctance to look around—and feels pressure to rival memorable stories. The daily question turns imaginative blankness into public embarrassment.
evidence: each morning I was forced to reply with a mortifying negative.

days.title: Frankenstein introduction: an idea takes form
days.challenge: Separate a report of what people said about an experiment from a verified experiment. Then reread Shelley’s distinctions among the idea, encouragement to expand it, and the authorship of the earlier preface.
days.focus: Analyze an origin story that combines influence, involuntary vision, and deliberate authorship.
days.context: Shelley continues her 1831 account by explaining invention as the reshaping of prior materials. Discussion of life, a frightening waking dream, and the work of expansion lead to the novel. This completes the introduction begun in the preceding selection.
