days.contentNote: Includes a frightening vision of an animated body, reflections on bereavement, and a historically reductive reference to Hindu cosmology.

excerpt.locator: Frankenstein (1831), Author’s Introduction, paragraphs 9–18; opens “Every thing must have a beginning, to speak in Sanchean phrase; and”; closes “and substance of it untouched. M. W. S. _London, October 15, 1831._”.

questions.prompt: What does invention “out of chaos” mean in the account that follows?
facilitatorNotes: Existing stories, conversations, and questions about life supply materials that the imagination shapes into a new relation. Originality is presented as transformation and form, not creation without influences.
evidence: does not consist in creating out of void, but out of chaos

questions.prompt: Why does Shelley qualify the reference to Dr. Darwin’s experiment?
facilitatorNotes: She explicitly records what was spoken of, not what he actually did. Her account concerns the effect of a circulating idea on imagination; it should not be treated as scientific confirmation.
evidence: I speak not of what the Doctor really did

questions.prompt: How does the phrase “hideous progeny” connect affection for the book with the imagined creator’s horror?
facilitatorNotes: She calls the book an offspring and sends it outward affectionately, whereas the dream’s artist flees his creation. The parallel invites reflection on different responsibilities toward what one brings into being, while her memories add grief to pride.
evidence: I bid my hideous progeny go forth and prosper.

days.title: Frankenstein, Letter I: the voyage imagined
days.challenge: Mark the shift from Walton’s imagined polar paradise to claims of practical benefit. Reread his evidence of preparation beside his request that Margaret confirm he deserves glory.
days.focus: Assess how aspiration, preparation, and self-persuasion coexist in a narrator’s account.
days.context: The novel opens with Robert Walton writing to his sister Margaret Saville before an Arctic expedition. The letter’s hopes and geographic conjectures belong to a fictional explorer in an earlier period, not to a modern account of the polar region.

excerpt.locator: Frankenstein (1831), Letter I, paragraphs 1–13; opens “_To Mrs. Saville, England._ St. Petersburgh, Dec. 11th, 17--. You will rejoice”; closes “gratitude for all your love and kindness. Your affectionate brother, R. WALTON.”.

questions.prompt: How does Walton’s imagined pole differ from the danger he acknowledges around it?
facilitatorNotes: He imagines perpetual light, calm seas, and beauty where others anticipate desolation. The contrast shows desire selecting a picture; his willingness to suppose the conjectures false does not wholly displace the fantasy.
evidence: the region of beauty and delight

questions.prompt: What evidence makes Walton more than an idle dreamer?
facilitatorNotes: He has trained on whaling voyages, endured hardship, studied relevant subjects, and earned responsibility. These concrete preparations complicate criticism of his ambition; competence and overconfidence can coexist.
evidence: Twice I actually hired myself as an under-mate

questions.prompt: What does asking whether he “deserve[s]” a great purpose reveal about his argument?
facilitatorNotes: He treats sacrifice and effort as grounds for a hoped-for achievement and asks for emotional reassurance. Preparation can support a venture without guaranteeing success or entitlement to discovery.
evidence: do I not deserve to accomplish some great purpose?

days.title: Frankenstein, Letter II: the missing friend
days.challenge: Reread the desired friend’s qualities beside the master’s generous conduct. Trace the contrast between practical labor and fascination with the marvellous in Walton’s final self-description.
days.focus: Identify contradictions between a speaker’s stated values and the people he overlooks.
days.context: Walton has hired a ship and is gathering a crew. He writes again to Margaret about loneliness, the qualities he wants in a companion, and the men already around him. His allusion to the Ancient Mariner refers to Coleridge’s poem of a troubled sea voyage.
days.contentNote: Walton uses a reductive stereotype about Turkish people and class-based assumptions about education; these belong to his historical voice.

excerpt.locator: Frankenstein (1831), Letter II, paragraphs 1–11; opens “_To Mrs. Saville, England._ Archangel, 28th March, 17--. How slowly the time”; closes “should you never hear from me again. Your affectionate brother, ROBERT WALTON.”.

questions.prompt: What does Walton want a friend to do beyond sharing his pleasure?
facilitatorNotes: He wants someone to approve or amend plans, regulate his mind, and correct impatience. Friendship is imagined as an intellectual and ethical check, not merely admiration.
evidence: to approve or amend my plans

questions.prompt: Why does the master’s story expose a limitation in Walton’s judgment of possible companions?
facilitatorNotes: The master shows generosity, restraint, courage, and humane command, but Walton discounts intimacy because he lacks formal cultivation. The story supplies moral worth that the speaker’s social expectations do not fully reward.
evidence: but then he is wholly uneducated

questions.prompt: How does the final self-description complicate Walton’s promise to act prudently?
facilitatorNotes: He identifies himself as a painstaking worker yet admits an unexplained love of the marvellous that drives him beyond common paths. The two motives may cooperate or conflict; the text keeps both in view.
evidence: a love for the marvellous, a belief in the marvellous

days.title: Lines on the Mermaid Tavern
days.challenge: Read aloud twice for rhyme and the repeated question. Then trace the sign-board’s impossible journey and the changes in scale from pies and drinking vessels to the Zodiac.
days.focus: Read comic elevation as a defense of ordinary fellowship and artistic memory.
days.context: The Mermaid Tavern evokes a celebrated London gathering place associated with literary fellowship. Keats playfully imagines its pleasures continuing among dead poets in heaven; Canary is wine, and Elysium a classical afterlife.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem: Lines on the Mermaid Tavern; opens “Souls of Poets dead and gone,”; closes “Choicer than the Mermaid Tavern?”.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker compare Paradise with specific food and drink rather than abstract bliss?
facilitatorNotes: Canary wine and venison pies make remembered fellowship tangible. The comic comparison suggests that shared earthly pleasure can rival an ideal afterlife, without requiring the poem to deny spiritual experience.
evidence: Sweeter than those dainty pies

questions.prompt: How does the flying sign-board link the tavern to the heavens?
facilitatorNotes: A familiar commercial object becomes a celestial emblem, carrying the tavern’s identity into the Zodiac. The astrologer’s fanciful report lets imagination relocate a beloved gathering place.
evidence: The Mermaid in the Zodiac.

questions.prompt: Does the repeated final question mean exactly what it meant at the beginning?
facilitatorNotes: After the invented celestial tavern, the question can sound like a delighted confirmation that no better place exists. It also keeps the claim playful and speculative rather than converting fantasy into factual history.
evidence: Choicer than the Mermaid Tavern?

days.title: A difficult road to Philadelphia
days.challenge: Notice how literary digressions interrupt physical danger without erasing it.
days.focus: Narrative pacing and knowledge under uncertainty.
days.context: The seventeen-year-old Franklin has left Boston and is traveling through New York and New Jersey toward Philadelphia.
days.contentNote: Includes near drowning, alcohol use, illness, and historical religious judgments. His fever treatment is a memoir detail, not medical advice.

excerpt.locator: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin, Arrival in Philadelphia, consecutive paragraphs; opens “In crossing the bay, we met with a squall that tore our”; closes “nine o'clock on the Sunday morning, and landed at the Market-street wharf.”.

questions.prompt: Why might the account pause over the Dutch edition of Pilgrim’s Progress immediately after a rescue?
facilitatorNotes: The digression identifies Franklin’s enduring bookish attention and temporarily slows the danger. Compare its leisurely evaluation with the crowded night that follows.
evidence: a dress better than I had ever seen it wear in its own language

questions.prompt: Where does Franklin refuse to claim knowledge of what other people thought?
facilitatorNotes: At the shore he offers two explanations rather than asserting the rescuers’ motives. Contrast this with the travelers’ mistaken confidence about passing the city.
evidence: they either did not understand us, or thought it impracticable

questions.prompt: How do appearances alternately expose Franklin to suspicion and gain him hospitality?
facilitatorNotes: His miserable clothes suggest a runaway; conversation about books earns Brown’s friendship; the woman’s kindness does not depend on a polished appearance.
evidence: finding I had read a little, became very sociable and friendly

days.title: Judging strangers and printers
days.challenge: Track who knows whose identity in the printing-house conversation.
days.focus: Dramatic irony and the practical test of skill.
days.context: Newly arrived in Philadelphia after an exhausting journey, Franklin seeks lodging and work as a printer.
days.contentNote: Includes suspicion that a young traveler is a runaway servant and dismissive descriptions of a historical religious movement.

excerpt.locator: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin, Arrival in Philadelphia, consecutive paragraphs; opens “Thus refreshed, I walked again up the street, which by this time”; closes “she first happen'd to see me eating my roll in the street.”.

questions.prompt: How do the two Quaker encounters qualify the suspicion Franklin meets at his lodging?
facilitatorNotes: The meeting-goer wakes him kindly and the young man guides him toward a reputable inn. These acts complicate an account centered only on distrust.
evidence: if thee wilt walk with me, I'll show thee a better

questions.prompt: Why is the conversation between Bradford and Keimer ironic?
facilitatorNotes: Keimer tells a competitor’s father his strategy because he misidentifies him as a helpful stranger; Franklin and the reader can see the error.
evidence: not discovering that he was the other printer's father

questions.prompt: What concrete details support Franklin’s claim to useful expertise?
facilitatorNotes: The composing-stick test and repairing the press supply evidence beyond his disparaging judgments of the employers. Ask whether those judgments also promote his own image.
evidence: to put his press (which he had not yet us'd, and of which he understood nothing) into order

days.title: A governor’s promise and a father’s refusal
days.challenge: Compare three audiences for the same signs of youthful success.
days.focus: Patronage, display, and competing judgments.
days.context: Governor Keith has read a letter by the young Franklin and encourages him to establish a printing business; Franklin returns to Boston seeking his father’s financial support.
days.contentNote: Includes wine drinking and family estrangement.

excerpt.locator: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin, First Visit to Boston, consecutive paragraphs; opens “SIR WILLIAM KEITH, governor of the province, was then at Newcastle, and”; closes “embark'd again for New York, now with their approbation and their blessing.”.

questions.prompt: How do clothes, money, and polite attention acquire different meanings in the governor’s visit and Franklin’s homecoming?
facilitatorNotes: Keith’s finery and familiarity confer status; Franklin displays silver and a watch to former coworkers; his brother reads that display as an insult.
evidence: Then I took an opportunity of letting them see my watch

questions.prompt: Why does the father judge the governor as well as his son?
facilitatorNotes: The proposal itself becomes evidence of Keith’s discretion: he recommends an expensive business for someone legally and practically inexperienced.
evidence: he must be of small discretion

questions.prompt: Does the refusal amount to a rejection of Franklin’s ambition?
facilitatorNotes: The father recognizes industry, permits the return, and promises later assistance after saving. His alternative changes the timetable and conditions.
evidence: if I came near the matter, he would help me out with the rest

days.title: Promises, borrowed money, and convenient reasons
days.challenge: Read the final fish anecdote back against the earlier financial decisions.
days.focus: Self-justification and retrospective correction.
days.context: Returning toward Philadelphia, Franklin travels with his childhood friend Collins. Vernon has entrusted Franklin with money to collect and deliver. Governor Keith still proposes to finance a printing business.
days.contentNote: Includes alcohol misuse, gambling, misuse of entrusted funds, and a dangerous assault in which a swimmer is kept from a boat.

excerpt.locator: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin, First Visit to Boston, consecutive paragraphs; opens “At New York I found my friend Collins, who had arriv'd there”; closes “or make a reason for everything one has a mind to do.”.

questions.prompt: How does the description of Collins’s early promise sharpen the account of his later conduct?
facilitatorNotes: Intellectual gifts and shared reading initially support trust; the later borrowing and dependence show that learning does not guarantee reliable conduct.
evidence: a wonderful genius for mathematical learning

questions.prompt: What does Franklin’s admission about Vernon’s money do to the disagreement between his father and Keith?
facilitatorNotes: It retrospectively supports the father’s caution, immediately before Keith flatters Franklin with a contrary interpretation. Separate the young man’s confidence from the older narrator’s verdict.
evidence: my father was not much out in his judgment

questions.prompt: How can the cod-fishing anecdote change our reading of the governor’s promises?
facilitatorNotes: The final maxim distinguishes finding reasons from honestly testing them. Students can connect appetite for fish with appetite for advancement without claiming the text explicitly equates them.
evidence: find or make a reason for everything one has a mind to do

days.title: Who gets credit for the poem?
days.challenge: Distinguish an experiment about prejudice from proof of literary greatness.
days.focus: Attribution, judgment, and comic irony.
days.context: Franklin and three reading companions agree to write versions of the same psalm and criticize one another’s language.
days.contentNote: Includes religious disagreement and brief accounts of friends’ deaths.

excerpt.locator: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin, Early Friends in Philadelphia, consecutive paragraphs; opens “My chief acquaintances at this time were Charles Osborne, Joseph Watson, and”; closes “found things in that separate state. But he never fulfill'd his promise.”.

questions.prompt: Why do the friends choose a shared subject for their writing?
facilitatorNotes: They try to isolate language and expression by holding invention constant. Consider how changing the author’s name introduces a second variable into the exercise.
evidence: we excluded all considerations of invention

questions.prompt: What does Ralph’s criticism of his own disguised poem accomplish in the scene?
facilitatorNotes: It sustains the deception and draws Osborne into defending the work against the person he usually disparages. The reader knows more than Osborne.
evidence: Ralph only made some criticisms, and propos'd some amendments

questions.prompt: Does the trick justify Ralph’s decision to become a professional poet?
facilitatorNotes: It exposes possible bias, but a favorable response to one exercise does not settle a career. Franklin’s continued discouragement and later prose assessment limit the triumph.
evidence: This transaction fixed Ralph in his resolution of becoming a poet.

days.title: Eulalie—A Song
days.challenge: Read aloud to hear short and long line patterns; reread the absolutes and separate present celebration from lasting prediction.
days.focus: A song of transformed loneliness tests how repetition and extravagant comparison create certainty.
days.context: Astarté is a mythological divine figure in the poem’s celebratory imagery. The complete short lyric rewards voiced rereading and attention to its repeated endings.

excerpt.locator: Eulalie—A Song; complete poem in The Raven and Other Poems (1845); https://www.eapoe.org/works/poems/eulaliee.htm; opens “I DWELT alone In a world of moan, And my soul was”; closes “eye — While ever to her young Eulalie upturns her violet eye.”.

questions.prompt: How does the tide image establish the speaker’s emotional life before the marriage?
facilitatorNotes: A stagnant tide is a paradox of water that should move but does not. The later language of radiant stars and flowing reciprocal sighs replaces that arrested condition.
evidence: And my soul was a stagnant tide,

questions.prompt: What effect does comparing a careless curl with stars and moonlit vapour create?
facilitatorNotes: An ordinary detail of the beloved exceeds cosmic beauty. Readers can call this idealization, intimate attention or deliberate extravagance, supported by the repeated comparisons.
evidence: most humble and careless curl.

questions.prompt: How secure does the claim that Doubt and Pain will never return sound?
facilitatorNotes: The poem’s song form confidently celebrates transformation, but a reader can question the absolute claim without disproving the speaker’s present joy. Distinguish what the speaker feels from a prediction we can verify.
evidence: Come never again,

days.title: A Dream
days.challenge: Reread the shifting meanings of dream, day and light; explain the contrast without correcting the historical printing’s unusual phrasing.
days.focus: A short lyric makes dream both a cause of pain and a source of guidance.
days.context: The 1845 printing’s wording is preserved, including its unusual plural dreams in the first stanza and its final Truths. Use context to discuss meaning rather than silently substituting another edition.
days.contentNote: Loss and loneliness.

excerpt.locator: A Dream; complete poem in The Raven and Other Poems (1845); https://www.eapoe.org/works/poems/dreame.htm; opens “IN visions of the dark night I have dreamed of joy departed”; closes “afar — What could there be more purely bright In Truths day-star?”.

questions.prompt: Why does the first stanza make a waking dream more painful than a night vision?
facilitatorNotes: The night vision recovers lost joy, while waking imagination leaves the speaker aware of absence. Discuss how the usual opposition between dream illusion and waking reality is unsettled.
evidence: Hath left me broken-hearted.

questions.prompt: How do past-directed eyes affect the speaker’s experience of daytime surroundings?
facilitatorNotes: Attention looks through present things toward the past, making the day itself dreamlike. The poem frames this as a question rather than a plain factual statement.
evidence: Turned back upon the past?

questions.prompt: What changes when the dream becomes a distant guiding light?
facilitatorNotes: It becomes a resource under criticism and storm despite its trembling distance. Readers may stress fragility or persistence; both should acknowledge the qualified brightness.
evidence: A lonely spirit guiding.

days.title: The Haunted Palace
days.challenge: Map concrete features to the proposed allegory, then reread sounds and colour changes to test rather than assume that interpretation.
days.focus: An architectural allegory represents a change from ordered expression to painful disorder.
days.context: The poem names its ruler Thought, inviting an allegorical reading. It uses Gothic imagery of distress; the figures should not be treated as a clinical description.
days.contentNote: Frightening imagery and a figurative account of mental distress.

excerpt.locator: The Haunted Palace; complete poem in The Raven and Other Poems (1845); https://www.eapoe.org/works/poems/palacej.htm; opens “IN the greenest of our valleys By good angels tenanted, Once a”; closes “hideous throng rush out forever And laugh — but smile no more.”.

questions.prompt: Which details suggest that the palace also represents a human mind or head?
facilitatorNotes: Thought rules it; two windows resemble eyes, the pearl-and-ruby door suggests mouth or lips, and voices carry its wisdom. Require several correspondences rather than one asserted symbol.
evidence: In the monarch Thought's dominion

questions.prompt: How does music register the change from the earlier palace to the later one?
facilitatorNotes: Ordered movement follows a tuned law at first, then becomes fantastic and discordant. Sound measures the loss of order across the two descriptions.
evidence: To a discordant melody,

questions.prompt: Why distinguish laughter from smiling in the final line?
facilitatorNotes: The contradiction separates outward sound from warmth or joy and makes the ending disturbing. Avoid diagnosing a real illness from a literary allegory.
evidence: And laugh — but smile no more.

days.title: Sonnet—To Science
days.challenge: Reread each accusation and identify its imagined loss; evaluate the speaker’s rhetoric without treating the poem as evidence against scientific findings.
days.focus: A sequence of questions turns a cultural dispute into a personal account of threatened imagination.
days.context: Diana, Hamadryad, Naiad and Elfin name mythic figures associated with sky, trees, water and grass. The speaker uses them to ask what explanatory knowledge may seem to displace.

excerpt.locator: Sonnet—To Science; complete poem in The Raven and Other Poems (1845); https://www.eapoe.org/works/poems/sciencej.htm; opens “SCIENCE! true daughter of Old Time thou art! Who alterest all things”; closes “green grass, and from me The summer dream beneath the tamarind tree?”.

questions.prompt: What happens when Science is addressed first as a daughter and then as a vulture?
facilitatorNotes: The personifications shift from ancestry and change to predatory harm. The speaker frames inquiry as a threat to a poet’s imaginative possession.
evidence: Vulture, whose wings are dull realities?

questions.prompt: Why list displaced mythological figures instead of naming scientific discoveries?
facilitatorNotes: The list emphasizes loss of imagined inhabitants and emotional relations to nature rather than arguing technical facts. A response should distinguish this rhetorical grievance from a scientific rebuttal.
evidence: And driven the Hamadryad from the wood

questions.prompt: How does the last image change the scale of the complaint?
facilitatorNotes: The poem moves from celestial and mythical figures to the speaker’s own summer dream under one tree. This makes the public accusation intimate.
evidence: The summer dream beneath the tamarind tree?

days.title: Romance
days.challenge: Read the two stanzas as contrasting phases, then reread the final conditional sentence to explain the apparent guilt about making art.
days.focus: A bird metaphor traces the changing relation between imagination, time and emotional commitment.
days.context: Romance here names an imaginative faculty, not simply a love relationship. The poem’s birds connect childhood language and adult poetic labour.

excerpt.locator: Romance; complete poem in The Raven and Other Poems (1845); https://www.eapoe.org/works/poems/romanceg.htm; opens “ROMANCE, who loves to nod and sing, With drowsy head and folded”; closes “would feel to be a crime Unless it trembled with the strings.”.

questions.prompt: How does the childhood bird connect romance with learning language?
facilitatorNotes: The familiar colourful bird teaches alphabet and first words, so imaginative life precedes formal poetic mastery. The child is both inexperienced and described as knowing.
evidence: Taught me my alphabet to say —

questions.prompt: What changes when the bird imagery becomes Condor years?
facilitatorNotes: The small intimate bird becomes a vast, tumultuous figure of time. The changed scale and sound make adulthood feel less hospitable to playful attention.
evidence: Of late, eternal Condor years

questions.prompt: What condition makes time spent with lyre and rhyme acceptable to the speaker?
facilitatorNotes: It must involve the heart’s trembling, not merely occupy an idle hour. The ending both resists external pressure and requires sincere emotional participation.
evidence: Unless it trembled with the strings.

days.title: Frankenstein, Letter IV: two sledges
days.challenge: Draw the order of sightings and rescue without filling in the strangers’ identities. Then reread Walton’s judgments about the rescued man in light of his earlier longing for a friend.
days.focus: Distinguish observation, inference, and emotional investment in a frame narrator.
days.context: After a brief intervening letter reports the voyage underway, Walton’s ship is caught among Arctic ice. The crew sees one traveler at a distance and later rescues another. This selection is the first dated entry of Letter IV.
days.contentNote: Includes exposure, severe illness, and Walton’s prejudiced contrast between an imagined “savage” and a European.

excerpt.locator: Frankenstein (1831), Letter IV, paragraphs 1–25; opens “_To Mrs. Saville, England._ August 5th, 17--. So strange an accident has”; closes “the stranger at intervals, should I have any fresh incidents to record.”.

questions.prompt: What does the crew see directly, and what does it infer from the first sledge?
facilitatorNotes: They see a distant human-shaped figure of unusual stature on a dog sledge. They infer nearby land despite earlier estimates; that inference is understandable but not established by the sight alone.
evidence: this apparition seemed to denote

questions.prompt: Why is the rescued man’s first question surprising, and what does it suggest about his priorities?
facilitatorNotes: He asks where the ship is going before accepting safety, implying that pursuit matters even at the edge of death. It introduces an overriding purpose without yet explaining its cause or justice.
evidence: will you have the kindness to inform me whither you are bound?

questions.prompt: How does Walton’s need for friendship affect his portrayal of the stranger?
facilitatorNotes: He rapidly sees nobility, benevolence, and a brother of the heart in a man whose story he does not yet know. Kindness and suffering are observed, but the idealizing language may reflect a hope as well as a discovery.
evidence: I begin to love him as a brother

days.title: Frankenstein, Letter IV: a warning offered
days.challenge: Track Walton’s praise alongside the stranger’s self-description. Reread the promise to record the story “as nearly as possible” and consider the layers between events and reader.
days.focus: Evaluate how sympathy and a proposed lesson frame a story before it begins.
days.context: The rescued stranger is recovering aboard Walton’s ship. Walton explains his ambitions; the stranger responds with distress and offers to tell his history. This completes Letter IV and establishes the frame for Victor Frankenstein’s narrative.
days.contentNote: The passage includes despair and a character’s willingness to sacrifice life for discovery.

excerpt.locator: Frankenstein (1831), Letter IV, paragraphs 26–39; opens “August 13th, 17--. My affection for my guest increases every day. He”; closes “storm which embraced the gallant vessel on its course, and wrecked it--thus!”.

questions.prompt: Why does Walton’s willingness to sacrifice a life trigger the stranger’s warning?
facilitatorNotes: The stranger recognizes a destructive pattern in ambition presented as service to knowledge. His image of an intoxicating draught suggests impaired judgment, not merely a lack of courage or preparation.
evidence: Do you share my madness?

questions.prompt: What tension exists between Walton’s praise of judgment and the stranger’s account of his own fate?
facilitatorNotes: Walton calls his discernment never-failing, while the stranger describes a course that led to irreversible disaster. Admiration may predispose Walton to receive the narrative uncritically, though the warning itself asks for reflection.
evidence: a quick but never-failing power of judgment

questions.prompt: How does Walton’s recording plan qualify the apparent immediacy of the coming first-person story?
facilitatorNotes: He will reconstruct speech from listening and sometimes notes, writing when duties permit. The reader receives Victor’s account through an admiring recorder and a letter to Margaret, not unmediated access to events.
evidence: as nearly as possible in his own words

days.title: Frankenstein, Chapter I: care and possession
days.challenge: Separate Victor’s praise of benevolence from the assumptions embedded in descriptions of poverty and beauty. Reread the parents’ duty to a child beside the final language of possessing Elizabeth.
days.focus: Read an idealized family history for its definitions of care, obligation, and ownership.
days.context: The rescued stranger, Victor Frankenstein, begins the story of his childhood. His account is relayed through Walton’s letters. In this 1831 version Elizabeth Lavenza joins his family after being raised by foster parents in Italy.
days.contentNote: The family history includes bereavement, paternalistic charity, and class- and appearance-based hierarchies, including idealization of fair skin and hair.

excerpt.locator: Frankenstein (1831), Chapter I, paragraphs 1–11; opens “I am by birth a Genevese; and my family is one of”; closes “more than sister, since till death she was to be mine only.”.

questions.prompt: What responsibility does Victor’s account assign to parents for the future of a being they bring into life?
facilitatorNotes: They must guide the child toward good and happiness through patience, charity, and self-control. The statement establishes a demanding model of care whose significance can be reconsidered as Victor’s own actions unfold.
evidence: according as they fulfilled their duties towards me

questions.prompt: How does the description of Elizabeth turn physical appearance into a claim of special worth?
facilitatorNotes: Fair hair, blue eyes, and beauty are treated as celestial distinction and even a different species. Readers should distinguish the narrator’s idealizing hierarchy from evidence that one poor child deserves care more than the others.
evidence: a distinct species, a being heaven-sent

questions.prompt: What tension is present in Victor’s promise to protect Elizabeth?
facilitatorNotes: Love and protection appear alongside the repeated claim that she is his possession. The adult recounts a child’s literal reading of a gift, but the final “mine only” carries the possessive idea beyond an innocent moment.
evidence: a possession of my own

days.title: Frankenstein, Chapter II: the first teachers
days.challenge: Map the interests assigned to Victor, Elizabeth, and Clerval. Reread the river metaphor and the claim about what a better parental explanation might have changed.
days.focus: Compare contrasting kinds of knowledge and examine a narrator’s explanation of formative influence.
days.context: Victor describes childhood with Elizabeth and Henry Clerval, then recalls discovering an old book of natural philosophy at thirteen. His adult narration repeatedly anticipates the disaster that followed these early interests.
days.contentNote: Includes idealized gender roles and a historical crusading description that calls religious opponents “infidels.”

excerpt.locator: Frankenstein (1831), Chapter II, paragraphs 1–8; opens “We were brought up together; there was not quite a year difference”; closes “with its contents; and I continued to read with the greatest avidity.”.

questions.prompt: How do the three children’s interests define different relationships to the world?
facilitatorNotes: Victor pursues causes and secrets, Elizabeth appreciates appearances and poetry, and Clerval attends to action and moral relations. The contrasts suggest complementary forms of attention rather than a simple ranking of intelligence.
evidence: the moral relations of things

questions.prompt: What does the mountain-river metaphor imply about the relation between a small beginning and later disaster?
facilitatorNotes: An almost forgotten source grows into a sweeping torrent. The metaphor makes development seem cumulative and overwhelming, but it is the adult narrator’s retrospective pattern, not proof that every step was inevitable.
evidence: from ignoble and almost forgotten sources

questions.prompt: Why does the father’s dismissal of Agrippa fail to redirect Victor?
facilitatorNotes: It names the book trash without explaining the grounds or offering a convincing alternative. Victor doubts the father knows its contents; the adult’s certainty about what explanation would have prevented remains a counterfactual claim.
evidence: the cursory glance my father had taken of my volume

days.title: Frankenstein, Chapter II: certainty overturned
days.challenge: Track what Victor does when experiments fail, then how he reacts to an explanation of lightning. Reread the final language of destiny alongside his reported choices.
days.focus: Distinguish revising a theory from replacing one absolute certainty with another.
days.context: Victor has begun reading Agrippa, Paracelsus, and Albertus Magnus. He hopes for knowledge that can overcome disease and mortality. An electrical storm then challenges the authority of his old books. This completes the chapter’s account of his early studies.

excerpt.locator: Frankenstein (1831), Chapter II, paragraphs 9–16; opens “When I returned home, my first care was to procure the whole”; closes “potent, and her immutable laws had decreed my utter and terrible destruction.”.

questions.prompt: How does Victor protect his favorite authors from the evidence of failed incantations?
facilitatorNotes: He attributes failure to his own inexperience rather than the claims themselves. This preserves the authority of the books against disconfirmation and reveals an uneven standard for judging evidence.
evidence: rather to my own inexperience and mistake

questions.prompt: Why is his response to the lightning explanation not simply a measured acceptance of new science?
facilitatorNotes: He moves from trusting grand promises to despising the entire field and believing nothing can be known, then turns to mathematical certainty. The reaction replaces one sweeping judgment with another.
evidence: It seemed to me as if nothing would or could ever be known.

questions.prompt: What effect does the final appeal to destiny have on our view of responsibility?
facilitatorNotes: It frames later ruin as decreed and casts a temporary change as failed rescue. Readers can hear sincere retrospective anguish while asking whether this language minimizes choices the narrative itself describes.
evidence: Destiny was too potent

days.title: The letters that never arrived
days.challenge: Trace how repeated postponement becomes evidence of a broken promise.
days.focus: Suspense and the gap between courtesy and credit.
days.context: Franklin sails for London believing that Governor Keith will provide recommendations and credit to buy printing equipment.
days.contentNote: Includes an account of a husband abandoning his family.

excerpt.locator: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin, First Visit to London, consecutive paragraphs; opens “THE governor, seeming to like my company, had me frequently to his”; closes “our best laws were of his planning and passed during his administration.”.

questions.prompt: Which repeated pattern should make a reader doubtful before Franklin becomes doubtful?
facilitatorNotes: Each promised delivery moves to another time or place. Courtesy and apparent importance repeatedly replace the actual letters.
evidence: a future time was still named

questions.prompt: What is the force of Denham’s phrase “no credit to give”?
facilitatorNotes: A letter of credit requires financial standing and reliable backing; the phrase also exposes Keith’s lack of credibility. Neither follows automatically from political office.
evidence: no credit to give

questions.prompt: How does the final paragraph complicate the reader’s judgment of Keith?
facilitatorNotes: Franklin condemns the personal deception but credits intelligence and beneficial laws. Discuss whether the explanation excuses, limits, or intensifies the charge.
evidence: having little to give, he gave expectations

days.title: The Water-American and the chapel ghost
days.challenge: Distinguish an argument’s strength from the social conditions that let it succeed.
days.focus: Informal power in a workplace.
days.context: In a London printing house, Franklin moves from presswork to composing type. The workers call their association a chapel.
days.contentNote: Includes heavy drinking, workplace harassment, and historical diet claims rather than health guidance.

excerpt.locator: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin, First Visit to London, consecutive paragraphs; opens “At my first admission into this printing-house I took to working at”; closes “which was generally better paid. So I went on now very agreeably.”.

questions.prompt: How does Franklin use his own work to challenge the belief that beer makes men strong?
facilitatorNotes: He contrasts carrying two forms of type with the others’ one, then gives an economic argument about bread. The companion’s unchanged behavior tests persuasion’s limits.
evidence: He drank on, however

questions.prompt: Why does the master’s agreement fail to protect Franklin from the admission fee?
facilitatorNotes: Formal authority cannot prevent repeated concealed sabotage by coworkers. The ghost story disguises an enforceable social rule.
evidence: notwithstanding the master's protection

questions.prompt: What makes Franklin’s later position more complicated than simply defeating the drinking custom?
facilitatorNotes: Some adopt his breakfast, but he also guarantees other workers’ beer debts. His influence involves compromise, skill, humor, and financial mediation.
evidence: having to pay sometimes near thirty shillings a week on their accounts

days.title: Swimming, commerce, and the road not taken
days.challenge: Follow the alternative futures the memoir opens and then closes.
days.focus: Contingency in a success narrative.
days.context: Near the end of his first stay in London, Franklin earns admiration as a swimmer while considering work and travel with friends.
days.contentNote: Includes unpaid debts and historical descriptions of risky river swimming.

excerpt.locator: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin, First Visit to London, consecutive paragraphs; opens “At Watts's printing-house I contracted an acquaintance with an ingenious young man,”; closes “conversation was of great advantage to me; and I had read considerably.”.

questions.prompt: Why place Denham’s repayment dinner before the account of his job offer?
facilitatorNotes: The unexpected repayment supplies a concrete reason to trust this adviser and prospective employer. Compare reputation established by action with flattering promises.
evidence: the full amount of the unpaid remainder with interest

questions.prompt: Why does Franklin accept lower immediate pay?
facilitatorNotes: He weighs training and future prospects against current composing wages, with his wish to return to Pennsylvania also shaping the decision.
evidence: less, indeed, than my present gettings as a compositor, but affording a better prospect

questions.prompt: How does the possible swimming school challenge a simple story of an inevitable career?
facilitatorNotes: Timing, interest, and an unexpected patron could have altered his destination. The closing paragraph also defines the London stay’s gains in books and acquaintances rather than accumulated money.
evidence: had the overture been sooner made me, probably I should not so soon have returned to America

days.title: Training workers who may replace you
days.challenge: Track how the value of the same skill changes under different business arrangements.
days.focus: Labor, leverage, and partnership.
days.context: After a return to Philadelphia and the end of a mercantile job, Franklin resumes printing for Keimer.
days.contentNote: Includes indentured servitude, exploitation of young workers, alcohol dependence, and dismissive national characterizations.

excerpt.locator: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin, Beginning Business in Philadelphia, consecutive paragraphs; opens “My brother-in-law, Holmes, being now at Philadelphia, advised my return to my”; closes “to be enabled thereby to keep his head much longer above water.”.

questions.prompt: What motive does Franklin infer behind his unusually high wages?
facilitatorNotes: He thinks Keimer wants him to train cheaper contracted workers who will then replace him. Later wage pressure supports the inference, though the memoir cannot directly reveal Keimer’s mind.
evidence: as soon as I had instructed them

questions.prompt: How does Meredith’s proposed partnership value Franklin differently?
facilitatorNotes: Skill becomes a contribution equivalent to invested capital, supporting an equal share rather than a temporary salary to be reduced.
evidence: your skill in the business shall be set against the stock I furnish

questions.prompt: Why does Keimer ask Franklin to return, and how does that return help both sides despite their conflict?
facilitatorNotes: Specialized currency-printing skills protect Keimer’s contract; Franklin can earn while equipment arrives and keep training Meredith. Reconciliation has practical incentives.
evidence: various types that I only could supply

days.title: How a business gains credit
days.challenge: Connect the memoir’s detour through a discussion club to its business narrative.
days.focus: Networks, visible labor, and reputation.
days.context: Franklin and Hugh Meredith have opened their own printing shop. Franklin also recalls founding the Junto, a club for mutual improvement.

excerpt.locator: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin, Beginning Business in Philadelphia, consecutive paragraphs; opens “We had not been long return'd to Philadelphia before the new types”; closes “virtue, when they see its effects in my favour throughout this relation.”.

questions.prompt: What different roles do House and Mickle play at the beginning of the business?
facilitatorNotes: House supplies a first customer at a decisive moment; Mickle supplies discouraging certainty that later property prices undermine. Avoid concluding that every warning is therefore foolish.
evidence: this countryman's five shillings, being our first-fruits

questions.prompt: How are the Junto’s discussion rules related to the club’s long life?
facilitatorNotes: Prepared questions encourage informed contributions; restrictions on direct contradiction discourage humiliating contests. The portraits also distinguish expertise from agreeable collaboration.
evidence: without fondness for dispute, or desire of victory

questions.prompt: Why does Franklin admit that describing his industry sounds like self-praise?
facilitatorNotes: The admission anticipates reader resistance and reframes the example as instruction to descendants. Discuss how neighbors’ observations both support his claim and serve his self-presentation.
evidence: tho' it seems to be talking in my own praise

days.title: Rip Van Winkle: a useful neighbour and an idle farmer
days.challenge: Compare labels applied to Rip and his wife with the actions and material consequences actually described.
days.focus: An apparently affectionate portrait contains evidence that complicates the narrator’s sympathy.
days.context: First of five consecutive scenes from Rip Van Winkle’s main narrative. The introductory Knickerbocker frame is outside this excerpt; the village begins under British rule.
days.contentNote: Historical sexist stereotypes, derogatory descriptions of a wife, and a passing stereotyped reference to Indigenous people.

excerpt.locator: Rip Van Winkle, main narrative, consecutive paragraphs; opens “Whoever has made a voyage up the Hudson must remember the Kaatskill”; closes “pity, I verily believe he reciprocated the sentiment with all his heart.”.

questions.prompt: Why is simply calling Rip lazy inadequate?
facilitatorNotes: He perseveres at fishing and helps neighbours with difficult work while neglecting his own farm. The distinction between chosen communal tasks and family obligations complicates his charm.
evidence: Rip was ready to attend to anybody’s business but his own

questions.prompt: Which details let a reader question the narrator’s treatment of Dame Van Winkle?
facilitatorNotes: Her complaints about ruin have support in the shrinking farm and neglected children, while the narrator repeatedly caricatures her voice. Ask what the sympathetic portrayal of Rip encourages us to overlook.
evidence: His children, too, were as ragged and wild as if they belonged to nobody.

questions.prompt: How is authority exercised at the inn without much speech?
facilitatorNotes: Vedder’s smoking becomes a code others interpret, and his position controls the group. The mock solemnity satirizes a supposedly wise public forum.
evidence: knew how to gather his opinions.

days.title: Rip Van Winkle: the mountain company
days.challenge: Trace what Rip observes, what he guesses and what remains unexplained; reread the thunder comparison.
days.focus: Familiar helpfulness leads into an uncanny scene built through contradictory sound, silence and gesture.
days.context: Second consecutive Rip Van Winkle scene. Having escaped village responsibilities for a mountain ramble, Rip encounters a strangely dressed company.
days.contentNote: Alcohol intoxication, hunting and recurring sexist caricature of Rip’s wife.

excerpt.locator: Rip Van Winkle, main narrative, consecutive paragraphs; opens “In a long ramble of the kind on a fine autumnal day,”; closes “head, his head gradually declined, and he fell into a deep sleep.”.

questions.prompt: What draws Rip toward the stranger even while he feels apprehensive?
facilitatorNotes: His readiness to help a presumed neighbour overrides fear. The same trait that endeared him to the village propels him into the uncanny encounter.
evidence: supposing it to be some one of the neighbourhood in need of his assistance

questions.prompt: How does the sound of thunder gain a second explanation?
facilitatorNotes: What initially seems weather becomes the sound of ninepins. The landscape and the game remain linked, inviting a supernatural explanation without an explicit narrator’s announcement.
evidence: echoed along the mountains like rumbling peals of thunder.

questions.prompt: Why is the company’s pleasure unsettling?
facilitatorNotes: Grave faces, silence and fixed stares contradict amusement. Rip’s gradual drinking then replaces fear with impaired awareness, closing the scene in sleep rather than understanding.
evidence: the most melancholy party of pleasure he had ever witnessed.

days.title: Rip Van Winkle: an unfamiliar home
days.challenge: Track the order of clues and distinguish Rip’s assumptions from details a reader can interpret differently.
days.focus: Accumulated discrepancies undermine a character’s familiar account of reality.
days.context: Third consecutive Rip Van Winkle scene. Rip wakes after drinking with the mountain company, believing that only one night has passed.
days.contentNote: Abandoned home, family absence and disparaging language about Rip’s wife.

excerpt.locator: Rip Van Winkle, main narrative, consecutive paragraphs; opens “On waking, he found himself on the green knoll whence he had”; closes “a cocked hat, and underneath was painted in large characters, “GENERAL WASHINGTON.””.

questions.prompt: Why do Rip’s explanations become less convincing as the scene develops?
facilitatorNotes: He attributes bodily stiffness to his bed and the altered gun to a trick, but the grown beard, changed stream and village require a larger explanation. List evidence before deciding what happened.
evidence: These mountain beds do not agree with me

questions.prompt: How does the altered response of animals and children intensify estrangement?
facilitatorNotes: Formerly friendly children and dogs now mock or reject him. Recognition is social as well as visual, and the possibly mistaken identification of Wolf sharpens his loneliness.
evidence: My very dog

questions.prompt: What makes the repainted inn sign both a change and a continuity?
facilitatorNotes: The same face and material sign are adapted from king to Washington. This visual joke makes political transformation visible while showing the reuse of familiar forms.
evidence: The red coat was changed for one of blue and buff

days.title: Rip Van Winkle: the election crowd
days.challenge: Read the crowd’s questions from both its perspective and Rip’s; examine how interrupted syntax represents bewilderment.
days.focus: Political vocabulary and mistaken recognition turn social change into a crisis of identity.
days.context: Fourth consecutive Rip Van Winkle scene. Rip reaches the former inn and meets an election gathering after finding his home and village transformed.
days.contentNote: Threatening crowd behaviour and reports of war deaths.

excerpt.locator: Rip Van Winkle, main narrative, consecutive paragraphs; opens “There was, as usual, a crowd of folk about the door, but”; closes “changed, and I can’t tell what’s my name, or who I am!””.

questions.prompt: How has public conversation changed from the old inn society?
facilitatorNotes: Urgent dispute, handbills and political categories replace slow newspaper reading and smoking. The narrator lets Rip hear the vocabulary as incomprehensible, separating historical change from his understanding of it.
evidence: a perfect Babylonish jargon

questions.prompt: Why does Rip’s declaration of loyalty provoke danger rather than trust?
facilitatorNotes: The crowd hears allegiance to a rejected king where Rip intends reassurance. The exchange shows that words depend on political circumstances the speaker does not know.
evidence: a loyal subject of the king

questions.prompt: Why is seeing a man like himself more destabilizing than hearing that friends have disappeared?
facilitatorNotes: His own name and appearance seem to belong to another person, so the problem shifts from altered surroundings to personal identity. His broken speech enacts that confusion.
evidence: I’m not myself--I’m somebody else

days.title: Rip Van Winkle: recognition and a settled story
days.challenge: Distinguish recognition, corroboration and repetition; reread the narrator’s excuses and the final political–domestic analogy.
days.focus: A community restores a man’s place while turning uncertain memory into a familiar legend.
days.context: Final consecutive excerpt of Rip Van Winkle’s main narrative. The editorial Note and Postscript that follow in the source are not included.
days.contentNote: Sexist stereotypes; mention of possible suicide, colonial fears of Indigenous people, death and bereavement. The claim that Hudson first discovered an inhabited region reflects colonial framing.

excerpt.locator: Rip Van Winkle, main narrative, consecutive paragraphs; opens “The bystanders began now to look at each other, nod, wink significantly,”; closes “they might have a quieting draught out of Rip Van Winkle’s flagon.”.

questions.prompt: Which kinds of evidence restore Rip’s identity, and which supposedly confirm his extraordinary explanation?
facilitatorNotes: His daughter and the older woman establish personal recognition; Vanderdonk supplies inherited folklore for the mountain story. Those are different evidential tasks, not one proof.
evidence: He recollected Rip at once, and corroborated his story

questions.prompt: How does the closing account of Rip’s freedom narrow the political change he has missed?
facilitatorNotes: The narrative shifts from national independence to escape from a wife it caricatures. Readers can question this gendered comparison, especially alongside the unchanged idleness inherited by his son.
evidence: Rip, in fact, was no politician

questions.prompt: Why mention that the story varied before becoming fixed?
facilitatorNotes: The detail leaves uncertainty about memory, invention and communal repetition. A stable popular version need not prove the events, even though the narrator gives a reassuring excuse.
evidence: vary on some points every time he told it

days.title: Frankenstein, Chapter III: leaving the house of mourning
days.challenge: Read the mother’s final requests beside Elizabeth’s subsequent actions. Trace Victor’s changing feelings during the journey rather than treating departure as either simple freedom or simple abandonment.
days.focus: Analyze how an account of education begins with loss and unequal expectations of care.
days.context: At seventeen Victor prepares for university in Ingolstadt, but his mother dies after nursing Elizabeth through scarlet fever. The selection follows the family’s grief and Victor’s eventual journey, ending with his arrival.
days.contentNote: A parent dies from illness; the passage describes bereavement and expectations placed on a young woman to assume family care.

excerpt.locator: Frankenstein (1831), Chapter III, paragraphs 1–9; opens “When I had attained the age of seventeen, my parents resolved that”; closes “conducted to my solitary apartment, to spend the evening as I pleased.”.

questions.prompt: What future roles does Caroline’s deathbed request assign to Victor and Elizabeth?
facilitatorNotes: She imagines their marriage and asks Elizabeth to replace her care for the younger children. The request joins affection with a heavy gendered responsibility; readers may recognize devotion without treating the expectation as neutral.
evidence: you must supply my place to my younger children

questions.prompt: How does the account distinguish the first shock of grief from its later reality?
facilitatorNotes: At first the mind cannot accept absence; time confirms it and deepens bitterness. The narrator then turns toward continuing duties, describing a process rather than a single uniform emotion.
evidence: when the lapse of time proves the reality of the evil

questions.prompt: Why do Victor’s spirits rise during the journey even though he initially resists leaving?
facilitatorNotes: The new solitude frightens him, but the long-desired opportunity to learn and enter the world returns to view. Conflicting feelings can coexist; the change does not prove his earlier love or grief insincere.
evidence: as I proceeded, my spirits and hopes rose

days.title: Frankenstein, Chapter III: two professors
days.challenge: Mark what both professors reject and what Waldman honors in earlier inquiry. Reread Victor’s response to “unlimited powers” beside Waldman’s later advice for broad study.
days.focus: Compare the content of instruction with the rhetoric that makes it persuasive.
days.context: Newly arrived at Ingolstadt, Victor consults Krempe and attends Waldman’s lecture. Both teach modern science, but their manners and accounts of earlier thinkers differ. Victor narrates these encounters after the disastrous events of his story.

excerpt.locator: Frankenstein (1831), Chapter III, paragraphs 10–21; opens “The next morning I delivered my letters of introduction, and paid a”; closes “Thus ended a day memorable to me: it decided my future destiny.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Krempe’s technically relevant correction fail to win Victor’s interest?
facilitatorNotes: Contempt and an unappealing manner alienate Victor, who also dislikes modest practical aims. The scene distinguishes the truth of a correction from the conditions under which a learner will accept it.
evidence: the teacher, therefore, did not prepossess me

questions.prompt: How does Waldman reconcile respect for older thinkers with rejection of their impossible promises?
facilitatorNotes: He credits their zeal and groundwork while distinguishing modern achievements from mistaken systems. This lets Victor revise his allegiance without treating all previous effort as worthless.
evidence: however erroneously directed

questions.prompt: What gap appears between Waldman’s advice and the ambition Victor takes from the lecture?
facilitatorNotes: Waldman recommends broad study and careful preparation; Victor hears a summons to surpass all predecessors and uncover creation’s deepest mysteries. His response intensifies the rhetoric of power beyond ordinary instruction.
evidence: more, far more, will I achieve

days.title: Frankenstein, Chapter IV: discovery and withheld knowledge
days.challenge: Separate evidence of sustained study from the unsupported details of the extraordinary discovery. Reread the direct address to Walton to see how the tale becomes a warning instead of a technical explanation.
days.focus: Examine how a narrator both excites curiosity and refuses to satisfy it.
days.context: Victor describes two years of increasingly absorbing scientific study and his claimed discovery of how to animate lifeless matter. He is telling the story to Walton, who seeks knowledge and glory himself. The selection stops before Victor chooses what to make.
days.contentNote: Describes anatomical study, graves, and bodily decay in a Gothic account of scientific obsession; it supplies no usable procedure.

excerpt.locator: Frankenstein (1831), Chapter IV, paragraphs 1–6; opens “From this day natural philosophy, and particularly chemistry, in the most comprehensive”; closes “than he who aspires to become greater than his nature will allow.”.

blocks.text: THE MUTABILITY OF LITERATURE
A COLLOQUY IN WESTMINSTER ABBEY
WASHINGTON IRVING

"I know that all beneath the moon decays,
And what by mortals in this world is brought,
In time's great period shall return to nought.
I know that all the muse's heavenly lays,
With toil of sprite which are so dearly bought,
As idle sounds, of few or none are sought,
That there is nothing lighter than mere praise."
--DRUMMOND OF HAWTHORNDEN.

There are certain half-dreaming moods of mind, in which we naturally steal away from noise and glare, and seek some quiet haunt, where we may indulge our reveries and build our air castles undisturbed. In such a mood I was loitering about the old gray cloisters of Westminster Abbey, enjoying that luxury of wandering thought which one is apt to dignify with the name of reflection; when suddenly an interruption of madcap boys from Westminster School, playing at football, broke in upon the monastic stillness of the place, making the vaulted passages and mouldering tombs echo with their merriment. I sought to take refuge from their noise by penetrating still deeper into the solitudes of the pile, and applied to one of the vergers for admission to the library. He conducted me through a portal rich with the crumbling sculpture of former ages, which opened upon a gloomy passage leading to the chapter-house and the chamber in which doomsday book is deposited. Just within the passage is a small door on the left. To this the verger applied a key; it was double locked, and opened with some difficulty, as if seldom used. We now ascended a dark narrow staircase, and, passing through a second door, entered the library.

I found myself in a lofty antique hall, the roof supported by massive joists of old English oak. It was soberly lighted by a row of Gothic windows at a considerable height from the floor, and which apparently opened upon the roofs of the cloisters. An ancient picture of some reverend dignitary of the church in his robes hung over the fireplace. Around the hall and in a small gallery were the books, arranged in carved oaken cases. They consisted principally of old polemical writers, and were much more worn by time than use. In the center of the library was a solitary table with two or three books on it, an inkstand without ink, and a few pens parched by long disuse. The place seemed fitted for quiet study and profound meditation. It was buried deep among the massive walls of the abbey, and shut up from the tumult of the world. I could only hear now and then the shouts of the school-boys faintly swelling from the cloisters, and the sound of a bell tolling for prayers, echoing soberly along the roofs of the abbey. By degrees the shouts of merriment grew fainter and fainter, and at length died away; the bell ceased to toll, and a profound silence reigned through the dusky hall.

I had taken down a little thick quarto, curiously bound in parchment, with brass clasps, and seated myself at the table in a venerable elbow-chair. Instead of reading, however, I was beguiled by the solemn monastic air, and lifeless quiet of the place, into a train of musing. As I looked around upon the old volumes in their mouldering covers, thus ranged on the shelves, and apparently never disturbed in their repose, I could not but consider the library a kind of literary catacomb, where authors, like mummies, are piously entombed, and left to blacken and moulder in dusty oblivion.

How much, thought I, has each of these volumes, now thrust aside with such indifference, cost some aching head! how many weary days! how many sleepless nights! How have their authors buried themselves in the solitude of cells and cloisters; shut themselves up from the face of man, and the still more blessed face of nature; and devoted themselves to painful research and intense reflection! And all for what? to occupy an inch of dusty shelf--to have the title of their works read now and then in a future age, by some drowsy churchman or casual straggler like myself; and in another age to be lost, even to remembrance. Such is the amount of this boasted immortality. A mere temporary rumor, a local sound; like the tone of that bell which has just tolled among these towers, filling the ear for a moment--lingering transiently in echo--and then passing away like a thing that was not.

While I sat half murmuring, half meditating these unprofitable speculations with my head resting on my hand, I was thrumming with the other hand upon the quarto, until I accidentally loosened the clasps; when, to my utter astonishment, the little book gave two or three yawns, like one awaking from a deep sleep; then a husky hem; and at length began to talk. At first its voice was very hoarse and broken, being much troubled by a cobweb which some studious spider had woven across it; and having probably contracted a cold from long exposure to the chills and damps of the abbey. In a short time, however, it became more distinct, and I soon found it an exceedingly fluent conversable little tome. Its language, to be sure, was rather quaint and obsolete, and its pronunciation, what, in the present day, would be deemed barbarous; but I shall endeavor, as far as I am able, to render it in modern parlance.

It began with railings about the neglect of the world--about merit being suffered to languish in obscurity, and other such commonplace topics of literary repining, and complained bitterly that it had not been opened for more than two centuries; that the dean only looked now and then into the library, sometimes took down a volume or two, trifled with them for a few moments, and then returned them to their shelves. "What a plague do they mean," said the little quarto, which I began to perceive was somewhat choleric, "what a plague do they mean by keeping several thousand volumes of us shut up here, and watched by a set of old vergers, like so many beauties in a harem, merely to be looked at now and then by the dean? Books were written to give pleasure and to be enjoyed; and I would have a rule passed that the dean should pay each of us a visit at least once a year; or if he is not equal to the task, let them once in a while turn loose the whole school of Westminster among us, that at any rate we may now and then have an airing."

"Softly, my worthy friend," replied I, "you are not aware how much better you are off than most books of your generation. By being stored away in this ancient library, you are like the treasured remains of those saints and monarchs, which lie enshrined in the adjoining chapels; while the remains of your contemporary mortals, left to the ordinary course of nature, have long since returned to dust."

"Sir," said the little tome, ruffling his leaves and looking big, "I was written for all the world, not for the bookworms of an abbey. I was intended to circulate from hand to hand, like other great contemporary works; but here have I been clasped up for more than two centuries, and might have silently fallen a prey to these worms that are playing the very vengeance with my intestines, if you had not by chance given me an opportunity of uttering a few last words before I go to pieces."

"My good friend," rejoined I, "had you been left to the circulation of which you speak, you would long ere this have been no more. To judge from your physiognomy, you are now well stricken in years: very few of your contemporaries can be at present in existence; and those few owe their longevity to being immured like yourself in old libraries; which, suffer me to add, instead of likening to harems, you might more properly and gratefully have compared to those infirmaries attached to religious establishments, for the benefit of the old and decrepit, and where, by quiet fostering and no employment, they often endure to an amazingly good-for-nothing old age. You talk of your contemporaries as if in circulation--where do we meet with their works? what do we hear of Robert Groteste, of Lincoln? No one could have toiled harder than he for immortality. He is said to have written nearly two hundred volumes. He built, as it were, a pyramid of books to perpetuate his name: but, alas! the pyramid has long since fallen, and only a few fragments are scattered in various libraries, where they are scarcely disturbed even by the antiquarian. What do we hear of Giraldus Cambrensis, the historian, antiquary, philosopher, theologian, and poet? He declined two bishoprics, that he might shut himself up and write for posterity; but posterity never inquires after his labors. What of Henry of Huntingdon, who, besides a learned history of England, wrote a treatise on the contempt of the world, which the world has revenged by forgetting him? What is quoted of Joseph of Exeter, styled the miracle of his age in classical composition? Of his three great heroic poems one is lost forever, excepting a mere fragment; the others are known only to a few of the curious in literature; and as to his love verses and epigrams, they have entirely disappeared. What is in current use of John Wallis, the Franciscan, who acquired the name of the tree of life? Of William of Malmsbury;--of Simeon of Durham;--of Benedict of Peterborough;--of John Hanvill of St. Albans;--of----"

"Prithee, friend," cried the quarto, in a testy tone, "how old do you think me? You are talking of authors that lived long before my time, and wrote either in Latin or French, so that they in a manner expatriated themselves, and deserved to be forgotten; but I, sir, was ushered into the world from the press of the renowned Wynkyn de Worde. I was written in my own native tongue, at a time when the language had become fixed; and indeed I was considered a model of pure and elegant English."
(I should observe that these remarks were couched in such intolerably antiquated terms, that I have had infinite difficulty in rendering them into modern phraseology.)
