blocks.text: The family meeting was warm and affectionate; as the evening was far advanced, the Squire would not permit us to change our travelling dresses, but ushered us at once to the company, which was assembled in a large old-fashioned hall. It was composed of different branches of a numerous family connection, where there were the usual proportion of old uncles and aunts, comfortably married dames, superannuated spinsters, blooming country cousins, half-fledged striplings, and bright-eyed boarding-school hoydens. They were variously occupied; some at a round game of cards; others conversing around the fireplace; at one end of the hall was a group of the young folks, some nearly grown up, others of a more tender and budding age, fully engrossed by a merry game; and a profusion of wooden horses, penny trumpets, and tattered dolls, about the floor, showed traces of a troop of little fairy beings, who having frolicked through a happy day, had been carried off to slumber through a peaceful night.

While the mutual greetings were going on between Bracebridge and his relatives, I had time to scan the apartment. I have called it a hall, for so it had certainly been in old times, and the Squire had evidently endeavoured to restore it to something of its primitive state. Over the heavy projecting fireplace was suspended a picture of a warrior in armour, standing by a white horse, and on the opposite wall hung helmet, buckler, and lance. At one end an enormous pair of antlers were inserted in the wall, the branches serving as hooks on which to suspend hats, whips, and spurs; and in the corners of the apartment were fowling-pieces, fishing-rods, and other sporting implements. The furniture was of the cumbrous workmanship of former days, though some articles of modern convenience had been added, and the oaken floor had been carpeted; so that the whole presented an odd mixture of parlour and hall.

The grate had been removed from the wide overwhelming fireplace, to make way for a fire of wood, in the midst of which was an enormous log glowing and blazing, and sending forth a vast volume of light and heat; this I understood was the Yule-log, which the Squire was particular in having brought in and illumined on a Christmas eve, according to ancient custom.

It was really delightful to see the old Squire seated in his hereditary elbow-chair by the hospitable fireside of his ancestors, and looking around him like the sun of a system, beaming warmth and gladness to every heart. Even the very dog that lay stretched at his feet, as he lazily shifted his position and yawned, would look fondly up in his master's face, wag his tail against the floor, and stretch himself again to sleep, confident of kindness and protection. There is an emanation from the heart in genuine hospitality which cannot be described, but is immediately felt, and puts the stranger at once at his ease. I had not been seated many minutes by the comfortable hearth of the worthy cavalier before I found myself as much at home as if I had been one of the family.

Supper was announced shortly after our arrival. It was served up in a spacious oaken chamber, the panels of which shone with wax, and around which were several family portraits decorated with holly and ivy. Beside the accustomed lights, two great wax tapers, called Christmas candles, wreathed with greens, were placed on a highly-polished buffet among the family plate. The table was abundantly spread with substantial fare; but the Squire made his supper of frumenty, a dish made of wheat cakes boiled in milk with rich spices, being a standing dish in old times for Christmas eve. I was happy to find my old friend, minced-pie, in the retinue of the feast; and finding him to be perfectly orthodox, and that I need not be ashamed of my predilection, I greeted him with all the warmth wherewith we usually greet an old and very genteel acquaintance.

The mirth of the company was greatly promoted by the humours of an eccentric personage whom Mr. Bracebridge always addressed with the quaint appellation of Master Simon. He was a tight, brisk little man, with the air of an arrant old bachelor. His nose was shaped like the bill of a parrot; his face slightly pitted with the small-pox, with a dry perpetual bloom on it, like a frost-bitten leaf in autumn. He had an eye of great quickness and vivacity, with a drollery and lurking waggery of expression that was irresistible. He was evidently the wit of the family, dealing very much in sly jokes and innuendoes with the ladies, and making infinite merriment by harpings upon old themes; which, unfortunately, my ignorance of the family chronicles did not permit me to enjoy. It seemed to be his great delight during supper to keep a young girl next him in a continual agony of stifled laughter, in spite of her awe of the reproving looks of her mother, who sat opposite. Indeed, he was the idol of the younger part of the company, who laughed at everything he said or did, and at every turn of his countenance. I could not wonder at it; for he must have been a miracle of accomplishments in their eyes. He could imitate Punch and Judy; make an old woman of his hand, with the assistance of a burnt cork and pocket-handkerchief; and cut an orange into such a ludicrous caricature, that the young folks were ready to die with laughing.

I was let briefly into his history by Frank Bracebridge. He was an old bachelor of a small independent income, which by careful management was sufficient for all his wants. He revolved through the family system like a vagrant comet in its orbit; sometimes visiting one branch, and sometimes another quite remote; as is often the case with gentlemen of extensive connections and small fortunes in England. He had a chirping, buoyant disposition, always enjoying the present moment; and his frequent change of scene and company prevented his acquiring those rusty unaccommodating habits with which old bachelors are so uncharitably charged. He was a complete family chronicle, being versed in the genealogy, history, and intermarriages of the whole house of Bracebridge, which made him a great favourite with the old folks; he was a beau of all the elder ladies and superannuated spinsters, among whom he was habitually considered rather a young fellow, and he was a master of the revels among the children; so that there was not a more popular being in the sphere in which he moved than Mr. Simon Bracebridge. Of late years he had resided almost entirely with the Squire, to whom he had become a factotum, and whom he particularly delighted by jumping with his humour in respect to old times, and by having a scrap of an old song to suit every occasion. We had presently a specimen of his last-mentioned talent; for no sooner was supper removed, and spiced wines and other beverages peculiar to the season introduced, than Master Simon was called on for a good old Christmas song. He bethought himself for a moment, and then, with a sparkle of the eye, and a voice that was by no means bad, excepting that it ran occasionally into a falsetto, like the notes of a split reed, he quavered forth a quaint old ditty,--

Now Christmas is come,
Let us beat up the drum,
And call all our neighbours together;
And when they appear,
Let us make them such cheer,
As will keep out the wind and the weather, etc.

questions.prompt: What does the mixture of old furnishings and newer comforts suggest about the Squire’s preservation of the past?
facilitatorNotes: The room is neither a museum nor wholly modern. Details such as the carpet show selective adaptation, complicating the claim that old customs survive unchanged.
evidence: an odd mixture of parlour and hall

questions.prompt: How do the sun and comet comparisons distinguish the Squire from Master Simon?
facilitatorNotes: The Squire is a stable centre around which relatives gather, while Simon moves between households and occasions. Both sustain connection, but through different kinds of presence and influence.
evidence: like the sun of a system

questions.prompt: Why can the narrator enjoy hospitality without fully enjoying the family’s jokes?
facilitatorNotes: Shared history makes the humour intelligible to insiders. His confessed ignorance marks a limit to instant belonging, even within an exceptionally welcoming gathering.
evidence: my ignorance of the family chronicles did not permit me to enjoy

days.title: Christmas Eve: Dancing and a Midnight Song
days.challenge: Read the courtship scene for discrepancies between assertion and gesture; reread the last paragraph aloud to hear its slowing movement.
days.focus: Gesture and musical pacing allow a comic gathering to end in intimate, uncertain perception.
days.context: Final consecutive Christmas Eve scene. Dancing and an embedded old song lead into the narrator’s retreat to his room. The song is quoted within Irving’s narrative, not presented as a separate daily selection.
days.contentNote: Historical courtship conventions, drinking, and a reference to a war injury.

excerpt.locator: Old Christmas (1886), consecutive paragraphs of “Christmas Eve”; opens “The supper had disposed every one to gaiety, and an old harper”; closes “died away, my head sank upon the pillow and I fell asleep.”.

questions.prompt: What does the contrast between Master Simon’s formal steps and the younger dancers reveal about tradition?
facilitatorNotes: The older style survives through performance and affectionate amusement, while energetic dancing continues around it. The passage presents continuity as a mixture of generations rather than exact repetition.
evidence: a kind of connecting link between the old times and the new

questions.prompt: How do Julia’s actions complicate the narrator’s claim that she is indifferent to the officer?
facilitatorNotes: The emphatic claim of indifference is undercut by her blushes and destruction of the bouquet while he sings. Discuss dramatic irony while allowing that an observer cannot fully know her feelings.
evidence: the nosegay lay in ruins on the floor

questions.prompt: How does the final listening scene change the pace and scale of the evening?
facilitatorNotes: Public movement and conversation give way to a private, half-waking experience of music. Repetition prolongs attention as the sounds recede, making the close feel suspended between memory and sleep.
evidence: I listened and listened

days.title: Frankenstein, Chapter XII: language and an invisible gift
days.challenge: Track one revision of an initial misunderstanding, then follow how it changes behavior. Reread the hopes of becoming visible beside the pain of seeing a reflection.
days.focus: Trace the connection between learning, empathy, and the desire for recognition.
days.context: Hidden beside the cottage, the creature observes the family through winter. It gradually recognizes their poverty, learns words and relationships, helps them secretly, and imagines introducing itself once speech can overcome fear of its appearance.
days.contentNote: The narrator internalizes harsh judgments about its appearance and compares itself to a mistreated animal.

excerpt.locator: Frankenstein (1831), Chapter XII, paragraphs 1–19; opens “"I lay on my straw, but I could not sleep. I thought”; closes “the future gilded by bright rays of hope, and anticipations of joy."”.

questions.prompt: What changes when the creature understands that the family is poor?
facilitatorNotes: The cottage first looks luxurious by comparison with its own life. Recognizing the younger people’s hunger reveals that taking food harms them, so it stops and begins supplying wood. Knowledge changes conduct through sympathy.
evidence: when I found that in doing this I inflicted pain on the cottagers, I abstained

questions.prompt: Why are the first learned words and the discovery of written signs meaningful beyond a vocabulary list?
facilitatorNotes: Concrete necessities and family names map the household’s life; written signs suggest speech can be stored and recovered. Language promises access to feelings and relationships the creature already observes but cannot join.
evidence: he found on the paper signs for speech

questions.prompt: How do the secret gifts and imagined introduction expose a gap between contribution and belonging?
facilitatorNotes: The creature already helps materially and is unknowingly called a good spirit, yet expects its appearance to cause disgust. It hopes gentle speech can make visible worth recognized; the hopeful ending does not establish that others will respond fairly.
evidence: until, by my gentle demeanour and conciliating words

days.title: Frankenstein, Chapter XIII: the burden of understanding
days.challenge: Distinguish the history lesson’s sweeping categories from the creature’s questions about them. Reread the progression from words and letters to property, belonging, and self-definition.
days.focus: Assess education as access to knowledge that can also expose the learner’s vulnerability.
days.context: Safie arrives at the cottage and learns its language. The hidden creature follows her lessons, including history read from Volney and explanations of social rank and family life. Greater understanding brings both intellectual pleasure and a sharper sense of exclusion.
days.contentNote: Contains ethnic stereotypes in a historical lesson, colonial violence, class exclusion, and a distressed reflection on death as escape. Discussion should examine these claims and feelings without endorsing them.

excerpt.locator: Frankenstein (1831), Chapter XIII, paragraphs 1–22; opens “"I now hasten to the more moving part of my story. I”; closes “so I loved, in an innocent, half painful self-deceit, to call them)."”.

questions.prompt: Why does Safie’s arrival accelerate the creature’s learning?
facilitatorNotes: Lessons intended for a visible newcomer make language explicit and repeatable for the hidden listener. The two learn from the same instruction while having very different access to welcome and conversation.
evidence: I should make use of the same instructions to the same end

questions.prompt: How does learning history complicate the creature’s earlier admiration of human beings?
facilitatorNotes: Accounts of accomplishment coexist with conquest, vice, and bloodshed, prompting a question about human greatness and cruelty. The lesson itself contains stereotypes; readers should examine its framing rather than endorse every generalization.
evidence: so powerful, so virtuous, and magnificent, yet so vicious and base?

questions.prompt: Why does knowledge of property and family make the question “What was I?” more painful?
facilitatorNotes: Social categories reveal that it lacks money, ancestry, friends, and recognized kinship, not just comfort. Knowledge names forms of exclusion previously obscure; the repeated question remains unresolved by its intellectual progress.
evidence: But where were my friends and relations?

days.title: Ode to a Nightingale
days.challenge: Read once for the speaker’s changing wishes, again aloud for recurring sounds, and a third time across the transitions at “Away,” “Darkling,” and “Forlorn.” Distinguish the mortal bird from the imagined continuity of its song.
days.focus: Follow an imaginative journey whose ending questions the power that made it possible.
days.context: Keats’s speaker hears a bird and imagines escaping human suffering through wine, poetry, and the continuity of song. Lethe is the mythological river of forgetting; Bacchus is associated with wine; Ruth is a biblical exile.
days.contentNote: The speaker reflects on death and briefly imagines dying while hearing the song; the discussion treats this as a literary expression of distress, not advice.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem: Ode to a Nightingale; opens “My heart aches, and a drowsy numbness pains”; closes “Fled is that music:--Do I wake or sleep?”.

questions.prompt: Why does the poem move from a wish for wine to the “viewless wings of Poesy”?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker first imagines bodily escape through intoxication, then makes imagination the vehicle. The shift tests different routes beyond suffering, while the dull brain and final return qualify the success of either.
evidence: But on the viewless wings of Poesy,

questions.prompt: How does the imagined “immortal Bird” differ from a claim that one animal literally lives forever?
facilitatorNotes: The voice seems to connect different generations, social ranks, and imagined worlds. The bird becomes a figure for recurring song or artistic experience; the poem’s imaginative address need not be read as zoological assertion.
evidence: The voice I hear this passing night was heard

questions.prompt: What does “Forlorn” do to the poem’s movement, and why does the ending remain a question?
facilitatorNotes: A word from the fantasy rings like a bell and returns the speaker to the isolated self. The fading sound leaves the status of the experience uncertain; escape has been powerful but temporary.
evidence: To toll me back from thee to my sole self!

days.title: Ode on a Grecian Urn
days.challenge: Reread each stanza as a change in the speaker’s relation to the urn. Mark unanswered questions and compare “happy” with “Cold Pastoral” before interpreting the final declaration.
days.focus: Examine the attractions and costs of permanence in an imagined artwork.
days.context: The speaker addresses an ancient decorated vessel and imagines stories in its figures. The poem supplies the verbal object of study; no particular external image is needed. Tempe and Arcady evoke idealized Greek landscapes.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem: Ode on a Grecian Urn; opens “Thou still unravish'd bride of quietness,”; closes “Ye know on earth, and all ye need to know.”.

questions.prompt: How can the unheard music be “sweeter” than heard music, and what is lost with that advantage?
facilitatorNotes: Imagination can idealize music that never ends or disappoints, but actual sound and change are absent. The poem entertains permanence as a pleasure while making its incompleteness visible.
evidence: Heard melodies are sweet, but those unheard

questions.prompt: How does the empty town complicate the earlier praise of figures that never change?
facilitatorNotes: The lovers keep beauty but cannot complete a kiss; the town remains permanently emptied with nobody able to explain it. Stillness preserves a scene at the cost of return, fulfillment, and knowledge.
evidence: and not a soul to tell

questions.prompt: How should the final claim about beauty and truth be read in relation to “Cold Pastoral”?
facilitatorNotes: Accept a consoling artistic maxim or a deliberately troubling, limited statement if supported by the poem’s shifts. The urn’s endurance coexists with its silence and coldness; the ending should not erase those tensions.
evidence: Cold Pastoral!

days.title: Ode to Psyche
days.challenge: Read the lists beginning “Nor” and “Thy” aloud, then map how the final stanza turns parts of a landscape into parts of a mind. Attend to the difference between an existing shrine and a promised one.
days.focus: Analyze a poem that makes its own imaginative act the answer to an absence.
days.context: Psyche, whose name evokes soul, is the beloved of Cupid in classical myth. Keats imagines her as arriving too late for the ancient forms of worship and offers an inward sanctuary through poetry.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem: Ode to Psyche; opens “O Goddess! hear these tuneless numbers, wrung”; closes “To let the warm Love in!”.

questions.prompt: How does the second stanza establish what Psyche lacks despite her beauty?
facilitatorNotes: Repeated negatives list missing temple, altar, choir, instrument, shrine, and oracle. Beauty alone has not secured a public institution of devotion, creating the need the speaker later undertakes to meet.
evidence: though temple thou hast none,

questions.prompt: What changes when the speaker repeats the earlier missing objects as things he will become?
facilitatorNotes: The list of absence becomes an offer of voice and imaginative labor. The speaker does not discover a lost temple; he proposes to create the functions of worship through the poem and his mind.
evidence: So let me be thy choir

questions.prompt: How does the final garden image combine deliberate construction with unpredictable creativity?
facilitatorNotes: Priest, sanctuary, and trellis suggest making and arranging, while branching thoughts and Fancy’s never-repeated flowers suggest growth beyond a fixed plan. Multiple supported readings of the open casement are welcome.
evidence: Who breeding flowers, will never breed the same:

facilitatorNotes: Washington connects family security, comfort, property, and access to voting. Identify these distinct arguments without assuming his historical description guarantees rights in every case.
evidence: one of the conditions for voting

questions.prompt: What distinction does he make when he calls the minister’s dwelling a house but not a home?
facilitatorNotes: For him ownership alone is insufficient: care, usable surroundings, and leadership by example are required. Ask what the visible exterior can and cannot prove about its occupants.

facilitatorNotes: The home should support continuing education and shared family life, not simply a pleasing exterior or increasing property value.

days.title: Calling Things by Their Right Names

days.context: Washington addresses Tuskegee students about what he regards as misleading claims to educational and religious authority. This address is complete.

facilitatorNotes: The speaker permits ambition while rejecting a present claim unsupported by resources or achievement. Naming is tied to public trust.
evidence: I do not by any means intend to say that schools do not have the right to aspire

facilitatorNotes: Both claim intellectual work or authority that the person has not earned. Examine how the repeated foundation metaphor joins appearance to actual preparation.
evidence: all come from this false foundation

facilitatorNotes: No: Washington explicitly makes room for seminaries and colleges preparing clergy. His stated objection is competition that diverts children from a better-equipped common school.

days.title: The Value of System in Home Life
days.challenge: Follow the argument from misplaced objects to time available for learning.
days.focus: Domestic organization as an educational resource.

facilitatorNotes: The opening gives practical arrangements a social purpose. Order is presented as a way to reduce worry and make a home useful to others.
evidence: the greatest amount of happiness in these homes

facilitatorNotes: The accumulating sequence makes delay and dependence visible. The example dramatizes a system failing at several linked steps.

facilitatorNotes: The household examples support a possible saving of time; the regional explanation makes a much broader causal claim without comparable evidence about income and opportunity.

days.title: Education That Educates
days.challenge: Distinguish a defense of practical learning from a dismissal of every book-based study.
days.focus: Original problems and visible demonstrations of learning.
days.context: After President McKinley’s 1898 visit to Tuskegee, Washington reflects on students’ preparations and displays. This is the complete address; the source’s separate explanatory editorial footnote is not part of the address.
days.contentNote: Includes support for opportunities connected with American colonial possessions and an unqualified promise that skill will overcome exclusion.

excerpt.locator: Character Building, complete address “Education That Educates”; opens “EDUCATION THAT EDUCATES Perhaps I am safe in saying that during the”; closes “you will find that nothing under the sun will keep us back.”.
