blocks.text: EDUCATION THAT EDUCATES

Perhaps I am safe in saying that during the last ten days you have not given much systematic effort to book study in the usual sense. When interruptions come such as we have just had, taking you away from your regular routine work and study, and the preparation of routine lessons is interrupted, the first thought to some may be that this time is lost, in so far as it relates to education in the ordinary sense; that it is so much time taken away from that part of one's life that should be devoted to acquiring education. I suppose that during the last few days the questions have come to many of you: "What are we gaining? What are we getting from the irregularity that has characterized the school grounds within the last week, that will in any degree compensate for the amount of book study that we have lost?"

To my mind I do not believe that you have lost anything by the interruption. On the other hand, I am convinced that you have got the best kind of education. I do not mean to say that we can depend upon it for all time to come for systematic training of the mind, but so far as real education, so far as development of the mind and heart and body are concerned, I do not believe that a single student has lost anything by the irregularity of the last week or more.

You have gained in this respect: in preparing for the reception and entertainment of the President of the United States and his Cabinet, and the distinguished persons who accompanied the party, you have had to do an amount of original thinking which you, perhaps, have never had to do before in your lives. You have been compelled to think; you have been compelled to put more than your bodily strength into what you have been doing. You could not have made the magnificent exhibition of our work which you have made if you had not been compelled to do original thinking and execution. Most of you never saw such an exhibition before; I never did. Those of you who had to construct floats that would illustrate our agricultural work and our mechanical and academic work, had to put a certain amount of original thought into the planning of these floats, in order to make them show the work to the best advantage; and two-thirds of you—yes, practically all of you—had never seen anything of the kind before. For this reason it was a matter that had to be thought out by you and planned out by you, and then put into visible shape.

Now compare that kind of education with the mere committing to memory of certain rules, or something which some one else thought out and executed a thousand years ago perhaps—and that is what a large part of our education really is. Education in the usual sense of the word is the mere committing to memory of something which has been known before us. Now during the last ten days we have had to solve problems of our own, not problems and puzzles that some one else originated for us. I do not believe that there is a person connected with the institution who is not stronger in mind, who is not more self-confident and self-reliant, so far as the qualities relate to what he is able to do with his mind or his hands, than he was ten or twelve days ago. There is the benefit that came to all of us. It put us to thinking and planning; it brought us in to contact with things that are out of the ordinary; and there is no education that surpasses this. I see more and more every year that the world is to be brought to the study of men and of things, rather than to the study of mere books. You will find more and more as the years go by, that people will gradually lay aside books, and study the nature of man in a way they have never done as yet. I tell you, then, that in this interruption of the regular school work you have not lost anything:—you have gained; you have had your minds awakened, your faculties strengthened, and your hands guided.

I do not wish to speak of this matter egotistically, but it is true that I have heard a great many persons from elsewhere mention the pleasure which they have received in meeting Tuskegee students, because when they come in contact with a student who has been here, they are impressed with the fact that he or she does not seem to be dead or sleepy. They say that when they meet a Tuskegee boy or girl they find a person who has had contact with real life. The education that you have been getting during the last few days, you will find, as the years go by, has been of a kind that will serve you in good stead all through your lives.

Just in proportion as we learn to execute something, to put our education into tangible form—as we have been doing during the last few days—in just the same proportion will we find ourselves of value as individuals and as a race. Those people who came here to visit us knew perfectly well that we could commit to memory certain lines of poetry, they knew we were able to solve certain problems in algebra and geometry, they understood that we could learn certain rules in chemistry and agriculture; but what interested them most was to see us put into visible form the results of our education. Just in proportion as an individual is able to do that, he is of value to the world. That is the object of the work which we are trying to do here. We are trying to turn out men and women who are able to do something that the world wants done, that the world needs to have done. Just in proportion as you can comply with that demand you will find that there is a place for you—there is going to be standing room. By the training we are giving you here we are preparing you for a place in the world. We are going to train you so that when you get to that place, if you fail in it, the failure will not be our fault.

It is a great satisfaction to have connected with a race men and women who are able to do something, not merely to talk about doing it, not merely to theorize about doing it, but actually to do something that makes the world better to live in, something that enhances the comforts and conveniences of life. I had a good example of this last week. I wanted something done in my office which required a practical knowledge of electricity. It was a great satisfaction when I called upon one of the teachers, to have him do the work in a careful, praiseworthy manner. It is very well to talk or lecture about electricity, but it is better to be able to do something of value with one's knowledge of electricity.

And so, as you go on, increasing your ability to do things of value, you will find that the problem which often now-a-days looks more and more difficult of solution will gradually become easier. One of the Cabinet members who were here a few days ago said, after witnessing the exhibition which you made here, that the islands which this country had taken into its possession during the recent war are soon going to require the service of every man and woman we can turn out from this institution. You will find it true, not only in this country but in other countries, that the demand will be more and more for people who can do something. Just in proportion as we can, as a race, get the reputation which I spoke to you about a few days ago, you will find there will be places for us. Regardless of colour or condition, the world is going to give the places of trust and remuneration to the men and women who can do a certain thing as well as anybody else or better. This is the whole problem. Shall we prepare ourselves to do something as well as anybody else or better? Just in proportion as we do this, you will find that nothing under the sun will keep us back.

questions.prompt: Why does preparing the exhibition count as education in Washington’s argument?
facilitatorNotes: Students solve unfamiliar design problems and turn plans into physical results. The claim rests on original thought and execution, not simply being busy.
evidence: a matter that had to be thought out by you and planned out by you

questions.prompt: Where does Washington limit his criticism of routine study?
facilitatorNotes: He says the event cannot replace systematic mental training indefinitely. Compare that concession with the later claim that people will lay aside books.
evidence: I do not mean to say that we can depend upon it for all time to come

questions.prompt: What is the difference between showing that students can do valuable work and proving that nothing can keep them back?
facilitatorNotes: The exhibition provides evidence of capacity; the final claim assumes institutions will always reward capacity regardless of exclusion. Keep achievement and guaranteed opportunity distinct.
evidence: nothing under the sun will keep us back

days.title: The Importance of Being Reliable
days.challenge: Track when reported employer opinions become the speaker’s own causal explanations.
days.focus: Reputation, evidence, and collective judgment.
days.context: Washington reports conversations with employers in North and South Carolina and asks Tuskegee students to influence work habits. This address is complete.
days.contentNote: Repeats racial stereotypes about workers and attributes poverty to unreliability. Discussion separates reported prejudice, particular behavior, and unsupported generalization.

excerpt.locator: Character Building, complete address “The Importance of Being Reliable”; opens “THE IMPORTANCE OF BEING RELIABLE. I am going to call your attention”; closes “make us as a race firmer and stronger in these important directions.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Washington initially distinguish the truth of a reputation from its effects?
facilitatorNotes: An employer’s belief can restrict hiring even if counterexamples exist. That identifies the power of a stereotype without establishing its accuracy.
evidence: whether it is true or not, the results are the same

questions.prompt: Where does the speech move beyond reporting what employers said?
facilitatorNotes: He later directly attributes irregular employment and poverty largely to the described habits. Ask what additional evidence would be needed for that causal conclusion.
evidence: Wherever our people are not getting regular, paying employment

questions.prompt: What double task does Washington assign to educated students?
facilitatorNotes: They must establish their own steadiness and reshape expectations and conduct in communities. Examine the burden of making individuals responsible for a whole group’s reputation.
evidence: you young men and young women who are being educated in institutions of learning

days.title: Robinson Crusoe: from deliverance to provisions
days.challenge: Trace shifts between emotional judgment and practical action; reread the order in which provisions, clothing and tools are selected.
days.focus: A survivor’s changing priorities turn an inventory of objects into a study of value and grief.
days.context: First of three consecutive salvage scenes from Robinson Crusoe. A shipwreck has left the narrator alone on a shore. This begins after his escape from the sea and ends with loading essential supplies.
days.contentNote: Shipwreck deaths, fear of starvation and predators, tobacco and alcohol. The novel’s earlier voyage involved a proposed slave-trading expedition; the selected scene does not narrate that expedition.

excerpt.locator: Robinson Crusoe, main narrative, consecutive paragraphs; opens “I walked about on the shore, lifting up my hands and my”; closes “to look into it, for I knew in general what it contained.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Crusoe call his rescue a dreadful deliverance?
facilitatorNotes: Immediate gratitude gives way to exposure, hunger and isolation. The paradox preserves both survival and continuing danger rather than treating rescue as a finished success.
evidence: a dreadful deliverance

questions.prompt: How does finding the wreck change grief into action without removing grief?
facilitatorNotes: He imagines that staying aboard might have saved his companions, then searches for access and supplies. Practical activity follows renewed tears; it does not prove he has ceased to mourn.
evidence: a fresh renewing of my grief

questions.prompt: Why is the carpenter’s chest more valuable than gold here?
facilitatorNotes: Tools can produce future necessities, whereas gold depends on a social exchange system he cannot access. His loading decisions establish a situational scale of value.
evidence: much more valuable than a ship-loading of gold

days.title: Robinson Crusoe: landing the raft
days.challenge: Sketch the raft’s changing position while rereading, then distinguish observed dangers from imagined ones.
days.focus: Detailed movement of a raft demonstrates the interaction of observation, uncertainty and revised design.
days.context: Second consecutive salvage scene. Crusoe has built and loaded a raft; he must land it, survey the island and return for another load.
days.contentNote: Firearms, hunting, fears of animals, and a colonial claim about the first gun fired on the island.

excerpt.locator: Robinson Crusoe, main narrative, consecutive paragraphs; opens “My next care was for some ammunition and arms. There were two”; closes “and brought them all safe on shore, to my very great comfort.”.

questions.prompt: How does the tide function as both a danger and a resource?
facilitatorNotes: Uneven grounding nearly tips the cargo, but rising water frees the raft and falling water finally leaves it safely ashore. The solution depends on changing conditions as well as strength.
evidence: the rising of the water brought me a little more upon a level

questions.prompt: Which fears in his survey are observations, and which remain conjectures?
facilitatorNotes: The view establishes an island, but he sees no dangerous beasts. The older narrator explicitly says his fear of being devoured was unnecessary; distinguish that retrospective correction from what he knew then.
evidence: there was really no need for those fears.

questions.prompt: What changes on his second raft, and what does that reveal about learning?
facilitatorNotes: He reduces size and load after the first near disaster. His knowledge emerges from specific difficulty rather than from a complete plan formed at the start.
evidence: I neither made this so unwieldy, nor loaded it so hard

days.title: Robinson Crusoe: money and the disappearing ship
days.challenge: Compare stated judgments with actions; reread the money speech and its immediate reversal.
days.focus: Practical accumulation is complicated by overloading, habitual value and the final loss of the wreck.
days.context: Final consecutive salvage scene. Crusoe continues recovering supplies until changing weather destroys the ship as a usable store.
days.contentNote: Firearms, alcohol and the remains of a shipwreck.

excerpt.locator: Robinson Crusoe, main narrative, consecutive paragraphs; opens “I was under some apprehensions during my absence from the land, that”; closes “her afterwards did; but those things were of small use to me.”.

questions.prompt: How does the cat encounter expose a limit of Crusoe’s apparent power?
facilitatorNotes: He points a gun, but the animal does not recognize the threat and responds instead to food. His imagined human-style acquaintance gives the brief encounter a comic and companionable turn.
evidence: as she did not understand it

questions.prompt: How does the overturned raft complicate the pattern of successful salvage?
facilitatorNotes: The desire to recover more produces an unwieldy load and loss. Hard work and previous experience do not prevent a new error, and recovery consumes still more effort.
evidence: so unwieldy and so overladen

questions.prompt: What should a reader make of his taking the money immediately after dismissing it?
facilitatorNotes: The action contradicts the speech and can suggest habit, hope for future society or reluctance to abandon familiar value. The text does not state one definitive motive, so distinguish inference from fact.
evidence: However, upon second thoughts, I took it away

days.title: Robinson Crusoe: designing a refuge
days.challenge: Map each feature to a stated need, then reread the narrator’s qualifications about danger and security.
days.focus: A detailed refuge design reveals competing priorities and a revised understanding of vulnerability.
days.context: An independent scene after the salvage sequence. Crusoe chooses a longer-term habitation, builds a fence and tent, and changes his storage after a storm.
days.contentNote: Uses the dehumanizing historical term savages and groups imagined human threats with beasts. Discuss this as Crusoe’s prejudiced assumption; firearm and powder storage are narrative details, not practical instructions.

excerpt.locator: Robinson Crusoe, main narrative, consecutive paragraphs; opens “My thoughts were now wholly employed about securing myself against either savages,”; closes “wet might come to it, marking very carefully where I laid it.”.

questions.prompt: How do his four requirements for a home balance staying alive with leaving the island?
facilitatorNotes: Water, shade and protection support settlement, while a sea view preserves hope of rescue. The design serves both present habitation and a possible departure.
evidence: of which I was not willing to banish all my expectation yet.

questions.prompt: What does the later narrator add to the account of his fortress?
facilitatorNotes: He reports secure sleep but also says the feared enemies did not require such caution. The defence can therefore have a psychological function even where its imagined threat lacks evidence.
evidence: there was no need of all this caution

questions.prompt: Why does the lightning thought make him interrupt the building project?
facilitatorNotes: Concentrated powder creates a different vulnerability from outside attack. He reallocates labour to separate storage after imagining a single failure destroying his means of defence and food supply.
evidence: O my powder!

days.title: Robinson Crusoe: ordering goods and keeping a journal
days.challenge: Compare the material arrangement of the cave with the narrator’s arrangement of experience; notice qualifications to his confidence in reason.
days.focus: Physical order and written order emerge together in a retrospective account of adaptation.
days.context: An independent scene in which Crusoe enlarges and organizes his dwelling before introducing the journal he says he kept. No following journal entries are included.
days.contentNote: Brief description of distressed self-directed hitting and fear after shipwreck.

excerpt.locator: Robinson Crusoe, main narrative, consecutive paragraphs; opens “I have already described my habitation, which was a tent under the”; closes “for having no more ink, I was forced to leave it off.”.

questions.prompt: Why are a chair and table more than optional luxuries in this account?
facilitatorNotes: They enable writing, eating and enjoyment as well as bodily convenience. The passage expands survival from having supplies to arranging a usable daily life.
evidence: I could not write or eat

questions.prompt: How does the one-board example qualify his sweeping claim about reason and skill?
facilitatorNotes: He celebrates inventiveness but consumes a whole tree and much time for one plank. Achievement is real, yet the inefficient process reveals the cost of missing tools and experience.
evidence: one board out of a whole tree

questions.prompt: How does he explain the delay in starting his journal, and what might that omit?
facilitatorNotes: He cites mental discomposure as well as labour, calling earlier experiences dull. Discuss how the later narrator selects and judges the frightened earlier self rather than offering an unfiltered record.
evidence: my journal would have been full of many dull things.

days.title: Fancy
days.challenge: Read aloud for quick rhymes and accumulation. On rereading, mark changes of season and place that could not happen simultaneously in ordinary experience, then examine the final return to the opening claim.
days.focus: Test the promise that imagination can renew pleasures dulled by repetition.
days.context: Keats personifies the imaginative faculty as a winged being. The poem begins beside a winter fire and gathers sensations from different seasons. Ceres’s daughter is Persephone; Hebe is associated with youth in Greek myth.
days.contentNote: Classical allusions include an idealized beloved and a brief nonexplicit image of Hebe’s loosened clothing.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem: Fancy; opens “Ever let the Fancy roam,”; closes “Pleasure never is at home.”.

questions.prompt: Why is winter beside the fire a useful setting for the poem’s command to release Fancy?
facilitatorNotes: The still, dark, restricted present contrasts with the abundance memory and imagination can summon. The scene gives the imaginative journey a concrete deprivation to answer rather than presenting images at random.
evidence: Beauties that the earth hath lost;

questions.prompt: How does the poem make its impossible mixture of seasons feel abundant rather than confused?
facilitatorNotes: Repeated commands and sensory lists bring spring birds, summer delight, and autumn wealth together; the comparison to blended wines gives combination a pleasurable logic. Students should cite the deliberate simultaneity.
evidence: She will mix these pleasures up

questions.prompt: Does the return to “Pleasure never is at home” solve the problem of pleasure fading?
facilitatorNotes: It offers continual imaginative movement as an answer, yet the repeated claim also suggests no lasting satisfaction is secured. Accept celebration or qualified unease if the ending is connected to the earlier problem of use and fading.
evidence: Pleasure never is at home.

days.title: To Autumn
days.challenge: Read each stanza aloud at a different pace suggested by its verbs. Reread the final stanza for sound, then connect its movement toward evening with the earlier abundance.
days.focus: Explain how ripeness, pause, and departure coexist within a celebration.
days.context: Keats addresses autumn as a season, a companion of the sun, and several human figures at harvest. A gleaner gathers grain remaining after reaping; a cyder-press extracts juice from apples.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem: To Autumn; opens “Season of mists and mellow fruitfulness,”; closes “And gathering swallows twitter in the skies.”.

questions.prompt: How do the first stanza’s verbs make abundance feel active?
facilitatorNotes: Loading, bending, filling, swelling, and plumping show ripeness being produced, not merely displayed. The sun and season collaborate, while the bees’ belief in endless warmth quietly exceeds what a season can promise.
evidence: Until they think warm days will never cease,

questions.prompt: What changes when autumn becomes a resting reaper or patient watcher at the press?
facilitatorNotes: The energetic accumulation slows into suspension and lingering. Work, rest, and the last stages of harvest give the season a human rhythm and introduce an ending without abrupt loss.
evidence: Thou watchest the last oozings hours by hours.

questions.prompt: How does the final stanza answer the missing songs of spring without denying decline?
facilitatorNotes: It names autumn’s own varied sounds while keeping soft-dying daylight, mourning gnats, and gathering swallows. The affirmation values the present season rather than pretending it is spring or that departure has stopped.
evidence: Think not of them, thou hast thy music too,

days.title: Ode on Melancholy
days.challenge: Read the opening negatives and the second stanza’s “But” as an argument. Reread the last stanza to trace the personifications of Beauty, Joy, Pleasure, and Melancholy.
days.focus: Analyze a paradox in which the depth of joy creates awareness of loss.
days.context: Keats’s ode rejects oblivion and then locates melancholy within intense experience of beauty and pleasure. Lethe represents forgetting; Psyche can mean soul. Mythic plants and figures belong to the poem’s imagery, not a practical set of instructions.
days.contentNote: The poem names poisonous plants while explicitly rejecting oblivion and death. It also includes a historically possessive image of a lover’s hand; discuss the imagery without treating it as guidance.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem: Ode on Melancholy; opens “No, no, go not to Lethe, neither twist”; closes “And be among her cloudy trophies hung.”.

questions.prompt: What does the opening reject, and why is “wakeful” important to that rejection?
facilitatorNotes: It rejects numbing oblivion and death-associated emblems that would drown awareness. Wakefulness preserves the capacity to feel; the poem’s later response depends on engaging experience rather than erasing it.
evidence: the wakeful anguish of the soul.

questions.prompt: How does the weeping-cloud image make sadness both obscuring and nourishing?
facilitatorNotes: The cloud hides the hill yet fosters flowers. The double action prepares a conception of melancholy as bound up with growth and beauty rather than simply their opposite.
evidence: That fosters the droop-headed flowers all,

questions.prompt: Why is Melancholy’s shrine inside the temple of Delight?
facilitatorNotes: Pleasure’s intensity includes knowledge that beauty dies and joy departs. The final image makes grief inseparable from fully tasting transient joy; it need not mean that all happiness is worthless.
evidence: Ay, in the very temple of Delight

days.title: To Wordsworth
days.challenge: Read the sonnet aloud, locate the turn at “One loss,” and trace the light and refuge images. On rereading, distinguish literal death from the loss of a valued public voice.
days.focus: Analyze how praise can become the basis of a pointed reproach.
days.context: Shelley addresses an older poet whose earlier writing he admired. The sonnet moves from shared grief about passing life to a specific accusation that Wordsworth has abandoned commitments to truth and liberty. This is the speaker’s judgment, not a neutral biography.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem: To Wordsworth; opens “Poet of Nature, thou hast wept to know”; closes “Thus having been, that thou shouldst cease to be.”.

questions.prompt: What do the first four lines allow the speaker to share with Wordsworth before disagreeing?
facilitatorNotes: Both experience the loss of youth, friendship, and love. The common grief establishes kinship and respect, making the later charge a disappointed appeal rather than an attack without prior attachment.
evidence: These common woes I feel.

questions.prompt: How do the star and refuge images explain the importance of the older poet’s former role?
facilitatorNotes: He provided guidance and shelter to a vulnerable traveler or public. The images turn artistic influence into a responsibility, which sharpens the accusation of desertion.
evidence: Thou wert as a lone star, whose light did shine

questions.prompt: What does the final claim that Wordsworth has ceased to be mean within this address to him?
facilitatorNotes: It laments the disappearance of the principled voice the speaker valued, not the person’s literal existence. The paradox depends on the earlier praise and the specific charge of abandoning truth and liberty.
evidence: Thus having been, that thou shouldst cease to be.

days.title: Ozymandias
days.challenge: Read once following the chain of speakers, once contrasting inscription and landscape, and once aloud for the final spacious sounds. Mark what survives in art and what fails in political power.
days.focus: Explain how framed speech and material setting reverse a boast.
days.context: A speaker reports a traveler’s account of a ruined statue and its inscription. Ozymandias is a Greek form of a name associated with the Egyptian ruler Ramesses II. The supplied poem itself contains the scene needed for analysis.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem: Ozymandias; opens “I met a traveller from an antique land”; closes “The lone and level sands stretch far away.”.

questions.prompt: How does the sculptor preserve something the ruler may not have meant to expose?
facilitatorNotes: The carved frown and sneer preserve an attitude of command beyond the ruler’s life. Art transmits a reading of power, not just the ruler’s preferred public title; mocked can suggest imitation and invite an ironic reading.
evidence: its sculptor well those passions read

questions.prompt: Why does “despair” change force when read beside the surrounding landscape?
facilitatorNotes: The inscription demands awe before unmatched works, but nothing remains except wreck and sand. Despair can now arise from the failure of permanence rather than a rival’s inferiority.
evidence: Nothing beside remains.

questions.prompt: What does the traveler frame contribute that a direct description would not?
facilitatorNotes: The ruler’s claim reaches us through successive voices and time, reducing its immediate authority. Readers encounter a reported relic whose meaning is shaped by witnesses and setting rather than a command still in force.
evidence: I met a traveller from an antique land

days.title: The Highest Education
days.challenge: Read the repeated definition of education as a sequence of expanding tests.
days.focus: Knowledge, moral conduct, and appreciation of beauty.
days.context: In this complete address, Washington explains what he believes Tuskegee’s academic and practical training should ultimately accomplish.
days.contentNote: Includes dated disability terminology and judgments linking housing conditions to education; the passage also explicitly condemns mocking disabled people.

excerpt.locator: Character Building, complete address “The Highest Education”; opens “THE HIGHEST EDUCATION It may seem to some of you that I”; closes “the best, the purest and the most beautiful things out of life.”.

questions.prompt: What role remains for an orderly mind after Washington criticizes memorization?
facilitatorNotes: He values mental training as the means to find information, reason, and turn goodwill into effective action. His criticism is of treating stored facts as the final goal.
evidence: all heart and no head

questions.prompt: How does the response to an unfortunate stranger become a test of education?
facilitatorNotes: Conduct toward someone with less power reveals justice and sympathy more directly than recitation. Compare the rejection of ridicule with the address’s claims about universal service.
evidence: the one who is really cultivated, is gentle and sympathetic to everyone

questions.prompt: How does the ending connect books, beautiful surroundings, and truthful conduct?
facilitatorNotes: Books become means toward cultivated perception and ethical relationships. Students may also question whether the housing test confuses resources with disposition.
evidence: not an end, but a means to an end

days.title: Keeping Your Word
days.challenge: Compare what three personal experiences and one counterexample can logically establish.
days.focus: Reliability, notice, and the limits of examples.
days.context: Washington draws on travel experiences and reports about employment to address Tuskegee students. This is the complete address.
days.contentNote: Includes racial generalizations and a defense of employers withholding wages. The text is historical argument, not employment or legal guidance.

excerpt.locator: Character Building, complete address “Keeping Your Word”; opens “KEEPING YOUR WORD I do not want to speak to you continually”; closes “and to keep at it until reliability becomes a part of you.”.

questions.prompt: What alternative to perfectly keeping every engagement does Washington explicitly allow?
facilitatorNotes: He recognizes unavoidable failure but expects advance notice or a substitute. This makes the practical standard communication and responsibility rather than absolute control.
evidence: if they had sent another hackman to fill the engagement for them

questions.prompt: What does Mr. Lewis’s position disprove, and what does it fail to prove?
facilitatorNotes: It disproves an absolute claim that no Black person can attain responsibility; a single success does not show that equal opportunity exists generally or that prejudice has no effects.
evidence: This single instance shows

questions.prompt: How does the discussion of withheld wages treat the workers’ possible objections?
facilitatorNotes: It mentions employers’ power and self-interest but returns to workers’ reliability. Examine the unsupported assertion that delayed access to earned money means no loss.
evidence: Of course the men do not lose anything in the end by this method

days.title: The Gospel of Service
days.challenge: Track how one word crosses occupations with very different kinds of power.
days.focus: Redefinition, dignity, and occupational hierarchy.
days.context: In this complete address, Washington seeks to dignify useful work, including domestic service, for Tuskegee students.
days.contentNote: Contains racial and gender assumptions, claims discounting discrimination, and a proposal tying employment to a prior employer’s recommendation.

excerpt.locator: Character Building, complete address “The Gospel of Service”; opens “THE GOSPEL OF SERVICE The subject on which I am going to”; closes “future may be still greater than it has been in the past.”.

questions.prompt: How does the opening redefine the word servant?
facilitatorNotes: The list places presidents, governors, merchants, teachers, and domestic workers under a shared duty to others. Ask what the definition reveals and what differences in power remain.
evidence: Every individual serves another in some capacity

questions.prompt: Why does a lecture about dusting matter to the argument?
facilitatorNotes: An educated lecturer and cultivated audience illustrate that ordinary work can require organized knowledge; the example challenges the equation of domestic work with ignorance.
evidence: one of the most valuable hours I ever spent

questions.prompt: What tension appears between honoring present work and describing children as rising to higher things?
facilitatorNotes: The speech insists on equal honor for skilled service but retains a hierarchy of future advancement. Readers can explain the strategic argument without treating it as free of tension.
evidence: our children and grandchildren are to rise to higher things

days.title: Some Great Little Things
days.challenge: Distinguish the practical value of a habit from judgments about a person’s worth.
days.focus: Paradox, repeated practice, and self-examination.
days.context: Washington gives Tuskegee students a complete address about daily routines, personal care, reading, and reflection.
days.contentNote: Includes historical health assertions and harsh judgments based on cleanliness and clothing. These are not medical guidance or standards for judging classmates.

excerpt.locator: Character Building, complete address “Some Great Little Things”; opens “SOME GREAT LITTLE THINGS I am going to speak to you for”; closes “you are stronger in everything essential to good manhood and good womanhood.”.

questions.prompt: How does the title’s apparent contradiction organize the speech?
facilitatorNotes: Ordinary actions are small in scale but, he argues, large in cumulative effect. Trace this reasoning across grooming, order, reading, and reflection.
evidence: great, because of their supreme importance

questions.prompt: What does making a habit “a part of yourselves” mean here?
facilitatorNotes: Repetition should make the action nearly automatic and its omission feel unusual. Discuss whether that mechanism alone justifies his judgments about graduates’ worth.
evidence: to leave it undone would seem unnatural

questions.prompt: How does the final image of walking upon dead selves revise the earlier emphasis on fixed habits?
facilitatorNotes: Habits should persist, but self-examination should discard prior weaknesses. The striking metaphor makes continuity and deliberate change work together.
evidence: walk upon your dead selves of the week before

days.title: To Would-Be Teachers
days.challenge: Reconstruct a practical proposal from its resources, steps, and expected benefits.
days.focus: Community participation and educational tradeoffs.
days.context: This complete address offers future teachers a plan for extending short school terms in Southern communities.
days.contentNote: Describes children’s agricultural labor and gendered work roles in a historical school-funding proposal.

excerpt.locator: Character Building, complete address “To Would-be Teachers”; opens “TO WOULD-BE TEACHERS Since very many of you whom I see before”; closes “she cannot add much to her income by sewing, dressmaking or poultry-raising.”.

questions.prompt: How does the contribution of six eggs affect the definition of a useful donation?
facilitatorNotes: It makes participation possible for people without cash and anticipates contributions of labor, transport, land, and produce. The anecdote makes the collective plan tangible.
evidence: one old coloured woman brought me six eggs

questions.prompt: Why might helping build a school change pupils’ relationship to it?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker predicts that participation gives students a personal stake. Distinguish the material contribution from the proposed effect on interest.
evidence: they have had a hand in its erection

questions.prompt: What tradeoff does Washington ask parents to accept in the school-farm proposal?
facilitatorNotes: Shorter classroom days and agricultural labor fund a longer yearly term and practical instruction. Evaluate the stated benefits alongside burdens that the address does not measure.
evidence: keep the school open six or seven months

days.title: Robinson Crusoe: tools, excavation and a falling roof
days.challenge: Read the dates as a measure of hidden work; distinguish producing a tool, using it and repairing the result.
days.focus: A journal sequence makes dependencies, substitutions and revised criteria for completion visible.
days.context: A contiguous run of journal entries from November 17 through December 20, including the narrator’s inserted notes. Crusoe is enlarging his storage cave.
days.contentNote: Threat of accidental burial and references to hunting. Historical construction methods are treated as narrative choices, not as instructions.

excerpt.locator: Robinson Crusoe, main narrative, consecutive paragraphs; opens “Nov. 17. This day I began to dig behind my tent into”; closes “to be very scarce with me: also I made me another table.”.

questions.prompt: Why must work on the cave stop before it can advance?
facilitatorNotes: The desired space depends on tools that themselves require materials, design and time. This chain of prerequisites gives an ordinary excavation narrative tension.
evidence: I desisted from my work

questions.prompt: How does abandoning a wheelbarrow differ from simply giving up?
facilitatorNotes: He recognizes the wheel and axle problem and substitutes a hod. The less elaborate device accomplishes the immediate transport task, so adaptation includes narrowing an ambition.
evidence: I made me a thing like a hod

questions.prompt: What does the roof collapse reveal about his judgment that the cave was finished?
facilitatorNotes: Usable space had increased without adequate support. The repair produces partitions as well as safety, showing a new design emerging from a serious failure.
evidence: it seems I had made it too large

days.title: Robinson Crusoe: the unexpected grain
days.challenge: Track differences between the experiencing character and the later narrator; reread the final delay before the grain can be eaten.
days.focus: A discovery shifts from apparent miracle to remembered cause without losing the narrator’s devotional meaning.
days.context: An independent episode beginning with improvised lighting and a discarded feed bag, then following the discovery of barley and rice. The return to the journal marks its end.
days.contentNote: Devotional claims and hunting; readers can analyze the narrator’s beliefs without sharing them.

excerpt.locator: Robinson Crusoe, main narrative, consecutive paragraphs; opens “In the next place, I was at a great loss for candle;”; closes “did that also after some time. But to return to my journal.”.

questions.prompt: How does the placement of the discarded bag information affect the reader’s response to the barley?
facilitatorNotes: Readers already know about the husks before Crusoe recalls them. This creates a gap between the reader’s likely explanation and his astonishment at apparently spontaneous grain.
evidence: I shook the husks of corn out of it

questions.prompt: Does remembering the bag end the narrator’s religious interpretation?
facilitatorNotes: It reduces the earlier self’s wonder, but the retrospective voice argues that ordinary causes can still be providential. Distinguish a natural explanation from the narrator’s interpretation of its significance.
evidence: though I ought to have been as thankful

questions.prompt: Why does this apparent gift not become immediate food?
facilitatorNotes: The grain must be saved as seed, and failed seasonal judgment delays consumption for years. Promise and usable abundance are separated by labour, risk and time.
evidence: it was not till the fourth year

days.title: Robinson Crusoe: an earthquake changes the meaning of safety
days.challenge: Separate reported sensations from causal guesses; reread the final decision as a trade-off rather than complete reassurance.
days.focus: A natural disaster turns a secure enclosure into a competing source of danger.
days.context: A complete earthquake-and-immediate-decision episode from the journal sequence. The excerpt stops before the next project of sharpening tools.
days.contentNote: Earthquake, fear of burial and violent storm. Crusoe’s claim linking a hurricane causally to an earthquake is his historical belief, not scientific or safety guidance.

excerpt.locator: Robinson Crusoe, main narrative, consecutive paragraphs; opens “I worked excessive hard these three or four months to get my”; closes “it was finished and fit to remove to. This was the 21st.”.

questions.prompt: Why place the earthquake immediately after the completed enclosure?
facilitatorNotes: The apparent solution to outside danger becomes exposure to collapse from above. The sequence reverses security almost as soon as Crusoe declares it achieved.
evidence: The very next day after this wall was finished

questions.prompt: How do observation and inference differ in his decision to re-enter the cave?
facilitatorNotes: He observes rain and an absence of new shocks but assumes a causal sequence in which the earthquake is spent. Discuss how the need for shelter makes an uncertain explanation attractive; it is not sound modern hazard guidance.
evidence: these winds and rain being the consequence of the earthquake

questions.prompt: Why does he remain temporarily in a place he has decided is dangerous?
facilitatorNotes: A new protected site requires time, while open exposure also frightens him. The decision is a compromise among risks, attachment to completed work and limited capacity.
evidence: I must be contented to run the venture where I was

days.title: Robinson Crusoe: the inland valley and two homes
days.challenge: Distinguish discovery, knowledge and ownership; trace how attraction to a place is tested by transport, weather and rescue priorities.
days.focus: Exploration reveals the limits of knowledge and an unexamined claim of possession alongside practical compromise.
days.context: An independent inland exploration episode, ten months into Crusoe’s island life, ending with the dried-grape harvest and return of heavy rains.
days.contentNote: Colonial ownership assumptions, historical labels for Indigenous people, enslavement and reported illness deaths. Plant and health claims are elements of the historical novel, not guidance.

excerpt.locator: Robinson Crusoe, main narrative, consecutive paragraphs; opens “I had been now in this unhappy island above ten months; all”; closes “that I could not stir out of my cave for several days.”.

questions.prompt: How does the discovery of abundant plants expose a lack rather than simply solve one?
facilitatorNotes: He sees resources but cannot identify their uses, admitting he learned little while in Brazil. Availability and usable knowledge are distinct.
evidence: might perhaps have virtues of their own, which I could not find out.

questions.prompt: What assumptions let Crusoe call himself king and rightful possessor?
facilitatorNotes: He moves from believing no one has set foot there to claiming ownership and inheritance in English legal terms. The text supplies his assertion, not proof of a legitimate right; ask whose possible claims his reasoning excludes.
evidence: I was king and lord of all this country

questions.prompt: Why retain the coastal home despite finding the valley more pleasant?
facilitatorNotes: A sea view keeps open the possibility of rescue, while the inland bower provides temporary comfort and fruit. Later rain also reveals a practical advantage of the original shelter.
evidence: to render such an affair not only improbable, but impossible

days.title: Robinson Crusoe: failed sowing and a living fence
days.challenge: Reread to map initial expectation, observed result and revised action in each episode; compare their different forms of uncertainty.
days.focus: Two plant episodes contrast failed prediction with useful surprise and deliberate reuse.
days.context: An independent paired episode after the accidental grain discovery: Crusoe tests planting seasons and finds that cut fence stakes have grown.

excerpt.locator: Robinson Crusoe, main narrative, consecutive paragraphs; opens “The rainy season, and the dry season, began now to appear regular”; closes “served for a defence also, as I shall observe in its order.”.

questions.prompt: What does saying he bought his experience emphasize?
facilitatorNotes: Knowledge costs failed crops and time rather than arriving as abstract advice. The metaphor makes error part of the price of adapting to an unfamiliar climate.
evidence: I bought all my experience before I had it

questions.prompt: Why does keeping some seed matter as much as choosing a better planting place?
facilitatorNotes: A reserve makes a second trial possible after the first fails. The small successful harvest reflects both cautious allocation and changed conditions, not insight alone.
evidence: I would not sow it all at first

questions.prompt: How does the growing fence change the role of an object Crusoe thought he had finished making?
facilitatorNotes: Cut stakes become living trees, shade and future defence. He learns from an unplanned result and reproduces it elsewhere, unlike the failed first sowing.
evidence: the stakes which I had cut off of some trees

days.title: Hymn to Intellectual Beauty
days.challenge: Reread each stanza to name its function: description, question, rejection, appeal, memory, vow, or mature hope. Track the repeated images of a passing shadow rather than treating the power as fully defined.
days.focus: Follow a lyric argument that honors uncertainty while committing to a value.
days.context: Shelley uses hymn-like address for an elusive power associated with beauty, sympathy, and moral hope. “Awful” here suggests awe-inspiring. The poem moves from questions about passing experience to a remembered encounter and a vow.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem: Hymn to Intellectual Beauty; opens “The awful shadow of some unseen Power”; closes “To fear himself, and love all human kind.”.

questions.prompt: How do the opening comparisons make Beauty both real in its effects and difficult to possess?
facilitatorNotes: Wind, moonlight, fading music, and memory are sensed indirectly or briefly. Their effects matter even though the source remains unseen and inconstant; mystery is part of the attraction.
evidence: Dear, and yet dearer for its mystery.

questions.prompt: Why does the remembered search for ghosts matter to the later encounter?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker’s attempted summons receives no answer, whereas Beauty arrives unexpectedly during reflection and seasonal renewal. The contrast revises his way of seeking meaning without supplying a simple proof of a named supernatural being.
evidence: I was not heard--I saw them not--

questions.prompt: How does the final stanza change the speaker’s request from earlier ecstasy?
facilitatorNotes: The mature comparison to afternoon and autumn asks for calm, self-scrutiny, and love of humanity. The desired result is an enduring ethical disposition rather than a permanent repetition of the first intense thrill.
evidence: To fear himself, and love all human kind.

days.title: Ode to the West Wind
days.challenge: Read the first three movements for changes of scale, then the last two for changes in the speaker’s request. Follow leaf, cloud, and wave as they return in a new grammatical role.
days.focus: Explain how a natural process becomes a model for poetic and public renewal.
days.context: Shelley addresses the autumn wind across land, sky, and sea, then asks it to transform his own voice. A Maenad is a frenzied follower of Dionysus; Baiae evokes an ancient coastal place. The five numbered movements retain their internal verse breaks here without printed numbering.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem: Ode to the West Wind; opens “O wild West Wind, thou breath of Autumn's being,”; closes “If Winter comes, can Spring be far behind?”.

questions.prompt: How can the wind be both destroyer and preserver in the opening movement?
facilitatorNotes: It drives away dead leaves but also carries seeds into winter’s shelter before spring. The paired functions establish renewal through apparent destruction rather than a simple opposition between good and bad weather.
evidence: Destroyer and preserver; hear, oh, hear!

questions.prompt: What changes when the speaker wishes to be a leaf, cloud, or wave?
facilitatorNotes: Earlier objects demonstrate the wind’s reach; they become imagined forms in which the burdened speaker might share its energy. The turn makes a grand natural address into a personal plea without abandoning the earlier imagery.
evidence: Oh, lift me as a wave, a leaf, a cloud!

questions.prompt: How does the final request transform private distress into an ambition for the poem’s readers?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker asks for thoughts and words to scatter like seeds or sparks among humanity. The final seasonal question offers hope of change, but its interrogative form leaves readers to weigh that hope rather than receive a guaranteed political outcome.
evidence: Ashes and sparks, my words among mankind!

days.title: The Cloud
days.challenge: Read aloud for internal rhymes and paired movements. On rereading, map changes of substance and scale, and distinguish the imaginative account from a modern scientific explanation.
days.focus: Analyze how a first-person natural voice makes change a form of continuity.
days.context: A cloud speaks of weather, light, and continual transformation. Personified natural forces mingle with a poetic account of water moving among earth, sea, and sky. A cenotaph is a memorial for someone whose body is elsewhere.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem: The Cloud; opens “I bring fresh showers for the thirsting flowers,”; closes “I arise and unbuild it again.”.

questions.prompt: How does the opening prevent the cloud from being merely gentle or merely threatening?
facilitatorNotes: It nourishes flowers, shades leaves, brings hail, dissolves rain, and laughs in thunder. These changing functions belong to one speaker, joining benefit and force in a mobile identity.
evidence: I wield the flail of the lashing hail,

questions.prompt: What do the eagle and dove comparisons add to the movement from sunrise to sunset?
facilitatorNotes: The sunrise image is vivid, poised, and fiery; the evening image folds into stillness and rest. Bird forms translate shifting light and cloud into recognizable attitudes while maintaining the cloud’s changing scale.
evidence: As still as a brooding dove.

questions.prompt: Why can the cloud laugh at its own cenotaph?
facilitatorNotes: A clear sky seems to commemorate its disappearance, but evaporation and return make disappearance temporary. The final reappearance turns an image of death into one of recurring transformation.
evidence: I change, but I cannot die.

days.title: To a Skylark
days.challenge: Read the sequence of “Like” images aloud and identify what each makes perceptible. Then reread the questions and assertions about pain to see how uncertainty and idealization coexist.
days.focus: Examine how repeated comparisons reveal both an ideal and the limits of knowing it.
days.context: Shelley hears a bird beyond clear sight and repeatedly compares its song with human art and feeling. “Hymeneal” refers to a wedding song. The speaker’s claims about the bird’s happiness are poetic projections, not scientific observations.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem: To a Skylark; opens “Hail to thee, blithe Spirit!”; closes “The world should listen then--as I am listening now.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker call the skylark a spirit while repeatedly admitting it is unseen or unknown?
facilitatorNotes: Its disembodied sound invites an ideal beyond ordinary sight. The uncertainty motivates comparisons; the poem cannot describe the bird directly enough to settle what it is.
evidence: What thou art we know not;

questions.prompt: What common pattern connects the hidden poet, maiden, glow-worm, and rose?
facilitatorNotes: Each source is partly concealed while its effect spreads outward through song, light, or scent. The comparisons make invisible influence imaginable and connect the bird’s song to artistic communication.
evidence: Like a Poet hidden

questions.prompt: How does the final wish for “half the gladness” change the speaker’s position?
facilitatorNotes: The poet becomes a learner who hopes to transmit something of the song’s power to a listening world. Asking for half acknowledges distance from the ideal even while expressing a large artistic ambition.
evidence: Teach me half the gladness

days.title: To Night
days.challenge: Read aloud for the recurring calls to come quickly. Reread the dialogue with Death and Sleep and explain how it qualifies the earlier references to weariness and an opiate wand.
days.focus: Distinguish related symbolic figures instead of treating every dark image as the same desire.
days.context: Shelley addresses Night as a person whose family includes Death and Sleep. The speaker longs for night’s imaginative presence while explicitly refusing the substitutes offered by those related figures.
days.contentNote: Death and sleep are personified; the speaker explicitly rejects both as substitutes for Night.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem: To Night; opens “Swiftly walk o'er the western wave,”; closes “Come soon, soon!”.

questions.prompt: How is Night made both frightening and desired in the opening?
facilitatorNotes: Night weaves dreams of joy and fear, so its appeal includes imaginative uncertainty. The paired qualities resist reducing the poem to a simple wish for comfort.
evidence: terrible and dear

questions.prompt: What does the comparison of lingering Day to an unloved guest reveal about the speaker’s relation to time?
facilitatorNotes: Day’s departure feels delayed and unwelcome, reversing a common preference for daylight. The social comparison makes impatience intimate and emotional rather than merely a statement about sunset.
evidence: Lingering like an unloved guest

questions.prompt: Why is the refusal of Death and Sleep essential to interpreting the final plea?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker wants Night itself, not unconsciousness or death, even though the figures are related. The final urgency must be read through this explicit distinction rather than treated as a death wish.
evidence: No, not thee!

days.title: The Cultivation of Stable Habits
days.challenge: Test how far the detailed example supports the address’s universal language.
days.focus: Persistence, preparation, and explanations of success.
days.context: Washington uses two Tuskegee graduates’ millinery work to urge students to complete their training. The complete address includes his direct observations of a store display.
days.contentNote: Contains racial stereotypes about businesses and harsh judgments of poverty and interrupted education.

excerpt.locator: Character Building, complete address “The Cultivation of Stable Habits”; opens “THE CULTIVATION OF STABLE HABITS I am going to speak with you”; closes “this finds in the end that he has achieved a tremendous success.”.

questions.prompt: What observable evidence does the store-window episode offer about the graduates’ work?
facilitatorNotes: Washington reports a finished display and favorable reactions; the later account adds completion of training. These support competence more directly than every claim about its sole cause.
evidence: Hundreds of people stopped to comment favourably

questions.prompt: Why is the postgraduate course important to the example?
facilitatorNotes: One graduate returns after her academic diploma to finish industrial training. Completion means gaining the relevant skill, not merely possessing a credential.
evidence: she came back last year and took a postgraduate course in millinery

questions.prompt: Where does the speech move from supporting persistence to making an explanation too broad for its evidence?
facilitatorNotes: The two graduates illustrate one path; claims that failure or poverty simply follows instability exclude other circumstances. Ask students to identify the language that makes those claims absolute.
evidence: it all comes from their determination to succeed

days.title: Getting On in the World
days.challenge: Follow the balance between mastering work and remaining open to correction.
days.focus: Ambition, inquiry, and practical expertise.
days.context: In this complete address, Washington advises Tuskegee students about developing competence in their present work while seeking advancement.

excerpt.locator: Character Building, complete address “Getting on in the World”; opens “GETTING ON IN THE WORLD It is natural and praiseworthy for a”; closes “out of ten, men who have made worthless failures in other places.”.

questions.prompt: Why pair milking cows with going to Congress?
facilitatorNotes: The contrast acknowledges the audience’s ambitions while giving ordinary work public significance. The humor makes a concrete example serve an abstract argument.
evidence: many of you boys had rather I would tell you how to go to Congress

questions.prompt: How can someone seek to know everything about a job while believing there is more to learn?
facilitatorNotes: The first is an aspiration toward expertise; the second prevents complacency. Books, conversation, and experiments provide distinct routes to improvement.
evidence: ever feel that there is more for you to learn

questions.prompt: Does listening require accepting every suggestion?
facilitatorNotes: Washington explicitly distinguishes openness from agreement: compare plans and select the best-supported one. This qualification keeps humility compatible with judgment.
evidence: weigh their plans alongside of your own

days.title: Each One His Part
days.challenge: Separate conscientious action from the much larger judgments people draw from it.
days.focus: Interdependence and conduct outside public view.
days.context: This complete Tuskegee address considers how overlooked tasks support the work of an institution.
days.contentNote: Includes imprisonment and a sheriff’s claim that careful work indicates innocence; that inference is examined rather than endorsed.

excerpt.locator: Character Building, complete address “Each One His Part”; opens “EACH ONE HIS PART I desire to call your attention for a”; closes “should be done? These are the problems we must work out here.”.

questions.prompt: How do the examples of the teacher and the driver make interdependence visible?
facilitatorNotes: Uncelebrated maintenance supports public occasions and travel. The teacher gives up visible participation; the driver notices a defect his passenger misses.
evidence: one individual is dependent for success upon another

questions.prompt: Why does Washington say he fears failure more in private duties than on the platform?
facilitatorNotes: Public attention can motivate careful preparation; unseen tasks test whether responsibility continues without applause or surveillance.
evidence: the things which no one will see you do

questions.prompt: What can the prisoner’s careful work show, and why does it not establish innocence of an unspecified crime?
facilitatorNotes: It is evidence of diligence in that setting, not proof about another event. The sheriff’s inference reveals the speech’s tendency to treat one kind of conduct as a complete character test.
evidence: I do not believe that a man can be so honest and faithful about his work and be guilty of a crime.

days.title: Object Lessons
days.challenge: Evaluate what a visible example can answer and what it cannot settle.
days.focus: Economic independence and evidence against prejudice.
days.context: Washington presents individual achievements and donor letters as evidence of Tuskegee’s educational value. This address is complete.
days.contentNote: Contains racial stereotypes, dialect representation, a minimizing description of slavery’s effects, and claims about the absence of opposition to Black education.

excerpt.locator: Character Building, complete address “Object Lessons”; opens “OBJECT LESSONS Not long ago an old coloured man living in this”; closes “to demonstrate to them this value more and more clearly every year.”.

questions.prompt: What does the man’s phrase “second freedom” mean in the explanation that follows?
facilitatorNotes: Freedom from debt and ownership of land, alongside children’s education, extend freedom into material security. Do not confuse this with the narrator’s later problematic description of slavery.
evidence: had freed himself from debt

questions.prompt: How does the repeated “show them” change the way Washington proposes answering prejudice?
facilitatorNotes: He substitutes concrete achievements for abstract rebuttal and uses parallel examples across occupations. A counterexample can defeat an absolute stereotype without making dignity dependent on wealth.
evidence: I want you to be able to show them

questions.prompt: Do the donor letters establish the claim that a school in any Southern county would face no white opposition?
facilitatorNotes: They establish particular acts of support and reasons given by donors. They do not justify a universal claim about every community; distinguish evidence of possibility from evidence of absence.
evidence: which will not meet with opposition from the white residents of the community

days.title: Growth
days.challenge: Track repeated oppositions while considering what they include and leave out.
days.focus: Self-assessment and the rhetoric of continual improvement.
days.context: Washington asks Tuskegee students to carry habits of improvement from school into work, teaching, and home life. This is the complete address.
days.contentNote: Uses an imagined parental gaze and absolute judgments about progress and decline; readers need not disclose family circumstances or personal performance.

excerpt.locator: Character Building, complete address “Growth”; opens “GROWTH I want to impress upon you this evening the importance of”; closes “one thing or the other, continually going backward or continually going forward.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the opening ask students to imagine their parents’ thoughts and prayers?
facilitatorNotes: The imagined audience gives effort an emotional and relational purpose. Analyze the appeal without assuming every reader has the same family experience.
evidence: for the sake of those who are near and dear to you

questions.prompt: How does the address move from being observed by others to observing oneself?
facilitatorNotes: Washington explicitly asks students themselves to notice growth in courtesy. The standard is meant to become internal rather than depend only on teachers’ approval.
evidence: I want you to find yourselves so.

questions.prompt: What persuasive work does the repeated choice between forward and backward do, and what possibilities does it omit?
facilitatorNotes: The binary creates urgency and extends school habits through life. Students can question whether rest, consolidation, or temporary setbacks fit so simple a model.
evidence: it will be impossible for you to stand still

days.title: Robinson Crusoe: remembered basket-making
days.challenge: Read this short passage twice: first for the sequence of making, then to annotate where knowledge, material and judgment each contribute.
days.focus: A remembered craft shows that self-reliance depends on earlier observation, suitable materials and maintenance.
days.context: A complete basket-making episode extracted from the longer island narrative. Crusoe has previously found that some stakes cut for his fence continue growing; the next paragraph in the novel turns to different missing utensils.

excerpt.locator: Robinson Crusoe, main narrative, consecutive paragraphs; opens “In this time I found much employment, (and very suitable also to”; closes “of sacks, when I should come to have any quantity of it.”.

questions.prompt: Why is the childhood memory more useful than merely having seen finished baskets?
facilitatorNotes: He watched methods and sometimes helped, so he can recall a process rather than only an object’s appearance. Discuss what the passage suggests about attentive participation.
evidence: sometimes lent an hand

questions.prompt: What must he still discover before that memory can become useful work?
facilitatorNotes: He needs flexible local twigs, then tests the tree used for his growing fence. Skill and suitable material are separate requirements.
evidence: I wanted nothing but the materials

questions.prompt: Why does the passage end with replacement rather than with a single triumphant basket?
facilitatorNotes: Useful objects decay and demand continued making. His standard is serviceability rather than beauty, and recurring maintenance becomes part of self-sufficiency.
evidence: as my wicker-ware decayed I made more

days.title: Robinson Crusoe: protecting and reserving the harvest
days.challenge: Distinguish biological threats to grain from moral labels applied to animals; reread the ending to identify unsolved steps between crop and bread.
days.focus: A harvest episode makes labour, future planning and the narrator’s language of ownership visible.
days.context: An independent third-year episode, beginning with Crusoe’s work schedule and ending with his decision to reserve the harvested grain.
days.contentNote: Hunting and hanging dead birds as deterrents, compared with the public punishment of human thieves; devotional routine.

excerpt.locator: Robinson Crusoe, main narrative, consecutive paragraphs; opens “Thus, and in this disposition of mind, I began my third year;”; closes “to accomplish this great work of providing myself with corn and bread.”.

questions.prompt: How does the shelf-board example answer a possible impatient reader?
facilitatorNotes: Comparing forty-two days with two sawyers’ half-day explains why apparently small results require long narration and labour. Missing collaboration and tools matter alongside effort.
evidence: two sawyers, with their tools and saw-pit

questions.prompt: What is gained and lost when birds and animals are called enemies and thieves?
facilitatorNotes: The language conveys his fear for future food but assigns human wrongdoing to animals feeding. The punishment analogy imports English authority into his solitary cultivation.
evidence: served them as we serve notorious thieves in England

questions.prompt: Why does a successful harvest end with a decision not to eat it?
facilitatorNotes: More seed secures future supply, and he still lacks processing and baking methods. Achievement opens a new chain of dependencies rather than ending the problem.
evidence: to preserve it all for seed against the next season

days.title: Robinson Crusoe: pots made by trial and accident
days.challenge: Track several kinds of failure before success; reread the move from a broken shard to an entire firing process.
days.focus: A craft narrative distinguishes appearance, function, accidental evidence and deliberate experiment.
days.context: An independent pottery-making episode during Crusoe’s preparations to process grain. This scene ends with the first successful use of a fire-resistant pot.
days.contentNote: Animal food and historical gendered comparison. The firing process and mention of lead are historical narrative details, not a safe craft procedure.

excerpt.locator: Robinson Crusoe, main narrative, consecutive paragraphs; opens “Within-door, that is, when it rained, and I could not go out,”; closes “requisite to make it so good as I would have had it.”.

questions.prompt: Why introduce the parrot before describing pottery?
facilitatorNotes: A voice other than his own accompanies labour and recalls the social isolation underlying practical achievements. He calls this companionship an assistant rather than the main work.
evidence: the first word I ever heard spoken in the island by any mouth but my own

questions.prompt: How does the accidental shard become evidence for a new experiment?
facilitatorNotes: He sees that fire has hardened a broken piece and reasons that whole vessels might survive the same treatment. An accident becomes useful through observation and a testable extension.
evidence: they might be made to burn whole, if they would burn broken.

questions.prompt: Why is an ugly pot an occasion for extraordinary joy?
facilitatorNotes: The important threshold is holding liquid and surviving fire, opening new cooking possibilities. Shape and appearance are secondary to a function that earlier sun-dried pots could not perform.
evidence: an earthen pot that would bear the fire

days.title: Robinson Crusoe: the many steps to bread
days.challenge: Reread to map each missing tool to its substitute; distinguish genuinely new design from reuse and remembered practice.
days.focus: An ordinary loaf depends on linked technologies, inherited knowledge and decisions about sufficiency.
days.context: A contiguous continuation of the pottery scene, ending after Crusoe can bake and estimate a sufficient annual grain supply. It also makes sense independently with the knowledge that he has harvested grain and learned to fire pots.
days.contentNote: Historical labels for Indigenous people and descriptions of hot coals; discussion concerns narrative and attribution of knowledge, not cooking instructions.

excerpt.locator: Robinson Crusoe, main narrative, consecutive paragraphs; opens “My next concern was to get me a stone mortar to stamp”; closes “hopes that such a quantity would fully provide me with bread, &c.”.

questions.prompt: How does Crusoe’s replacement for a stone mortar complicate the image of invention from nothing?
facilitatorNotes: He uses hardwood and a burning technique he attributes to Indigenous canoe makers. His solution depends on knowledge encountered elsewhere, not only solitary ingenuity.
evidence: as the Indians in Brasil make their canoes

questions.prompt: What do the sieves reveal about the continuing importance of the wreck?
facilitatorNotes: Saved clothing supplies material he cannot spin or weave. The island household still depends on prior social manufacture even when he repurposes its products.
evidence: some neckcloths of calico or muslin

questions.prompt: Why does abundance lead him to limit sowing rather than maximize it?
facilitatorNotes: Once he estimates yearly consumption, more production is unnecessary labour and storage. The practical standard becomes sufficiency rather than endless accumulation.
evidence: to sow but once a year

days.title: Robinson Crusoe: the canoe that cannot be launched
days.challenge: Compare what the narrator says he never considered with what he admits dismissing; trace how numbers change their role in the account.
days.focus: A failed escape project exposes selective attention, colonial assumptions and the difference between effort and feasibility.
days.context: An independent canoe-building episode. Crusoe has failed to recover a usable existing boat and now attempts to build one from a large tree; the excerpt ends with his explicit reflection on failure.
days.contentNote: Contains historical racial labels and assertions of superiority over African and Indigenous makers. Questions directly examine the assumptions that the failed project exposes.

excerpt.locator: Robinson Crusoe, main narrative, consecutive paragraphs; opens “This at length set me upon thinking whether it was not possible”; closes “we judge lightly of our own strength to go through with it.”.

questions.prompt: How does the older narrator distinguish lack of foresight from refusing to think?
facilitatorNotes: He first describes not considering the launch, then admits the difficulty repeatedly occurred to him and was dismissed. The contradiction supports a reading of motivated avoidance rather than simple ignorance.
evidence: the difficulty of launching my boat came often into my head

questions.prompt: How does the comparison with Indigenous canoe builders undermine Crusoe’s confidence?
facilitatorNotes: He boasts of superior tools while overlooking the people needed to move the boat. The narrator’s later acknowledgment exposes the narrowness of his earlier assumption of superiority.
evidence: want of hands to move it into the water

questions.prompt: Why do the measurements become decisive only at the proposed canal?
facilitatorNotes: Earlier dimensions celebrate size and effort; calculating depth and years of work finally tests feasibility. The ending criticizes pursuing a desired result before evaluating the whole process.
evidence: ten or twelve years before I should have gone through with it
